All these curses will come upon you and pursue you and overtake you until you are destroyed, because you did not obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping his commandments and his statutes as he commanded you.
They will be on you as a sign and a wonder, and on your offspring, for ever.
Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart when you had everything in abundance,
you will serve your enemies, whom the LORD will send against you, in hunger and thirst, naked and lacking everything. He will put a yoke of iron on your neck until he has destroyed you.
The LORD will raise up against you a nation from far away, from the end of the earth, swooping like an eagle—a nation whose language you will not understand,
a nation fierce of face, which will show no regard for the old and no favour to the young.

It will eat the fruit of your livestock and the fruit of your ground until you are destroyed, leaving you no grain, no new wine, no fresh oil, no offspring of your cattle, no young of your flock—until it has made you perish.

It will besiege you in all your towns until your high, fortified walls come down—the ones you are trusting in—throughout your whole land. It will besiege you in all your towns, throughout the land the LORD your God has given you.
And you will eat the fruit of your womb—the flesh of your sons and your daughters whom the LORD your God gave you—in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy presses you.
The man among you who is gentle and very refined—his eye will turn grudging toward his brother, toward the wife of his bosom, and toward whatever children he has left,

so that he will not give any of them any of the flesh of his children he is eating, because nothing at all is left to him, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy presses you in all your towns.

The gentle and refined woman among you, who would not venture to set the sole of her foot on the ground because she was so refined and gentle—her eye will turn grudging toward the husband of her bosom, toward her son and toward her daughter,

and toward the afterbirth that comes out from between her feet, and toward the children she bears; for she will eat them in secret, lacking everything, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy presses you in your towns.
If you are not careful to do all the words of this law written in this book, to fear this glorious and awesome name, the LORD your God,
then the LORD will make your plagues extraordinary, and the plagues of your offspring—great and lasting plagues, harmful and lasting sicknesses.
He will bring back on you all the diseases of Egypt that you dreaded, and they will cling to you.
And every sickness and every plague not written in the book of this law—the LORD will bring them up on you until you are destroyed.
You will be left few in number, where you had been as numerous as the stars of the heavens, because you did not obey the voice of the LORD your God.

And just as the LORD rejoiced over you to do you good and to multiply you, so the LORD will rejoice over you to make you perish and to destroy you. You will be torn away from the land you are entering to take possession of it.
The LORD will scatter you among all the peoples, from one end of the earth to the other, and there you will serve other gods that neither you nor your fathers have known—wood and stone.
Among those nations you will find no rest, and there will be no resting place for the sole of your foot. There the LORD will give you a trembling heart, failing eyes and a despairing spirit.
Your life will hang in doubt before you. You will be in dread night and day, with no confidence that you will live.
In the morning you will say, 'If only it were evening!' and in the evening, 'If only it were morning!'—because of the dread in your heart, and the sight of your eyes.

And the LORD will bring you back to Egypt in ships, by the road I told you you would never see again. There you will offer yourselves for sale to your enemies as male and female slaves—and there will be no buyer.

deuteronomy_29.t: These are the words of the covenant the LORD commanded Moses to make with the people of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant he made with them at Horeb.
Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: 'You have seen everything the LORD did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh, to all his officials and to all his land—
the great trials your eyes saw, those great signs and wonders.
But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears to hear.
I led you forty years in the wilderness. Your clothes did not wear out on you, and your sandals did not wear out on your feet.
You ate no bread and drank no wine or strong drink, so that you might know that I am the LORD your God.
You came to this place, and Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan came out to meet us in battle, and we struck them down.
We took their land and gave it as an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
So keep the words of this covenant and do them, so that you may prosper in everything you do.
Today you are all standing before the LORD your God: your heads, your tribes, your elders and your officers, every man of Israel,
your little ones, your wives, and the sojourner in your camp, from the one who cuts your wood to the one who draws your water—
so that you may enter into the covenant of the LORD your God and into his oath, which the LORD your God is making with you today,
so as to establish you today as his people, and that he may be your God, just as he spoke to you and just as he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob.
And it is not with you alone that I am making this covenant and this oath,
but with whoever is here with us, standing today before the LORD our God, and with whoever is not here with us today.
You know how we lived in the land of Egypt and how we passed through the middle of the nations you passed through,
and you saw their detestable things and their idols—wood and stone, silver and gold—that they had with them.

Beware that there is not among you a man or a woman, a clan or a tribe, whose heart is turning away today from the LORD our God to go and serve the gods of those nations—no root among you bearing poison and wormwood,

and when he hears the words of this oath, he blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'—sweeping away the watered land along with the thirsty.

The LORD will not be willing to forgive him. The anger of the LORD and his jealousy will smoke against that man, every oath written in this book will settle on him, and the LORD will wipe out his name from under the heavens.
The LORD will single him out for harm from all the tribes of Israel, according to all the oaths of the covenant written in this book of the law.

And the generation to come—your children who rise up after you—and the foreigner who comes from a distant land will say, when they see the plagues of that land and the diseases with which the LORD has made it sick,

'Its whole land is sulphur and salt, a burnt waste. Nothing is sown there, nothing sprouts, no vegetation comes up in it—like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and his rage'—
and all the nations will say, 'Why has the LORD done this to this land? What is this great heat of anger?'
And they will say: 'Because they forsook the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them out of the land of Egypt,
and they went and served other gods and bowed down to them—gods they had not known, that he had not allotted to them.
So the anger of the LORD burned against that land, bringing on it every curse written in this book.
And the LORD uprooted them from their ground in anger, rage and great wrath, and cast them into another land, as it is this day.'
The hidden things belong to the LORD our God; the revealed things belong to us and to our children for ever, so that we may do all the words of this law.

deuteronomy_30.t: And when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse I have set before you, and you call them to mind among all the nations where the LORD your God has driven you,
and you return to the LORD your God and obey his voice, according to everything I am commanding you today, you and your children, with all your heart and with all your soul,
then the LORD your God will restore your fortunes and have compassion on you. He will gather you again from all the peoples where the LORD your God scattered you.
Even if your banished are at the end of the heavens, from there the LORD your God will gather you, and from there he will take you.
The LORD your God will bring you into the land your fathers possessed, and you will possess it. He will do you good and make you more numerous than your fathers.
And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, to love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live.
And the LORD your God will put all these oaths on your enemies and on those who hate you, who persecuted you.
And you will return and obey the voice of the LORD, and do all his commandments that I am commanding you today.

And the LORD your God will make you abound in good things in every work of your hand—the fruit of your womb, the fruit of your livestock and the fruit of your ground. The LORD will again rejoice over you for good, just as he rejoiced over your fathers,

if you obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping his commandments and his statutes written in this book of the law, and if you return to the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
For this commandment I am commanding you today is not too hard for you, and it is not far off.
It is not in the heavens, so that you should say, 'Who will go up to the heavens for us and get it and let us hear it, so that we can do it?'
Nor is it beyond the sea, so that you should say, 'Who will cross the sea for us and get it and let us hear it, so that we can do it?'
No, the word is very near you—in your mouth and in your heart—for you to do it.
See, today I have set before you life and good, death and evil—

which I am commanding you today: to love the LORD your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes and his ordinances. Then you will live and increase, and the LORD your God will bless you in the land you are entering to take possession of it.
But if your heart turns away and you will not listen, and you are drawn aside to bow down to other gods and serve them,
I declare to you today that you will certainly perish. You will not live long on the land you are crossing the Jordan to enter and possess.
I call the heavens and the earth as witnesses against you today: I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. So choose life, so that you may live, you and your offspring,

by loving the LORD your God, obeying his voice and clinging to him. He is your life and the length of your days, so that you may dwell on the land the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob, to give them.

deuteronomy_31.t: Then Moses went and spoke these words to all Israel.
He said to them, "I am a hundred and twenty years old today. I can no longer go out and come in, and the LORD has said to me, 'You shall not cross this Jordan.'

The LORD your God himself is crossing over ahead of you. He will destroy these nations before you, and you will dispossess them. Joshua is the one crossing over ahead of you, just as the LORD has spoken.
And the LORD will do to them just as he did to Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites, and to their land, when he destroyed them.
And the LORD will deliver them up before you, and you are to do to them according to all the commandment I have commanded you.
Be strong and bold. Do not fear them and do not be terrified, for the LORD your God himself is going with you; he will not abandon you and will not forsake you.

Then Moses summoned Joshua and said to him in the sight of all Israel, "Be strong and bold, for you will go with this people into the land the LORD swore to their ancestors to give them, and you will give it to them as an inheritance.
And the LORD himself is going before you. He will be with you; he will not abandon you and will not forsake you. Do not fear and do not be dismayed.
Moses wrote down this law and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and to all the elders of Israel.
And Moses commanded them, "At the end of seven years, at the appointed time of the year of remission, at the Festival of Booths,
when all Israel comes to appear before the LORD your God at the place he will choose, you are to read this law aloud before all Israel, in their hearing.
Assemble the people — the men, the women, the little ones, and the sojourner in your gates — so that they may hear and learn, and fear the LORD your God and take care to do all the words of this law,
and their children who have not known it will hear and learn to fear the LORD your God all the days you live on the ground you are crossing the Jordan to enter and take possession of.

And the LORD said to Moses, "Your days have drawn near for you to die. Summon Joshua and present yourselves at the tent of meeting, so that I may commission him." So Moses went, with Joshua, and they presented themselves at the tent of meeting.
And the LORD appeared at the tent in a pillar of cloud, and the pillar of cloud stood over the entrance of the tent.

And the LORD said to Moses, "You are about to lie down with your ancestors, and this people will rise and act the prostitute after the foreign gods of the land it is entering. It will forsake me and break my covenant that I made with it.

And my anger will burn against it on that day. I will forsake them and hide my face from them, and it will be devoured; many calamities and troubles will come upon it. And on that day it will say, 'Is it not because my God is not among us that these calamities have come upon me?'
And I will certainly hide my face on that day, because of all the evil it has done, for it has turned to other gods.
"Now write down this song for yourselves and teach it to the sons of Israel. Put it in their mouth, so that this song may be a witness for me against the sons of Israel.

For I will bring it to the ground I swore to its ancestors, flowing with milk and honey, and it will eat and be satisfied and grow fat. Then it will turn to other gods and serve them, and they will spurn me, and it will break my covenant.

And when many calamities and troubles come upon it, this song will testify before it as a witness, for it will not be forgotten from the mouth of its offspring. For I know the intention it is forming today, before I bring it into the land I swore.
So Moses wrote down this song that day and taught it to the sons of Israel.
And he commissioned Joshua son of Nun and said, "Be strong and bold, for you will bring the sons of Israel into the land I swore to them, and I myself will be with you."
And when Moses had finished writing down the words of this law in a book, right to the end,
Moses commanded the Levites who carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD,
"Take this book of the law and put it beside the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, and it will be there as a witness against you.
For I know your rebellion and your stiff neck. Even now, while I am still alive with you today, you have been rebellious against the LORD — how much more after my death!
Assemble to me all the elders of your tribes and your officials, so that I may speak these words in their hearing and call the heavens and the earth as witnesses against them.

For I know that after my death you will certainly act corruptly and turn aside from the way I have commanded you. The evil will come upon you in the latter days, because you will do what is evil in the eyes of the LORD, provoking him to anger by the work of your hands.
And Moses spoke the words of this song in the hearing of all the assembly of Israel, right to the end.

deuteronomy_32.t: Give ear, heavens, and let me speak; let the earth hear the sayings of my mouth.
May my teaching fall like the rain, my speech settle like the dew, like showers on the grass, like abundant showers on the green things.
For I proclaim the name of the LORD. Ascribe greatness to our God!
The Rock—his work is perfect, and all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness, without injustice; righteous and upright is he.
They have acted corruptly toward him. They are not his children—the fault is theirs— a perverse and crooked generation.
Is this how you repay the LORD, you foolish people, and not wise? Is he not your father, who created you, who made you and established you?
Remember the days of old, consider the years of generation after generation. Ask your father and he will tell you, your elders, and they will say to you.
When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, when he separated humankind, he fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of God.
For the LORD's share is his people; Jacob is the measured portion of his inheritance.
He found him in a wilderness land, in a howling waste of desolation. He surrounded him, he cared for him, he guarded him like the pupil of his eye.
Like an eagle that stirs up its nest and hovers over its young, he spread his wings, he took him, he carried him on his pinion.
The LORD alone guided him; there was no foreign god with him.
He made him ride on the heights of the land, and he ate the produce of the field. He made him suck honey out of a rock, oil out of flinty rock.
Curds of the herd and milk of the flock, with the fat of lambs, rams of Bashan and goats, with the choicest of the wheat— and you drank the blood of the grape as wine.
Jeshurun grew fat and kicked— you grew fat, you grew thick, you were gorged— and he abandoned the God who made him, and treated the Rock of his salvation with contempt.
They made him jealous with strange gods; with abominations they provoked him to anger.
They sacrificed to demons, not to God— gods they had not known, new ones, lately come, whom your fathers had not dreaded.
You neglected the Rock who fathered you; you forgot the God who gave you birth.
The LORD saw and spurned them, because of the provocation of his sons and his daughters.
And he said: I will hide my face from them and see what their end will be; for they are a generation of perversity, children with no faithfulness in them.
They made me jealous with what is no god, provoked me to anger with their vanities; so I will make them jealous with what is no people, with a foolish nation I will provoke them to anger.
For a fire has been kindled in my anger, burning down to the lowest Sheol; it consumes the earth and its produce and sets the foundations of the mountains ablaze.
I will heap calamities on them; I will spend my arrows on them.
Wasted with hunger, devoured by burning plague and bitter destruction; I will send against them the tooth of beasts, with the venom of things that crawl in the dust.
Outside, the sword will bereave; inside, terror— young man and virgin alike, the nursing child and the grey-haired man.
I said: I will cut them to pieces, I will make the memory of them cease from humankind—
—were it not that I feared the provocation of the enemy, that their adversaries would misread it, that they would say, Our own hand did it; it was not the LORD who did all this.
For they are a nation lost to counsel, with no understanding in them.
If only they were wise, they would comprehend this; they would understand what their end will be.
How could one man pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them and the LORD had handed them over?
For their rock is not like our Rock— and our enemies themselves are the judges of it.
Their vine comes from the vine of Sodom, from the terraces of Gomorrah; their grapes are poisonous grapes, their clusters are bitter.
Their wine is the venom of serpents, the cruel poison of cobras.
Is this not stored up with me, sealed in my storehouses?
Vengeance is mine, and recompense, for the time their foot slips. The day of their disaster is near, and what is prepared for them comes quickly.
For the LORD will judge his people and have compassion on his servants, when he sees that their strength is gone, and no one is left, bond or free.
And he will say: Where are their gods, the rock they took refuge in,
who ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their drink offering? Let them rise up and help you— let them be a shelter over you!
See now that I, I am he, and there is no god beside me. I put to death and I make alive, I have wounded and I heal, and no one delivers from my hand.
For I lift my hand to the heavens and say: As I live for ever—
When I sharpen my flashing sword and my hand takes hold of judgement, I will return vengeance to my foes and repay those who hate me.
I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword will devour flesh— with the blood of the slain and the captives, from the heads of the long-haired leaders of the enemy.
Rejoice, you nations, with his people, because he'll avenge the blood of his servants; he'll turn vengeance back on his foes and make atonement for his land and his people.
Moses came and spoke all the words of this song in the hearing of the people, he and Hoshea son of Nun.
When Moses had finished speaking all these words to all Israel,
he said to them: 'Set your heart on all the words I am testifying against you today, which you are to command your children to be careful to do—all the words of this law.
This is not an empty word for you—it is your life, and by this word you will live long on the land you are crossing the Jordan to take possession of it.'
And that very day the LORD spoke to Moses:
'Go up this mountain of the Abarim, Mount Nebo, in the land of Moab opposite Jericho, and see the land of Canaan that I am giving to the people of Israel as a holding.
And die on the mountain you are going up, and be gathered to your kin, as Aaron your brother died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his kin,
because you acted unfaithfully against me among the people of Israel at the waters of Meribath-kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, because you did not treat me as holy among the people of Israel.
You will see the land from a distance, but you will not go there, into the land I am giving to the people of Israel.'

deuteronomy_33.t: This is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the sons of Israel before his death.
He said: The LORD came from Sinai and dawned on them from Seir; he shone out from Mount Paran and came from among ten thousands of holy ones, from his right hand, fire of law for them.
Indeed he loves peoples; all his holy ones are in your hand; they followed at your feet; he receives of your words.
Moses commanded us a law, a possession for the assembly of Jacob.
And the LORD became king in Jeshurun when the heads of the people gathered, the tribes of Israel together.
Let Reuben live and not die, though his men be few.
And this for Judah; he said: Hear, LORD, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people. With his own hands he contended for himself; be a help against his foes.
Of Levi he said: Your Thummim and your Urim belong to your loyal one, whom you tested at Massah, with whom you contended at the waters of Meribah;
who said of his father and mother, I have not regarded him, who did not recognise his brothers or acknowledge his own children; for they kept your speech and kept watch over your covenant.
They will teach your judgements to Jacob and your law to Israel; they will set incense before you and the whole offering on your altar.
Bless, LORD, his substance, and accept the work of his hands. Shatter the loins of those who rise against him, and of those who hate him, so they never rise again.
Of Benjamin he said: The beloved of the LORD dwells in safety beside him; he shelters him all day long, and dwells between his shoulders.
Of Joseph he said: Blessed by the LORD is his land, with the choice gift of the heavens, with dew, and with the deep that lies beneath,
with the choice gift of what the sun brings forth, and the choice gift of what the months yield,
with the finest of the ancient mountains, and the choice gift of the everlasting hills,
with the choice gift of the earth and its fullness, and the favour of the one who dwelt in the bush. May it come on the head of Joseph, on the crown of the one set apart from his brothers.

His firstborn bull — majesty is his, and his horns are the horns of a wild ox; with them he will gore the peoples, all of them, to the ends of the earth. These are the ten thousands of Ephraim; these are the thousands of Manasseh.
Of Zebulun he said: Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar, in your tents.
They will summon peoples to the mountain; there they will offer sacrifices of righteousness. For they will draw on the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand.
Of Gad he said: Blessed is the one who enlarges Gad. He lies like a lion and tears the arm, and the crown of the head as well.
He chose the best for himself, for there a commander's portion was reserved; and he came at the head of the people. He carried out the LORD's righteousness and his judgements with Israel.
Of Dan he said: Dan is a lion's cub that leaps out from Bashan.
Of Naphtali he said: Naphtali is satisfied with favour and full of the blessing of the LORD; take possession of the west and the south.
Of Asher he said: Most blessed of sons is Asher; let him be the favourite of his brothers and dip his foot in oil.
Iron and bronze are your bolts, and your strength will last as long as your days.
There is none like God, Jeshurun, who rides the heavens to your help, and in his majesty the skies.
The God of old is a dwelling, and underneath are the everlasting arms; he drove out the enemy before you and said, Destroy.
So Israel dwelt in safety, alone, the fountain of Jacob, in a land of grain and new wine; and his heavens drop dew.

How blessed you are, Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD, the shield of your help, the sword of your eminence? Your enemies will cringe before you, and you will tread on their high places.

deuteronomy_34.t: Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, the top of Pisgah, opposite Jericho; and the LORD showed him all the land — Gilead as far as Dan,
all Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the western sea,
the Negev, and the district — the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees — as far as Zoar.

And the LORD said to him: This is the land I swore to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob, saying, To your offspring I will give it. I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross over there.
So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, at the mouth of the LORD.
And he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor; and no one knows his burial place to this day.
Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died. His eye was not dim, and his vigour had not fled.
The sons of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab for thirty days, and the days of weeping in mourning for Moses came to an end.
And Joshua son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, because Moses had laid his hands on him; and the sons of Israel listened to him and did just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
And no prophet has arisen since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face,
for all the signs and wonders the LORD sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and all his servants and all his land,
and for all the mighty hand and all the great terror that Moses displayed before the eyes of all Israel.

ecclesiastes_1.t: The words of Qoheleth, son of David, king in Jerusalem.
Vanity of vanities, said Qoheleth, vanity of vanities; everything is vanity.
What does anyone get out of all the toil they toil at under the sun?
One generation goes, another comes, but the earth stands for ever.
The sun rises, the sun sets, and pants its way back to where it rises again.
South it goes, then round to the north; round and round the wind goes, and back it comes on its circuits.
All the rivers run to the sea, and the sea is never full; to the place the rivers run to, there they go back to run again.
Everything is wearying — more than anyone can say. The eye is never satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
What has been is what will be; what has been done is what will be done; there's nothing new under the sun.
Is there anything you can point at and say, "Look, this is new"? It has already been, in the ages before our time.
Nobody remembers the former things, and the things still to come won't be remembered either by those who come after them.
I, Qoheleth, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
I gave my heart to seeking out and searching by wisdom everything that has been done under the heavens. It's a grievous business God has given the children of humankind to be occupied with.
I've seen all the works done under the sun, and there it is: everything is vanity, a chasing of wind.
What's bent can't be made straight; what's missing can't be counted.
I said to myself: "Look — I've made wisdom great, I've increased it beyond anyone who was over Jerusalem before me; my heart has seen a great deal of wisdom and knowledge."
I gave my heart to knowing wisdom, and to knowing madness and folly too. I knew that this as well is a striving after wind.
In much wisdom there's much vexation; increase knowledge and you increase pain.

ecclesiastes_2.t: I said to myself, "Come on, let me try you with pleasure; see what's good." And there it was: that too was vanity.
Of laughter I said, "It's madness"; of pleasure, "What does this accomplish?"

I searched in my heart for a way to gratify my flesh with wine — my heart still guiding me with wisdom — and a way to take hold of folly, until I could see what is good for people to do under the heavens for the few days of their lives.
I made my works great. I built myself houses; I planted myself vineyards.
I made myself gardens and parks and planted every kind of fruit tree in them.
I made myself pools of water to irrigate a forest of growing trees.
I acquired male and female slaves, and had slaves born in my house; I had livestock too, herds and flocks in abundance, more than anyone before me in Jerusalem.
I gathered silver and gold as well, the treasure of kings and provinces. I got myself singers, men and women, and what people delight in — many concubines.
I became great; I increased beyond anyone before me in Jerusalem; and my wisdom stayed with me.
Whatever my eyes asked for, I didn't withhold from them; I kept my heart from no pleasure. My heart was glad in all my toil, and that was my portion out of all my toil.
Then I turned to all the works my hands had done, and to the toil I had toiled at, and there it was: everything vanity, a chasing of wind, and no profit under the sun.
Then I turned to look at wisdom, and madness, and folly; for what can anyone coming after the king do beyond what's already been done?
I saw that wisdom has the advantage over folly, as light has the advantage over darkness.
The wise one has his eyes in his head; the dullard walks in the dark. And yet I knew: the same thing happens to them all.
I said to myself, "What happens to the dullard will happen to me as well. So why have I been so very wise?" And I said to myself that this too is vanity.
There's no lasting remembrance of the wise one any more than of the dullard; in the days to come it will all have been forgotten. And how the wise one dies — just like the dullard!
So I hated life, because the work done under the sun weighed on me; everything is vanity, a chasing of wind.
I hated all the toil I'd toiled at under the sun, because I have to leave it to whoever comes after me.
And who knows whether he'll be wise or a fool? Yet he'll have power over everything I toiled at, everything I worked at with wisdom under the sun. This too is vanity.
So I turned to let my heart despair over all the toil I'd toiled at under the sun.
Here is someone whose toil is done with wisdom, knowledge and skill, and he has to hand it over as a portion to someone who never toiled at it. This too is vanity — and a great evil.
What does anyone get out of all their toil, out of the striving of the heart they toil at under the sun?
All his days are pain; his work is vexation; even at night his heart doesn't rest. This too is vanity.
There's nothing better for a person than to eat and drink and find some good in their toil. This too I saw: it comes from the hand of God.
Who can eat, who can enjoy anything, apart from him?

To the person who pleases him he gives wisdom, knowledge and joy; to the sinner he gives the task of gathering and heaping up, only to hand it over to someone who pleases God. This too is vanity, a chasing of wind.

ecclesiastes_3.t: For everything there is an appointed time, a time for every matter under the heavens:
a time to give birth and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot what's planted;
a time to kill and a time to heal; a time to break down and a time to build;
a time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance;
a time to throw stones away and a time to gather stones; a time to embrace and a time to keep far from embracing;
a time to seek and a time to give up as lost; a time to keep and a time to throw away;
a time to tear and a time to sew; a time to be silent and a time to speak;
a time to love and a time to hate; a time of war and a time of peace.
What does the worker get out of what he toils at?
I've seen the task God has given the children of humankind to be occupied with.
He has made everything beautiful in its time; he has also put eternity into the human heart, and yet nobody can find out the work God has done from beginning to end.
I know there's nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live.
And that everyone should eat and drink and find some good in all their toil — that is a gift of God.
I know that everything God does lasts for ever; nothing can be added to it, nothing taken away; and God has done it so that people should fear before him.
What is has already been; what is to be has already been; and God seeks out what has been driven away.
And again I saw, under the sun: in the place of judgement — wickedness; in the place of righteousness — wickedness.
I said to myself: "God will judge the righteous and the wicked; there is a time for every matter, and for every deed — there."
I said to myself about the children of humankind that God is testing them, so they may see that in themselves they are animals.

What happens to human beings and what happens to animals — the same thing happens to them both. As one dies, so dies the other; they all have the same breath; human beings have no advantage over the animals; everything is vanity.
Everything goes to one place. Everything came from the dust, and everything returns to the dust.
Who knows whether the human spirit goes upward, and whether the animal's spirit goes down to the earth?
And I saw there's nothing better than for a person to rejoice in their own work, because that's their portion; for who will bring them to see what comes after them?

ecclesiastes_4.t: I turned again and saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. There they were: the tears of the oppressed, and no one to comfort them; and power on the side of their oppressors — and no one to comfort them.
And I called the dead who have already died better off than the living who are still alive;
and better than both is the one who has never been, who hasn't seen the evil work done under the sun.
I considered all toil and all skill in work, and saw it comes from envy of one's neighbour. This too is vanity, a chasing of wind.
The dullard folds his hands and eats his own flesh.
Better one handful with quiet than two fistfuls of toil and a chasing of wind.
And I turned again and saw vanity under the sun:

Here is someone alone, with no one else; no son, no brother; and no end to all his toil; and his eye is never satisfied with wealth. "So who am I toiling for, depriving myself of good?" This too is vanity — a grievous business.
Two are better than one, because they get a good reward for their toil.
If they fall, one will lift the other up; but woe to the one who falls with nobody to lift him.
If two lie down together they keep warm; but how can one alone be warm?
Someone may overpower a person on their own, but two will stand against him; and a threefold cord isn't quickly torn apart.
Better a poor young person with wisdom than an old king who's a dullard and no longer knows how to take a warning.
He came out of prison to reign, though in his own kingdom he'd been born poor.
I saw all the living who walk about under the sun going over to the second youth who rises in his place.
There's no end to all the people, all those who were before them; yet those who come after won't rejoice in him. This too is vanity, a striving after wind.

ecclesiastes_5.t: Watch your step when you go to the house of God. Draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of dullards; they don't even know they're doing evil.
Don't be hasty with your mouth; don't let your heart hurry to get a word out before God. God is in the heavens and you are on the earth. So let your words be few.
A dream comes with too much business, a dullard's voice with too many words.
When you vow a vow to God, don't delay in paying it; he takes no pleasure in dullards. Pay what you vow.
Better not to vow at all than to vow and not pay.
Don't let your mouth make your flesh sin; don't say to the messenger, "It was a mistake." Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?
In a mass of dreams and vanities there are words without number — but fear God.
If you see the poor oppressed and justice and righteousness robbed away in a province, don't be astonished at it: one official is watching another, and there are higher ones over them.
The profit of a land is in everything; even a king is served by a cultivated field.
Whoever loves silver never has enough silver; whoever loves abundance never has enough income. This too is vanity.
When goods increase, so do those who consume them; and what does the owner get out of it but the sight of his own eyes?
The labourer's sleep is sweet, whether he eats little or much; but the plenty of the rich won't let him sleep.
There's a grievous evil I've seen under the sun: wealth hoarded by its owner, to his own harm.
And that wealth was lost in a bad venture; he fathered a son, and there was nothing in his hand.
He came out of his mother's womb naked, and naked he goes back, just as he came; he carries nothing away from his toil that he can take in his hand.
This too is a grievous evil: exactly as he came, so he goes; and what profit does he get from toiling for the wind?
All his days he eats in the dark, with much vexation, sickness and anger.
Here's what I've seen to be good, and beautiful: to eat and drink and find good in all the toil one toils at under the sun, for the few days of life God has given — for that is one's portion.
Everyone to whom God has given wealth and riches, and the power to eat from it, to take their portion and rejoice in their toil — that is a gift of God.
He won't dwell much on the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart.

ecclesiastes_6.t: There's an evil I've seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on people:

Here is someone God gives wealth, riches and honour, so that he lacks nothing he could want, and yet God gives him no power to eat from it — a stranger eats it instead. This is vanity, a grievous affliction.

Suppose a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that his years are many, but he never has his fill of good, and he gets no burial either — I say the stillborn child is better off than he is.
It came in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered over.
It never even saw the sun or knew anything. It has more rest than the other does.
Even if he lived a thousand years twice over and saw no good — don't they all go to one place?
All a person's toil goes into their mouth, and still the appetite is never filled.
What advantage does the wise have over the dullard? And what does a poor person gain by knowing how to conduct himself among the living?
Better what the eyes can see than what the appetite goes wandering after. This too is vanity, a chasing of wind.
Whatever has come to be already has its name, and what a human being is, is known; and nobody can contend with one stronger than they are.
There are plenty of words that only increase vanity. What advantage does anyone get from them?
Who knows what is good for a person in life, through the numbered days of a life that is vanity, spent like a shadow? Who can tell anyone what will come after them under the sun?

ecclesiastes_7.t: Better a good name than good oil, and the day of death than the day of birth.
Better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting; that is the end of everyone, and the living take it to heart.
Better vexation than laughter; a sad face does the heart good.
The heart of the wise is in a house of mourning; the heart of dullards is in a house of gladness.
Better to hear a wise person's rebuke than to be someone listening to the song of dullards.
Like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the dullard. This too is vanity.
Oppression turns a wise person foolish; a bribe destroys the heart.
Better the end of a matter than its beginning; better patient in spirit than proud in spirit.
Don't be hasty in spirit to get angry; anger settles in the bosom of dullards.
Don't say, "Why were the old days better than these?" It isn't wisdom that makes you ask that.
Wisdom is good alongside an inheritance, an advantage to those who see the sun.
Wisdom is a shelter and money is a shelter, but the advantage of knowledge is this: wisdom keeps its owner alive.
Consider the work of God: who can straighten what he has bent?
On a good day, enjoy the good; on a day of adversity, consider: God has made the one alongside the other, so that nobody can find out anything about what comes after.
I've seen all this in my vain life: a righteous person perishing in his righteousness, a wicked person living long in his evil.
Don't be righteous overmuch; don't make yourself wise to excess. Why destroy yourself?
Don't be wicked overmuch; don't be a fool. Why die before your time?
It's good to take hold of the one and not let go of the other; whoever fears God comes through with both.
Wisdom gives the wise more strength than ten rulers in a city.
There's no righteous person on earth who does good and never sins.
And don't take to heart everything people say, or you'll hear your own servant cursing you.
Your own heart knows how many times you too have cursed others.
I tested all this by wisdom. I said, "Let me be wise" — but it was far from me.
Whatever has been is far off, and deep, deep down — who can find it out?
I turned, I and my heart, to know and to search out, to seek wisdom and a reckoning, and to know that wickedness is stupidity and folly is madness.
And I found more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net, whose hands are fetters. Whoever is good before God escapes her; a sinner is caught by her.
"Look, this is what I found," said Qoheleth, "putting one and one together to find a reckoning —
what I kept on looking for and never found: one man in a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I never found.
This alone I found: that God made humankind upright, but they have gone looking for many schemes."

ecclesiastes_8.t: Who is like the wise? Who knows the interpretation of a matter? A person's wisdom lights up their face; the hardness of it is changed.
Keep the king's command — and do it because of the oath of God.
Don't be in a hurry to leave his presence; don't take a stand on an evil matter — he does whatever he wants.
A king's word carries mastery; who is going to say to him, "What are you doing?"
Whoever keeps a command will meet no evil; a wise heart knows the right time and the right way.
There's a time and a way for every matter, yet human trouble lies heavy on us.
Nobody knows what will be; who can tell them how it will be?
No one has mastery over the wind, to hold the wind back; no one has mastery over the day of death; there's no discharge in the battle; and wickedness won't rescue the one who owns it.
I've seen all this, giving my heart to every deed done under the sun — a time when one person domineers over another, to their harm.
And so I saw the wicked buried, and people came; they used to go in and out of the holy place, and they were forgotten in the very city where they had done it. This too is vanity.
Because sentence on an evil deed isn't carried out quickly, the heart of humankind is fully set on doing evil.
Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and lives on and on, I also know that it will go well with those who fear God, who stand in fear before him.
But it won't go well with the wicked; he won't lengthen his days, which are like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.
There's a vanity done on the earth: righteous people who get what the deeds of the wicked deserve, and wicked people who get what the deeds of the righteous deserve. I said that this too is vanity.

So I commended gladness, because there's nothing better for anyone under the sun than to eat and drink and be glad; that is what will go with them through their toil for the days of life God has given them under the sun.
When I gave my heart to knowing wisdom and seeing the task that is done on the earth — for day and night one's eyes see no sleep —

then I saw all the work of God: that nobody can find out the work that is done under the sun. However hard a person toils at seeking, they don't find out; and even if the wise claim to know, they can't find out.

ecclesiastes_9.t: I gave all this to my heart, to make it all clear: the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Love or hatred — nobody knows; everything lies ahead of them.

Everything comes alike to everyone: the same thing happens to the righteous and to the wicked, to the good, and to the clean and the unclean, to the one who sacrifices and the one who doesn't; as with the good, so with the sinner; as with the one who swears an oath, so with the one who shrinks from it.

This is an evil in everything done under the sun: the same thing happens to everyone; and the heart of humankind is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that — to the dead.
Whoever is joined to the living still has hope; a living dog is better than the dead lion.
The living know that they will die; the dead know nothing at all. They have no further reward; their memory is forgotten.
Their love, their hatred, their envy — all perished already; they have no portion, ever again, in anything done under the sun.
Go on: eat your bread with gladness, drink your wine with a glad heart — God has already accepted what you do.
Let your clothes always be white; never let oil be lacking on your head.
Enjoy life with a wife you love, all the days of the vain life he has given you under the sun, all your days of vanity; that is your portion in life and in the toil you toil at under the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your strength; there is no work or reckoning or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, where you are going.

I turned and saw, under the sun, that the race isn't to the swift, nor the battle to the mighty, nor bread to the wise, nor wealth to the discerning, nor favour to the knowledgeable; time and chance happen to them all.
Nobody knows their time. Like fish caught in a cruel net, like birds caught in a snare, so people are ensnared at an evil time, when it falls on them suddenly.
This too I saw as wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me:
There was a small city with few people in it, and a great king came against it, surrounded it, and built great siege works against it.
And in it was found a poor wise man, and he delivered the city by his wisdom; yet nobody remembered that poor man.
And I said, "Wisdom is better than strength" — yet the wisdom of the poor is despised, and nobody listens to his words.
The words of the wise, spoken quietly, are heard more than a ruler's shouting among dullards.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys a great deal of good.

ecclesiastes_10.t: Dead flies make a perfumer's oil stink and go off; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honour.
The heart of the wise leans right; the heart of a dullard leans left.
Even walking down the road, a fool's sense fails him, and he tells everyone he's a fool.
If the ruler's temper rises against you, don't leave your post; calmness lays great offences to rest.
There's an evil I've seen under the sun, like a mistake that comes from a ruler:
Folly is put in many high places, while the rich sit down low.
I've seen slaves on horseback and princes going on foot like slaves.
Dig a pit and you fall into it; break through a wall and a snake bites you.
Quarry stones and they'll hurt you; split logs and they'll put you in danger.
If the iron is blunt and nobody sharpens the edge, you have to put in more strength; but wisdom has the advantage of getting it right.
If the snake bites before it's charmed, the charmer gets no profit from it.
The words of a wise man's mouth win favour; a dullard's own lips swallow him up.
What his mouth begins with is folly; what it ends with is evil madness.
And the fool piles up words. Nobody knows what will be; who can tell them what will come after?
The toil of dullards wears them out; they don't even know the way to town.
Woe to you, land, whose king is a youth and whose princes are feasting in the morning!
How blessed are you, land, whose king is of noble birth, whose princes eat at the proper time, for strength and not for drinking!
Laziness makes the roof-beams sag; idle hands let the house leak.
Bread is made for laughter; wine gladdens life; and money answers everything.
Don't curse a king even in your thoughts, or curse a rich person in your bedroom; a bird of the air will carry the sound, and something with wings will report what was said.

ecclesiastes_11.t: Send your bread out over the face of the waters; after many days you'll find it again.
Give a portion to seven, and to eight as well; you don't know what calamity may come on the earth.
If the clouds are full of rain, they empty it on the earth; and whether a tree falls south or north, where it falls, there it lies.
Watch the wind and you'll never sow; watch the clouds and you'll never reap.
You don't know the way of the wind, or how bones form in a pregnant woman's womb; so you don't know the work of God, who makes everything.
Sow your seed in the morning, and in the evening don't let your hand rest; you don't know which will succeed, this one or that, or whether both will do equally well.
Light is sweet, and it's good for the eyes to see the sun.
If a person lives many years, let them rejoice in all of them — and remember the days of darkness, for there will be many. Everything that comes is vanity.

Rejoice, young man, in your youth; let your heart make you glad in the days of your young manhood. Walk in the ways of your heart, in the sight of your eyes — but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgement.
So put vexation out of your heart and evil away from your flesh; youth and the dawn of life are vanity.

ecclesiastes_12.t: Remember your Creator in the days of your young manhood, before the days of evil come and the years arrive when you will say, "I take no pleasure in these";
before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds come back after the rain;
in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bowed, and the grinding women stop because they're few, and those looking out of the windows grow dim;
and the doors onto the street are shut, when the sound of the grinding drops low, and one wakes at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low;

and they are afraid of high places, and terrors are in the road; the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, the caper-berry fails; for a person is going to their everlasting house, and the mourners go about the street;
before the silver cord is snapped, the golden bowl crushed, the jar broken at the spring, the wheel crushed at the well;
and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
Vanity of vanities, said the Qoheleth; everything is vanity.
Besides being wise himself, Qoheleth went on teaching the people knowledge; he weighed and searched out and set in order many proverbs.
Qoheleth sought out pleasing words, and what was written was upright — words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads, like nails driven home are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd.
And beyond these, my son, take warning: there's no end to the making of books, and much study wearies the flesh.
The end of the matter; it has all been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments; that is the whole duty of a person.
For God will bring every deed into judgement, including everything hidden, whether good or evil.

esther_1.t: In the days of Ahasuerus — the Ahasuerus who ruled from India to Cush, a hundred and twenty-seven provinces —
in those days, when King Ahasuerus was seated on his royal throne in Susa the citadel,
in the third year of his reign he threw a feast for all his officials and his court — the army of Persia and Media, the nobles and the provincial officials, all before him —
showing off the wealth of his kingdom's splendour and the honour of his greatness and glory, for a long time — a hundred and eighty days.
When those days were over, the king held a seven-day feast for everyone present in Susa the citadel, from the greatest to the least, in the court of the garden of the king's pavilion.

White cloth, cotton and violet, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rods and marble pillars; gold and silver couches on a pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl and precious stones.
Drinks were served in gold vessels, no two alike, and the royal wine flowed freely — the king could afford it.
The drinking was by decree: nobody was forced. The king had told every steward of his household to let each man do as he pleased.
Queen Vashti also held a feast for the women, in the royal house belonging to King Ahasuerus.
On the seventh day, when the wine had put the king in a good mood, he said to Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carcas — the seven eunuchs who served in his presence —
to bring Queen Vashti before the king in the royal crown, to show the peoples and the officials how beautiful she was — she was good to look at.
But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's word, brought by the eunuchs. The king was furious; his rage burned inside him.
So the king spoke to the wise men who knew the times — that was how the king did things, before everyone who knew law and judgement —
and those closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan — the seven officials of Persia and Media who had access to the king and sat first in the kingdom —
"By law, what is to be done with Queen Vashti, since she didn't carry out King Ahasuerus's command brought by the eunuchs?"
Memucan said, in front of the king and the officials, "It isn't only the king Queen Vashti has wronged — it's all the officials and all the peoples in every province of King Ahasuerus.
"Word of what the queen did will get out to all the women, and they'll look down on their own husbands. They'll say, 'King Ahasuerus ordered Queen Vashti brought before him, and she didn't come.'
"This very day the noble ladies of Persia and Media who've heard about the queen will be saying the same to all the king's officials — and there'll be no end of contempt and anger.

"If it pleases the king, let a royal word go out from him and be entered in the laws of Persia and Media, so it can't be revoked: Vashti is not to come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her royal position to another woman, better than she is.
"The king's decree, once he issues it, will be heard all through his kingdom — and it's a vast one — and all the women will give honour to their husbands, from the greatest to the least."
The king and the officials liked the proposal, and the king did what Memucan said.

He sent letters to all the king's provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language: every man was to be master in his own house and speak in his own people's language.

esther_2.t: After all this, once King Ahasuerus's rage had died down, he remembered Vashti — what she had done, and what had been decreed against her.
The king's young men who attended him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king,

"and let the king appoint officers in every province of his kingdom to gather every beautiful young virgin to Susa the citadel, to the house of the women, into the charge of Hegai the king's eunuch, the keeper of the women — and let them be given their ointments.
"And whichever young woman pleases the king will reign in place of Vashti." The king liked the proposal, and that is what he did.
There was a Jewish man in Susa the citadel named Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,
who had been carried off from Jerusalem with the exiles taken with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried into exile.

He was bringing up Hadassah — that is, Esther — his uncle's daughter, because she had no father or mother. The young woman was beautiful in form and good to look at, and when her father and mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.

When the king's word and his law were made public, and many young women were gathered to Susa the citadel into Hegai's charge, Esther was taken to the king's house, into Hegai's charge, the keeper of the women.

The young woman pleased him and won his loyalty, so he hurried her ointments and her allowance to her, and the seven chosen young women from the king's house, and moved her and her young women to the best place in the house of the women.
Esther had not said who her people or her family were, because Mordecai had told her not to.
Every single day Mordecai walked back and forth in front of the court of the house of the women, to find out how Esther was and what was happening to her.

When each young woman's turn came to go in to King Ahasuerus — after the twelve months prescribed for the women, which is how the days of their ointments were completed: six months with oil of myrrh and six months with balsam oils and the women's ointments —
then this is how the young woman would go in to the king: anything she asked for was given her to take with her from the house of the women to the king's house.

In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would come back to the second house of the women, into the charge of Shaashgaz the king's eunuch, the keeper of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again unless the king delighted in her and called for her by name.

When Esther's turn came to go in to the king — Esther, daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, who had taken her as his own daughter — she asked for nothing but what Hegai the king's eunuch, the keeper of the women, advised. And Esther won favour with everyone who saw her.
Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal house, in the tenth month — the month of Tebeth — in the seventh year of his reign.
The king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won favour and loyalty before him more than all the virgins. He set the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.
The king threw a great feast for all his officials and his court — Esther's feast — and he granted the provinces a remission and gave gifts with royal liberality.
When virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.
Esther still did not say who her family or her people were, just as Mordecai had told her; she did what Mordecai said, exactly as she had when he was raising her.

In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh — two of the king's eunuchs, from the keepers of the threshold — became angry and looked for a chance to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
The matter got out to Mordecai, and he told Queen Esther, and Esther told the king, in Mordecai's name.
The matter was investigated and proved true, and the two of them were hanged on a gallows. It was recorded in the book of the events of the days, in the king's presence.

esther_3.t: After all this, King Ahasuerus promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, raised him up, and set his seat above all the officials with him.
All the king's servants at the king's gate knelt and bowed down to Haman, because the king had ordered it. But Mordecai would not kneel and would not bow down.
So the king's servants at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why are you breaking the king's command?"
When they had spoken to him day after day and he would not listen, they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's words would stand — he had told them he was a Jew.
When Haman saw that Mordecai would not kneel and bow down to him, he was filled with rage.

But he thought it beneath him to lay a hand on Mordecai alone, since they had told him who Mordecai's people were. So Haman set out to annihilate all the Jews in the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus — Mordecai's people.

In the first month — the month of Nisan — in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, the lot) before Haman, from day to day and from month to month, to the twelfth, the month of Adar.

Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered and kept apart among the peoples in every province of your kingdom. Their laws are different from every other people's, they don't keep the king's laws, and it isn't in the king's interest to let them remain.
"If it pleases the king, let an order be written to destroy them, and I'll weigh out ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those who do the work, to be brought into the king's treasuries."
The king took his signet ring off his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the adversary of the Jews.
The king said to Haman, "Keep the silver — and the people are yours, to do with as you see fit."

The king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and it was all written down as Haman ordered: to the king's satraps, to the governors over each province, to the officials of each people — each province in its own script, each people in its own language. It was written in King Ahasuerus's name and sealed with the king's signet ring.

Letters were sent out by courier to all the king's provinces: annihilate, kill and destroy all the Jews, young and old, little children and women, in a single day — the thirteenth of the twelfth month, the month of Adar — and take their goods as plunder.
A copy of the writing was to be issued as law in every single province and published to all the peoples, so they would be ready for that day.
The couriers went out, driven by the king's word, and the law was issued in Susa the citadel. The king and Haman sat down to drink — and the city of Susa was in confusion.

esther_4.t: When Mordecai learned everything that had been done, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, went out into the middle of the city and cried out — loud and bitter.
He came as far as the front of the king's gate — no one could enter the king's gate in sackcloth.
In every single province, wherever the king's word and his law reached, there was great mourning among the Jews — fasting, weeping, wailing. Many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
Esther's maids and her eunuchs came and told her, and the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments for Mordecai to wear, to get the sackcloth off him — but he would not accept them.
So Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs whom the king had appointed to attend her, and sent him to Mordecai to find out what this was and why.
So Hathach went out to Mordecai, to the open square of the city in front of the king's gate.
Mordecai told him everything that had happened to him, and the exact sum of silver Haman had said he would weigh out to the king's treasuries for the Jews, to destroy them.

He also gave him a copy of the writing of the law issued in Susa for their annihilation, to show Esther and explain it to her, and to command her to go to the king, to seek his favour and plead with him for her people.
Hathach came back and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
Then Esther spoke to Hathach and gave him a message for Mordecai:

"All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know this: for any man or woman who goes to the king in the inner court without being summoned, there is one law — death. The only exception is the one the king extends the golden sceptre to, and lives. And I have not been summoned to come to the king for thirty days now."
And they told Mordecai what Esther had said.
Mordecai sent this reply back to Esther: "Don't imagine that you, of all the Jews, will escape because you are in the king's house.

"If you keep altogether silent at this time, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, and you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you reached royalty for a time like this?"
Then Esther sent this reply back to Mordecai:

"Go, gather all the Jews in Susa and fast for me — don't eat, don't drink, for three days, night or day. I and my maids will fast the same way. Then I'll go to the king, against the law. And if I perish, I perish."
So Mordecai went off and did everything Esther had commanded him.

esther_5.t: On the third day Esther put on royal dress and stood in the inner court of the king's house, facing the king's house. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the royal house, facing the entrance.
When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favour in his eyes, and he held out to her the golden sceptre in his hand. Esther came near and touched the top of the sceptre.
The king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? Up to half the kingdom — and it will be given you."
Esther said, "If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come today to the feast I've prepared for him."
The king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so we can do what Esther says." And the king and Haman came to the feast Esther had prepared.
At the feast of wine the king said to Esther, "What is your petition? It will be given you. What is your request? Up to half the kingdom, and it will be done."
Esther answered, "My petition and my request —

"if I have found favour with the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and do what I request — let the king and Haman come to the feast I'll prepare for them, and tomorrow I'll do as the king says."
Haman went out that day happy and in good spirits. But when he saw Mordecai at the king's gate, and Mordecai neither rose nor trembled before him, Haman was filled with rage against Mordecai.
But Haman held himself in and went home, and sent for his friends and Zeresh his wife.
Haman went through it all for them: the splendour of his wealth, the many sons he had, everything the king had done to promote him, how he had raised him above the officials and the king's servants.
And Haman said, "What's more, Queen Esther let no one come with the king to the feast she'd prepared — no one but me. And tomorrow I'm invited again, with the king.
"But none of it counts for anything, every time I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."

Zeresh his wife and all his friends said to him, "Have a gallows made, fifty cubits high, and in the morning speak to the king and have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go with the king to the feast in good spirits." Haman liked the idea, and he had the gallows made.

esther_6.t: That night the king could not sleep, and he ordered the book of the records — the events of the days — to be brought and read aloud before him.
And it was found written that Mordecai had reported Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs from the keepers of the threshold, who had sought to lay a hand on King Ahasuerus.
The king said, "What honour and greatness has been done for Mordecai for this?" The king's young men who attended him said, "Nothing has been done for him."
The king said, "Who's in the court?" Now Haman had come into the outer court of the king's house to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared for him.
The king's young men said to him, "Haman is standing in the court." The king said, "Let him come in."
Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What is to be done for the man the king delights to honour?" And Haman said to himself, "Who would the king delight to honour more than me?"
Haman said to the king, "For the man the king delights to honour —
"let them bring royal clothing the king has worn, and a horse the king has ridden, with a royal crown set on its head;

"and let the clothing and the horse be handed to one of the king's officials, one of the nobles, and let them dress the man the king delights to honour, mount him on the horse, and lead him through the open square of the city, proclaiming before him, 'This is what is done for the man the king delights to honour.'"

Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry — take the clothing and the horse, just as you said, and do it for Mordecai the Jew who sits at the king's gate. Don't let a single thing you said fall to the ground."

So Haman took the clothing and the horse, dressed Mordecai, mounted him, led him through the open square of the city, and proclaimed before him, "This is what is done for the man the king delights to honour."
Mordecai went back to the king's gate. Haman hurried home, mourning, with his head covered.

Haman told Zeresh his wife and all his friends everything that had happened to him. And his wise men and Zeresh his wife said, "If Mordecai, before whom you've begun to fall, is of the offspring of the Jews, you won't prevail against him. You will surely fall before him."
They were still speaking with him when the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman off to the feast Esther had prepared.

esther_7.t: So the king and Haman came to drink with Queen Esther.
On the second day too, at the feast of wine, the king said to Esther, "What is your petition, Queen Esther? It will be given you. What is your request? Up to half the kingdom, and it will be done."
Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favour with you, O king, and if it pleases the king — let my life be given me: that is my petition. And my people: that is my request."

"For we have been sold, I and my people, to be annihilated, killed and destroyed. If we had only been sold as slaves, men and women, I would have kept quiet — the distress would not be worth troubling the king."
King Ahasuerus said — he said to Queen Esther — "Who is he? Where is he? Who has filled his heart to do this?"
Esther said, "A man — an adversary and an enemy — this evil Haman!" And Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.

The king rose in his rage from the feast of wine and went out into the garden of the pavilion. Haman stayed behind to plead for his life with Queen Esther — he could see that harm had been determined against him by the king.

The king came back from the garden of the pavilion into the house of the feast of wine — and there was Haman, falling on the couch Esther was on. The king said, "Will he even subdue the queen, with me in the house?" The word went out of the king's mouth, and they covered Haman's face.

Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs, said in front of the king, "What's more, the gallows Haman made for Mordecai — the man who spoke up for the king's good — is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." The king said, "Hang him on it."
So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. And the king's rage subsided.

esther_8.t: That same day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the house of Haman, the adversary of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, because Esther had told him what Mordecai was to her.
The king took off his signet ring, the one he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.
Esther spoke to the king again. She fell at his feet, wept, and pleaded with him to avert the evil of Haman the Agagite and the plan he had devised against the Jews.
The king held out the golden sceptre to Esther, and Esther rose and stood before the king.

She said, "If it pleases the king, and if I have found favour with him, and the matter seems proper to the king, and I am good in his eyes — let an order be written to revoke the letters, Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite's plan, which he wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces.
"How could I bear to watch the evil that will overtake my people? How could I bear to watch the destruction of my own family?"
King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "See — I've given Haman's house to Esther, and they've hanged him on the gallows, because he laid a hand on the Jews.

"You write concerning the Jews as you see fit, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's signet ring — because a writing written in the king's name and sealed with the king's signet ring cannot be revoked."

So the king's scribes were summoned at that time, on the twenty-third day of the third month, the month of Sivan, and it was all written as Mordecai ordered — to the Jews, to the satraps, the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Cush, a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, each province in its own script and each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their own script and language.
He wrote in King Ahasuerus's name, sealed it with the king's signet ring, and sent the letters by courier on horseback — riders of the royal steeds, bred from the royal mares.

In them the king permitted the Jews in every single city to assemble and make a stand for their life: to annihilate, kill and destroy every armed force of a people or province attacking them, little children and women included, and to take their goods as plunder.
on one day, in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus: the thirteenth of the twelfth month, the month of Adar.
A copy of the writing was to be issued as law in every single province and published to all the peoples, and the Jews were to be ready for that day, to avenge themselves on their enemies.
The couriers, riders of the royal steeds, went out at speed, driven by the king's word; and the law was issued in Susa the citadel.
Mordecai went out from the king's presence in royal clothing of violet and white, wearing a great crown of gold and a robe of fine linen and purple. And the city of Susa shouted for joy and rejoiced.
For the Jews there was light and gladness, joy and honour.

In every single province and every single city, wherever the king's word and his law reached, there was gladness and joy for the Jews, a feast and a holiday. And many of the peoples of the land became Jews, because dread of the Jews had fallen on them.

esther_9.t: In the twelfth month, the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day, when the king's word and his law were about to be carried out — the day the enemies of the Jews had hoped to master them, and it was reversed: the Jews themselves mastered those who hated them —
the Jews assembled in their cities, in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, to lay a hand on those who sought their harm. No one stood before them; dread of them had fallen on all the peoples.
All the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors and those who did the king's work supported the Jews, because dread of Mordecai had fallen on them.
Mordecai was great in the king's house, and word of him went out into all the provinces — the man Mordecai went on growing greater.
The Jews struck down all their enemies with sword, slaughter and destruction, and did to those who hated them as they pleased.
In Susa the citadel the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men.
and Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vaizatha —
— the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the adversary of the Jews. These they killed, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.
That day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel came before the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, "In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman. What have they done in the rest of the king's provinces? And what is your petition? It will be given you. What more do you request? It will be done."
Esther said, "If it pleases the king, let the Jews in Susa be permitted tomorrow as well to act according to the law of this day, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows."
The king said it should be done, a law was issued in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman.
The Jews in Susa assembled on the fourteenth of Adar as well and killed three hundred men in Susa — but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.

The rest of the Jews in the king's provinces assembled and made a stand for their life, had rest from their enemies, and killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them — but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.
That was on the thirteenth of the month of Adar. They rested on the fourteenth and made it a day of feasting and joy.
But the Jews in Susa assembled on the thirteenth and the fourteenth, and rested on the fifteenth, and made that a day of feasting and joy.
That is why the Jews of the open country, who live in the unwalled towns, keep the fourteenth of Adar as a day of joy and feasting, a holiday, and of sending portions to one another.
Mordecai wrote these things down and sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far,
requiring them to observe the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and the fifteenth day of it, every single year,

as the days on which the Jews had rest from their enemies, and the month that was turned for them from sorrow to joy and from mourning to a holiday — to make them days of feasting and joy, of sending portions to one another and gifts to the needy.
And the Jews accepted what they had already begun to do, and what Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the adversary of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur — that is, the lot — to crush them and destroy them.
But when it came before the king, he said in the letter, "Let his evil plan against the Jews come back on his own head" — and they hanged him and his sons on the gallows.
That is why these days are called Purim, after the name of the Pur. So, because of all the words of this letter, and what they had seen of it, and what had happened to them,
