the Jews imposed and accepted, for themselves and their offspring and everyone who joined them, that it should not lapse — that they would observe these two days as prescribed and at their appointed time, every single year;

and that these days would be remembered and observed in every generation, every clan, every province and every city — that these days of Purim would never lapse among the Jews, and the memory of them would never cease from their offspring.
Then Queen Esther, daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter of Purim.
Letters went out to all the Jews, to the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of Ahasuerus's kingdom — words of peace and faithfulness —

to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed times, just as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had imposed them, and as they had imposed on themselves and their offspring — the matters of the fasts and their cry of distress.
Esther's command confirmed these matters of Purim, and it was recorded in the book.

esther_10.t: King Ahasuerus laid a levy on the land and on the islands of the sea.

And all his powerful and mighty deeds, and the full account of the greatness of Mordecai, to which the king raised him — are they not written in the book of the events of the days of the kings of Media and Persia?
For Mordecai the Jew was second to King Ahasuerus, great among the Jews, acceptable to the multitude of his brothers — seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his offspring.

exodus_1.t: These are the names of Israel's sons who came to Egypt with Jacob, each one with his household.
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah;
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin;
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
In all, seventy people came from Jacob's own body. Joseph was in Egypt.
Then Joseph died, and all his brothers, and that whole generation.
But the Israelites were fruitful. They swarmed, they multiplied, they grew mighty — overwhelmingly so — and the land filled up with them.
Then a new king came to power over Egypt, a king who did not know Joseph.
He said to his people, 'Look — the people of Israel outnumber us, and they're mightier than we are.'
'Come, let's deal wisely with them, or they'll multiply, and if war comes they'll join our enemies too, fight us, and go up out of the land.'
So they put labour-gang overseers over them, to afflict them with forced labour. They built storage cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Rameses.
But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and spread. The Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.
So the Egyptians made the Israelites serve harshly.
They made their lives bitter with hard labour: mortar, bricks, every kind of work in the field. All of it, imposed with harshness.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives. One was named Shiphrah, the other Puah.
He said, 'When you deliver the Hebrew women, watch the birthstool. If it's a boy, kill him. If it's a girl, let her live.'
But the midwives feared God. They didn't do what the king of Egypt told them — they let the boys live.
So the king of Egypt called the midwives in and said, 'Why have you done this? You've let the boys live.'
The midwives told Pharaoh, 'Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women. They're vigorous — before the midwife gets there, they've already given birth.'
God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and grew very mighty.
And because the midwives feared God, he made households for them.
Then Pharaoh gave the order to all his people: 'Every boy that's born, throw him into the Nile. Every girl, let her live.'

exodus_2.t: A man from the house of Levi went and married a daughter of Levi.
The woman conceived and bore a son. She saw that he was good, and she hid him three months.
When she couldn't hide him any longer, she got a papyrus basket for him and sealed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child inside and set it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile.
His sister stood at a distance to see what would happen to him.
Pharaoh's daughter went down to bathe at the Nile, her attendants walking along the bank. She saw the basket among the reeds, sent her maidservant, and had it brought to her.
She opened it and saw the child — a boy, crying. She felt compassion for him. 'This is one of the Hebrew children,' she said.
Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, 'Shall I go and get one of the Hebrew women to nurse him for you?'
Pharaoh's daughter said, 'Go.' So the young woman went and called the child's mother.
Pharaoh's daughter said, 'Take this child and nurse him for me, and I'll pay your wages.' So the woman took the child and nursed him.
The child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, and said, 'Because I drew him out of the water.'
In those days, once Moses had grown up, he went out to his brothers and saw their forced labour. And he saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew — one of his own brothers.
He looked this way and that, saw no one, struck the Egyptian down, and hid him in the sand.
He went out the next day and found two Hebrew men fighting. He said to the one in the wrong, 'Why are you striking your companion?'
The man said, 'Who put you in charge as chief and judge over us? Are you going to kill me the way you killed the Egyptian?' Moses was afraid. 'So it's known,' he thought.
When Pharaoh heard about it he tried to kill Moses, so Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian. He sat down by a well.
The priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock.
But shepherds came and drove them off. Moses got up, delivered them, and watered their flock.
When they came back to their father Reuel, he said, 'Why are you home so early today?'
They said, 'An Egyptian delivered us from the shepherds. He even drew the water himself and watered the flock.'
He said to his daughters, 'Where is he? Why did you leave the man there? Call him in to eat.'
Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah.
She bore a son, and he named him Gershom, saying, 'I've been a sojourner in a foreign land.'
During those long years the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned under the labour and cried out, and their cry for help went up to God from the labour.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
And God saw the Israelites. And God knew.

exodus_3.t: Moses was pasturing the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He drove the flock out beyond the wilderness and came to the mountain of God, to Horeb.
The angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the middle of a bush. He looked: the bush was burning, and the bush wasn't being consumed.
Moses said, 'Let me turn aside and look at this great sight — why the bush isn't burning up.'
When the LORD saw that he had turned aside to look, God called to him out of the middle of the bush: 'Moses! Moses!' He answered, 'Here I am.'
He said, 'Don't come any closer. Take your sandals off your feet — the place where you're standing is holy ground.'
He said, 'I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' Moses hid his face — he was afraid to look at God.
The LORD said, 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people in Egypt. I've heard their cry because of its taskmasters. I know its pains.'

'So I've come down to deliver them from Egypt's hand and bring them up out of that land into a good, spacious land — a land flowing with milk and honey — to the place of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites.'
'And now the cry of the Israelites has come to me, and I've seen the oppression the Egyptians are pressing on them.'
'So go. I'm sending you to Pharaoh. Bring my people, the Israelites, out of Egypt.'
But Moses said to God, 'Who am I, to go to Pharaoh? To bring the Israelites out of Egypt?'
He said, 'Because I will be with you. And this is your sign that I've sent you: when you bring the people out of Egypt, you'll serve God on this mountain.'
Then Moses said to God, 'Suppose I go to the Israelites and tell them, "The God of your fathers sent me to you," and they ask me, "What's his name?" What do I say?'
God said to Moses, 'I AM WHO I AM.' Then he said, 'Tell the Israelites this: I AM has sent me to you.'

God said further to Moses, 'Tell the Israelites this: The LORD, the God of your fathers — the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob — has sent me to you. This is my name for ever. This is how I am to be remembered, generation after generation.'

'Go, gather the elders of Israel and tell them, "The LORD, the God of your fathers — the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — appeared to me and said: I have surely attended to you, and to what has been done to you in Egypt."'

'And I have said: I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites — a land flowing with milk and honey.'

'They will listen to you. Then you and the elders of Israel are to go to the king of Egypt and say, "The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Now let us go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God."'
'But I know the king of Egypt won't let you go — not even under a strong hand.'
'So I'll stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders that I will do in its midst. After that, he'll let you go.'
'And I'll give this people favour in the eyes of the Egyptians, so that when you go, you won't go empty-handed.'
'Each woman is to ask her neighbour, and the woman staying in her house, for articles of silver and gold and for clothing. Put them on your sons and daughters — and so you'll plunder Egypt.'

exodus_4.t: Then Moses answered, 'But they won't believe me. They won't listen to me. They'll say, "The LORD didn't appear to you."'
The LORD said to him, 'What's that in your hand?' 'A staff,' he said.
He said, 'Throw it on the ground.' He threw it down, and it became a serpent. Moses ran from it.
The LORD said to Moses, 'Stretch out your hand and take it by the tail.' He stretched out his hand, took hold of it, and it became a staff in his palm.
'— so that they will believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.'
The LORD said to him again, 'Put your hand inside your cloak.' He put his hand inside and brought it out — and there was his hand, struck with scale-disease, like snow.
He said, 'Put your hand back inside.' He put it back in, brought it out again, and it had returned to be like the rest of his flesh.
'And if they won't believe you or listen to the voice of the first sign, they'll believe the voice of the second.'

'And if they won't believe even these two signs, and won't listen to you, take some water from the Nile and pour it out on the dry ground. The water you take from the Nile will turn to blood on the dry ground.'
But Moses said to the LORD, 'Please, my Lord — I'm not a man of words. I never have been, and I'm not now that you've spoken to your servant. I am heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue.'
The LORD said to him, 'Who made the human mouth? Who makes someone mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?'
'Now go. I will be with your mouth, and I'll teach you what to say.'
But he said, 'Please, my Lord — send by the hand of whoever else you'll send.'

Then the LORD's anger burned against Moses. He said, 'Isn't there Aaron your brother, the Levite? I know he can speak well. In fact he's on his way out to meet you — and when he sees you he'll be glad in his heart.'
'You'll speak to him and put the words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I'll teach you both what to do.'
'He'll speak for you to the people. He will become a mouth for you, and you will become like God to him.'
'And take this staff in your hand. With it you'll do the signs.'
Moses went back to Jether his father-in-law and said, 'Let me go back to my brothers in Egypt and see whether they're still alive.' Jethro said to Moses, 'Go in peace.'
The LORD said to Moses in Midian, 'Go back to Egypt. All the men who were seeking your life are dead.'
So Moses took his wife and his sons, set them on the donkey, and headed back to the land of Egypt. And Moses took the staff of God in his hand.
The LORD said to Moses, 'When you go back to Egypt, see that you do all the wonders I've put in your hand in front of Pharaoh. But I will harden his heart, and he won't let the people go.'
'And say to Pharaoh, "This is what the LORD says: Israel is my son, my firstborn."'
'And I said to you, "Let my son go, so he can serve me" — and you refused. So I'm about to kill your son, your firstborn.'
On the way, at the place where they stopped for the night, the LORD met him and sought to kill him.
Then Zipporah took a flint, cut off her son's foreskin, and touched it to his feet. 'Truly you are a bridegroom of blood to me,' she said.
So he withdrew from him. That was when she said, 'A bridegroom of blood' — because of the circumcision.
The LORD said to Aaron, 'Go into the wilderness to meet Moses.' He went and met him at the mountain of God, and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD that he had sent him with, and all the signs he had commanded him.
Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the Israelites.
Aaron spoke all the words the LORD had spoken to Moses, and he did the signs where the people could see.
And the people believed. When they heard that the LORD had attended to the Israelites and had seen their affliction, they bowed low and prostrated themselves.

exodus_5.t: Afterwards Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, 'This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Let my people go, so they can hold a festival to me in the wilderness.'
But Pharaoh said, 'Who is the LORD, that I should listen to him and let Israel go? I don't know the LORD, and I'm not letting Israel go either.'
They said, 'The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Let us go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God — or he may fall upon us with pestilence or the sword.'
But the king of Egypt said, 'Moses and Aaron — why are you drawing the people away from their work? Get back to your forced labour.'
And Pharaoh said, 'Look how many the people of the land are now — and you'd have them stop their forced labour.'
That same day Pharaoh gave orders to the taskmasters over the people and to their foremen:
'Don't give the people straw for making bricks any more, the way you did before. Let them go and gather their own straw.'
'But the quota of bricks they were making before — hold them to it. Don't reduce it. They're idle. That's why they're crying out, "Let us go and sacrifice to our God."'
'Make the labour heavy on the men, so they work at it and pay no attention to lying words.'
So the taskmasters and the foremen went out and told the people, 'This is what Pharaoh says: I'm not giving you straw.'
'Go get your own straw, wherever you can find it. But nothing at all comes off your quota.'
So the people scattered all through the land of Egypt, gathering stubble in place of straw.
The taskmasters kept pressing them: 'Finish your work — each day's amount on its day — just as when there was straw.'

And the foremen of the Israelites, the ones Pharaoh's taskmasters had put over them, were beaten. 'Why haven't you finished your prescribed portion of bricks the way you did before — yesterday or today?' they were asked.
Then the foremen of the Israelites came and cried out to Pharaoh: 'Why are you treating your servants like this?'
'No straw is given to your servants, and still they tell us, "Make bricks!" And look — your servants are being beaten. The fault lies with your own people.'
But he said, 'You're idle. Idle! That's why you keep saying, "Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD."'
'Now go and work. You'll get no straw, and you'll still deliver the full measure of bricks.'
The foremen of the Israelites saw they were in trouble when they were told, 'Don't reduce your bricks — each day's portion on its day.'
Coming out from Pharaoh, they ran into Moses and Aaron, who were standing there waiting for them.
They said to them, 'May the LORD look at you and judge — you've made us a stench in the eyes of Pharaoh and his servants, putting a sword in their hand to kill us.'
Then Moses turned back to the LORD. 'My Lord, why have you brought harm on this people? Why did you ever send me?'
'From the moment I went to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has brought harm on this people. And you have not delivered your people at all.'

exodus_6.t: The LORD said to Moses, 'Now you'll see what I will do to Pharaoh. Under a strong hand he will let them go, and under a strong hand he will drive them out of his land.'
God spoke to Moses and said to him, 'I am the LORD.'
'I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob as God Almighty. But by my name, the LORD, I did not make myself known to them.'
'I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan — the land where they lived as sojourners.'
'And I've heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are making serve, and I have remembered my covenant.'

'So tell the Israelites: I am the LORD. I will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt. I will deliver you from their labour. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgement.'
'I will take you to myself as a people, and I will be God for you. And you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brings you out from under the burdens of Egypt.'
'And I will bring you into the land I swore with uplifted hand to give to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD.'
Moses told the Israelites all this, but they didn't listen to him — out of shortness of spirit and hard labour.
Then the LORD said to Moses:
'Go in and speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt, so he'll let the Israelites go out of his land.'
But Moses spoke before the LORD: 'The Israelites haven't listened to me. How is Pharaoh going to listen to me, when I am uncircumcised of lips?'
But the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a command concerning the Israelites and concerning Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
These are the heads of their fathers' houses. The sons of Reuben, Israel's firstborn: Hanoch and Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jakin and Zohar, and Shaul the son of the Canaanite woman. These are the clans of Simeon.
These are the names of the sons of Levi by their generations: Gershon, Kohath and Merari. Levi lived a hundred and thirty-seven years.
The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans.
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel. Kohath lived a hundred and thirty-three years.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites by their generations.
Amram took Jochebed his father's sister as his wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. Amram lived a hundred and thirty-seven years.
The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg and Zikri.
The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan and Sithri.
Aaron took Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, as his wife, and she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah and Abiasaph. These are the clans of the Korahites.
Eleazar the son of Aaron took one of the daughters of Putiel as his wife, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the Levite fathers' houses by their clans.
That is the Aaron and Moses the LORD spoke to when he said, 'Bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their hosts.'
They are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. That is Moses and Aaron.
On the day the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,
the LORD spoke to Moses: 'I am the LORD. Tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I tell you.'
But Moses said before the LORD, 'I am uncircumcised of lips. How is Pharaoh going to listen to me?'

exodus_7.t: The LORD said to Moses, "Look, I've made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet."
You'll say everything I command you, and your brother Aaron will say it to Pharaoh, so he lets the people of Israel go out of his land.
But I myself will harden Pharaoh's heart, and I'll multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh won't listen to you. So I'll set my hand against Egypt, and I'll bring out my hosts — my people, the people of Israel — from the land of Egypt, with great acts of judgement.
Then the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand over Egypt and bring the people of Israel out from among them.
Moses and Aaron did exactly as the LORD commanded them. That's what they did.
Moses was eighty and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron,
"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Give us a wonder,' tell Aaron, 'Take your staff and throw it down in front of Pharaoh' — and let it become a dragon."
So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just what the LORD had commanded. Aaron threw his staff down in front of Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a dragon.
Then Pharaoh called in the wise men and the sorcerers, and they did the same thing — the ritual experts of Egypt, with their secret arts.
Each of them threw down his staff, and they became dragons — and Aaron's staff swallowed theirs.
But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he didn't listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hard. He's refused to let the people go."
Go to Pharaoh in the morning. He goes out to the water. Stand and wait for him on the bank of the Nile, and take in your hand the staff that was turned into a serpent.
Tell him, "The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you to say: Let my people go, so they can serve me in the wilderness. And look — you still haven't listened."
This is what the LORD says: This is how you'll know that I am the LORD. I'm about to strike the water in the Nile with the staff in my hand, and it will turn to blood.
The fish in the Nile will die, the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will get tired of drinking water from the Nile.

The LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt — over their rivers, their canals, their ponds, every pool of their water — and it will all become blood. There'll be blood in the whole land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and stone.'"
Moses and Aaron did just what the LORD had commanded. He raised the staff and struck the water in the Nile, in full view of Pharaoh and his servants, and all the water in the Nile turned to blood.
The fish in the Nile died, the Nile stank, and the Egyptians couldn't drink water from the Nile. There was blood in the whole land of Egypt.
But the ritual experts of Egypt did the same thing with their secret arts. Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he didn't listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house. He didn't take even this to heart.
So all the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they couldn't drink the water of the Nile.
Seven days went by after the LORD struck the Nile.

exodus_8.t: The LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'This is what the LORD says: Let my people go, so they can serve me.'"
But if you refuse to let them go, I'm about to strike down your whole territory with frogs.

The Nile will swarm with frogs. They'll come up and get into your house, into your bedroom and onto your bed, into your servants' house and among your people, into your ovens and into your kneading troughs.
The frogs will come up on you, on your people, and on all your servants.
The LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, the canals and the ponds, and bring the frogs up onto the land of Egypt.'"
Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.
But the ritual experts did the same thing with their secret arts, and they brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take the frogs away from me and from my people, and I'll let the people go so they can sacrifice to the LORD."

Moses said to Pharaoh, "Take the honour over me. For when shall I plead for you and for your servants and for your people, so the frogs are cut off from you and from your houses? Only in the Nile will they stay."
He said, "Tomorrow." And Moses said, "According to your word — so you'll know there's no one like the LORD our God."
The frogs will leave you and your houses and your servants and your people. Only in the Nile will they stay.
Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the LORD about the matter of the frogs he had set on Pharaoh.
The LORD did what Moses asked, and the frogs died — out of the houses, out of the courtyards, out of the fields.
They piled them up in heap after heap, and the land stank.
But when Pharaoh saw there was relief, he hardened his heart and didn't listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
The LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, and it will become gnats in the whole land of Egypt.'"

They did it. Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and the gnats were on humankind and on livestock. All the dust of the earth became gnats in the whole land of Egypt.
The ritual experts tried the same thing with their secret arts, to bring out the gnats, but they couldn't. And the gnats were on humankind and on livestock.
The ritual experts said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he didn't listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
The LORD said to Moses, "Get up early in the morning and stand in front of Pharaoh — he goes out to the water — and tell him, 'This is what the LORD says: Let my people go, so they can serve me.'"

If you won't let my people go, I'm about to send the swarm on you and your servants and your people and into your houses. The houses of Egypt will be full of the swarm — and the ground they stand on too.
But on that day I'll distinguish the land of Goshen, where my people are standing, so no swarm will be there — so you'll know that I am the LORD in the midst of the land.
I'll set a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign will happen.
The LORD did it, and a heavy swarm came into Pharaoh's house and the house of his servants. In the whole land of Egypt the land was ruined because of the swarm.
Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God — here in the land."

Moses said, "It isn't right to do that. We'd be sacrificing to the LORD our God the very thing Egypt finds detestable. If we sacrifice what Egypt finds detestable right in front of them, won't they stone us?"
We'll go a three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God, just as he tells us.
Pharaoh said, "I'll let you go, and you can sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness — only you must not go far. Now plead for me."

Moses said, "I'm going out from you now, and I'll plead with the LORD, and tomorrow the swarm will leave Pharaoh and his servants and his people. Only let Pharaoh not deal deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."
Moses went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.
The LORD did what Moses asked, and he took the swarm away from Pharaoh and his servants and his people. Not one was left.
But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time too, and he didn't let the people go.

exodus_9.t: The LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, so they can serve me.'"
If you refuse to let them go and you're still keeping a strong hold on them,
then the hand of the LORD is about to fall on your livestock out in the field — on the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the cattle and the flocks — a very heavy pestilence.
But the LORD will distinguish between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt. Nothing that belongs to the people of Israel will die.
And the LORD set an appointed time: "Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land."
The LORD did it the next day. All the livestock of Egypt died, but of the livestock of the people of Israel not one died.
Pharaoh sent to check, and indeed, not even one of the livestock of Israel had died. But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he didn't let the people go.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from a furnace, and have Moses throw it toward the sky in front of Pharaoh."
It will become fine dust over the whole land of Egypt, and on humankind and on livestock it will become boils breaking out in blisters, in the whole land of Egypt.
So they took the soot of the furnace and stood in front of Pharaoh, and Moses threw it toward the sky, and it became boils breaking out in blisters on humankind and on livestock.
The ritual experts couldn't stand in front of Moses because of the boils, because the boils were on the ritual experts and on all the Egyptians.
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he didn't listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses.
The LORD said to Moses, "Get up early in the morning and stand in front of Pharaoh, and tell him, 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, so they can serve me.'"
This time I'm sending all my plagues to your heart, and on your servants and on your people, so you'll know there is no one like me in all the earth.
By now I could have stretched out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you'd have been wiped out from the earth.
But this is why I've kept you alive: to make you see my power, and so my name will be recounted in all the earth.
You're still exalting yourself over my people by not letting them go.
About this time tomorrow I'm going to rain down very heavy hail — hail like Egypt has never had from the day it was founded until now.

So now send word and get your livestock under shelter, and everything you have in the field. Every human and animal found in the field and not brought into the house — the hail will come down on them, and they will die.
Whoever among Pharaoh's servants feared the word of the LORD got his servants and his livestock into the houses.
But whoever didn't take the word of the LORD to heart left his servants and his livestock out in the field.

The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, and let there be hail in the whole land of Egypt — on humankind and on livestock and on all the vegetation of the field, in the land of Egypt."
Moses stretched out his staff toward the sky, and the LORD gave thunder and hail, and fire went to the ground. The LORD rained hail on the land of Egypt.
There was hail, and fire flashing in the middle of the hail — very heavy, like nothing that had been in the whole land of Egypt since it became a nation.
The hail struck everything in the field in the whole land of Egypt, from humankind to livestock. The hail struck all the vegetation of the field, and it shattered every tree of the field.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel were, there was no hail.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said to them, "I've sinned this time. The LORD is the righteous one, and I and my people are the guilty ones."
Plead with the LORD — there's been enough of God's thunder and hail — and I'll let you go, and you won't have to stay any longer.
Moses said to him, "As soon as I go out of the city I'll spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will stop and there'll be no more hail — so you'll know that the earth belongs to the LORD."
But as for you and your servants — I know you don't yet fear before the LORD God.
The flax and the barley were struck, because the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud.
But the wheat and the spelt weren't struck, because they're late crops.
Moses went out from Pharaoh, out of the city, and spread out his hands to the LORD. The thunder and the hail stopped, and no rain was poured out on the ground.
But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had stopped, he sinned again, and he hardened his heart — he and his servants.
Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he didn't let the people of Israel go, just as the LORD had said through Moses.

exodus_10.t: The LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh. I myself have hardened his heart, and the heart of his servants, so I can set these signs of mine in his midst,
and so you can tell your son and your son's son how I dealt ruthlessly with Egypt, and about my signs that I set among them. And you'll know that I am the LORD."
So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and told him, "This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, so they can serve me.
If you refuse to let my people go, I'm about to bring locusts into your territory tomorrow.

It will cover the eye of the land, so no one will be able to see the land. It will eat the remainder of what escaped, whatever the hail left you, and it will eat every tree that sprouts for you from the field.

Your houses will be full, and the houses of all your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians — something your fathers and your fathers' fathers never saw from the day they were on the land until this day." Then he turned and went out from Pharaoh.
Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long will this one be a snare to us? Let the men go, so they can serve the LORD their God. Don't you know yet that Egypt has perished?"
So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, and he said to them, "Go, serve the LORD your God. Who and who are the ones going?"
Moses said, "We'll go with our young and our old, with our sons and our daughters, with our flocks and our herds — because it's a festival of the LORD for us."
He said to them, "May the LORD be with you the way I'm going to let you go — you and your little ones! Look: you have evil in mind."
"Not so! Go — the men — and serve the LORD, since that's what you're asking for." And they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.
The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so they'll come up over the land of Egypt and eat all the vegetation of the land — everything the hail left."
So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD drove an east wind across the land all that day and all night. When morning came, the east wind had carried the locusts.
The locusts came up over the whole land of Egypt and settled in all the territory of Egypt, very heavy. There had never been locusts like it before, and there never will be again.

It covered the eye of the whole land, and the land grew dark. It ate all the vegetation of the land and all the fruit of the trees the hail had left, and no greenery was left on the trees or on the vegetation of the field in the whole land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh hurried to call for Moses and Aaron and said, "I've sinned against the LORD your God and against you."
So now forgive my sin just this once, and plead with the LORD your God to take this death away from me — just this.
So he went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.
And the LORD turned a very strong sea wind, and it carried the locusts away and drove them into the Sea of Reeds. Not one locust was left in all the territory of Egypt.
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he didn't let the people of Israel go.
The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, and let there be darkness over the land of Egypt — a darkness that can be felt."
So Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was darkness of gloom in the whole land of Egypt for three days.
They couldn't see one another, and no one got up from where he was for three days. But for all the people of Israel there was light in their dwellings.
Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD. Only your flocks and your herds will be held back — even your little ones can go with you."
But Moses said, "You yourself will also have to give us sacrifices and burnt offerings, and we'll offer them to the LORD our God.
And our livestock has to go with us too — not a hoof will be left behind — because we'll take from it to serve the LORD our God. And we don't know what we'll serve the LORD with until we get there."
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he wasn't willing to let them go.
Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me! Watch yourself — don't see my face again. On the day you see my face, you'll die."
Moses said, "Rightly spoken. I won't see your face again."

exodus_11.t: The LORD said to Moses, "There's one more affliction I'll bring on Pharaoh and on Egypt. After that he'll let you go from here — and when he lets you go completely, he'll drive you right out.
Now speak to the people, and have each man ask his neighbour and each woman ask her neighbour for articles of silver and articles of gold."
And the LORD gave the people favour in the eyes of the Egyptians. The man Moses was also very great in the land of Egypt — in the eyes of Pharaoh's servants and in the eyes of the people.
Moses said, "This is what the LORD says: About the middle of the night I'm going out into the midst of Egypt.
Every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die — from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne to the firstborn of the maidservant behind the hand-mill, and every firstborn of the livestock.
There'll be a great cry in the whole land of Egypt — one like there's never been and never will be again.
But against all the people of Israel not a dog will bark, from human to livestock — so you'll know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.

And all these servants of yours will come down to me and bow down to me and say, 'Go out — you and all the people who follow you.' And after that I'll go out." Then he went out from Pharaoh in heat of anger.
The LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh won't listen to you, so that my wonders will be many in the land of Egypt."
Moses and Aaron did all these wonders in front of Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he didn't let the people of Israel go from his land.

exodus_12.t: The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt,
This month will be the beginning of months for you. It will be the first for you of the months of the year.
Speak to the whole congregation of Israel and say: On the tenth of this month each man is to take for himself an animal from the flock — one for a father's household, one for the household.

If the household is too small for one animal, then he and the neighbour nearest his house are to take one according to the number of people — each according to what he eats, you're to reckon for the animal.
The animal is to be unblemished, male, a year old. You'll take it from the sheep or from the goats.
You're to keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel is to slaughter it at twilight.
They're to take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses where they eat it.
They're to eat the flesh that night, roasted with fire, with unleavened bread; they're to eat it with bitter herbs.
Don't eat any of it raw, or boiled at all in water — only roasted with fire, its head with its legs and its entrails.
Don't leave any of it until morning. Whatever is left of it until morning you're to burn with fire.
And this is how you're to eat it: your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, your staff in your hand. You're to eat it in haste. It is a Passover to the LORD.

For I'll pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I'll strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from humankind to livestock. And against all the gods of Egypt I'll execute acts of judgement. I am the LORD.
The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are. I'll see the blood and pass over you, and there'll be no blow among you for destruction when I strike in the land of Egypt.
This day will be a memorial for you, and you're to celebrate it as a festival to the LORD. Throughout your generations, as a perpetual statute, you're to celebrate it.

For seven days you're to eat unleavened bread. On the first day you're to remove leaven from your houses, because anyone who eats what is leavened — that person will be cut off from Israel, from the first day until the seventh day.
On the first day there'll be a holy assembly, and on the seventh day a holy assembly for you. No work is to be done on those days — only what every person eats; that alone may be done by you.
You're to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, because on this very day I brought your hosts out from the land of Egypt. You're to keep this day throughout your generations, a perpetual statute.
In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, in the evening, you're to eat unleavened bread — until the twenty-first day of the month, in the evening.
For seven days no leaven is to be found in your houses. Anyone who eats anything leavened — that person will be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether a sojourner or a native of the land.
Eat nothing leavened. In all your dwellings you're to eat unleavened bread.
Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Draw out and take animals from the flock for yourselves according to your clans, and slaughter the Passover.

Take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood that's in the bowl, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood in the bowl. And none of you is to go out the door of his house until morning.

The LORD will pass through to strike down Egypt, and he'll see the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, and the LORD will pass over the door and won't allow the destroyer to come into your houses to strike down.
You're to keep this word as a decree for you and for your sons forever.
And when you come into the land the LORD will give you, just as he said, you're to keep this service.
And when your children ask you, "What does this service mean to you?" —

then you'll say, "It's a sacrifice of Passover to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt when he struck down Egypt — and he delivered our houses." And the people bowed low and bowed down.
The people of Israel went and did exactly as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron. That's what they did.

In the middle of the night the LORD struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt — from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive in the house of the pit, and every firstborn of the livestock.
Pharaoh got up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians, and there was a great cry in Egypt — because there was no house without someone dead in it.
He called for Moses and Aaron in the night and said, "Get up, get out from among my people — both you and the people of Israel. Go, serve the LORD as you said.
"Take your flocks and your herds too, as you said, and go. And bless me as well."
And the Egyptians pressed hard on the people to hurry them out of the land, because they said, "We're all dying."
So the people carried off their dough before it was leavened, their kneading troughs bound up in their clothes on their shoulders.
The people of Israel did what Moses had said, and they asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and articles of gold and clothing.
And the LORD gave the people favour in the eyes of the Egyptians, and they granted their request. And they plundered Egypt.
The people of Israel set out from Rameses toward Succoth — about six hundred thousand on foot, the men, apart from the little ones.
A large mixed company went up with them too, along with flocks and herds — very heavy livestock.

They baked the dough they'd brought out from Egypt into unleavened cakes, because it wasn't leavened — they had been driven out from Egypt and couldn't delay, and they hadn't made provisions for themselves.
The dwelling of the people of Israel, which they dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years.
At the end of four hundred and thirty years, on this very day, all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt.
It was a night of vigil for the LORD, to bring them out from the land of Egypt. This is that night for the LORD — a vigil for all the people of Israel throughout their generations.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the statute of the Passover. No son of a foreigner is to eat of it.
But every slave of a man, bought with silver — circumcise him, and then he may eat of it.
A resident alien and a hired worker are not to eat of it.
It's to be eaten in one house. Don't bring any of the flesh out of the house to the outside, and don't break a bone in it.
The whole congregation of Israel is to do it.

When a sojourner is staying with you and wants to keep a Passover to the LORD, let every male of his be circumcised. Then he may draw near to keep it, and he'll be like a native of the land. But no uncircumcised man is to eat of it.
One law is to be for the native and for the sojourner who sojourns among you.
All the people of Israel did exactly as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron. That's what they did.
And on this very day the LORD brought the people of Israel out from the land of Egypt by their hosts.

exodus_13.t: The LORD said to Moses:
Set apart as holy to me every firstborn. Whatever opens the womb first among the Israelites — people or livestock — is mine.
Moses said to the people, "Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of a house of slaves. The LORD brought you out of here by the strength of his hand. Don't eat anything leavened."
Today you're going out, in the month of Abib.

When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites and Jebusites — the land he swore to your fathers he would give you, a land flowing with milk and honey — keep this service in this month.
For seven days eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there's a festival to the LORD.
Eat unleavened bread for the seven days. No leavened bread is to be seen with you, and no leaven anywhere in your territory.
On that day tell your son, "This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt."
It's to be a sign on your hand and a reminder between your eyes, so the LORD's law stays in your mouth — because the LORD brought you out of Egypt with a strong hand.
Keep this statute at its appointed time, year after year.
When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your fathers, and gives it to you,
then hand over to the LORD everything that first opens the womb. Every firstborn of the animals you own — the males belong to the LORD.
Redeem every firstborn donkey with a sheep. If you don't redeem it, break its neck. And redeem every firstborn among your sons.
When your son asks you later on, "What is this?" tell him, "The LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of a house of slaves, by the strength of his hand."

When Pharaoh made it hard to let us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of humans to the firstborn of animals. That's why I sacrifice to the LORD every male that first opens the womb, and why I redeem every firstborn of my sons.
It's to be a sign on your hand and marks between your eyes, because the LORD brought us out of Egypt by the strength of his hand.

When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by the road through Philistine country, even though it was close. God said, "The people might change their minds when they see fighting, and go back to Egypt."
So God took the people around by the wilderness road toward the Sea of Reeds. The Israelites went up out of Egypt in battle array.
Moses took Joseph's bones with him, because Joseph had made the Israelites swear: "God will surely take notice of you, and when he does, carry my bones up from here with you."
They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness.
The LORD went ahead of them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them on the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, so they could travel day or night.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night never left their place ahead of the people.

exodus_14.t: The LORD said to Moses:
"Tell the Israelites to turn back and camp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, facing Baal-zephon. Camp there, opposite it, by the sea."
Pharaoh will say about the Israelites, "They're wandering around lost in the land. The wilderness has closed in on them."
"I'll harden Pharaoh's heart, and he'll come after them. I'll gain honour through Pharaoh and his whole army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD." And they did it.
When the king of Egypt was told the people had fled, Pharaoh and his officials had a change of heart about them. They said, "What have we done, letting Israel go from serving us?"
So he harnessed his chariot and took his people with him.
He took six hundred picked chariots and all the rest of Egypt's chariotry, with officers over all of them.
The LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he went after the Israelites — who were marching out with a high hand.
The Egyptians came after them and caught up with them camped by the sea — all Pharaoh's chariot horses, his horsemen and his army — at Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon.
As Pharaoh got close, the Israelites looked up — and there were the Egyptians, marching right behind them. They were terrified, and they cried out to the LORD.
They said to Moses, "Was there a shortage of graves in Egypt, that you took us out here to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us, bringing us out of Egypt?"
"Isn't this exactly what we told you in Egypt — 'Leave us alone, let us serve the Egyptians'? Better for us to serve the Egyptians than die in the wilderness."
Moses said to the people, "Don't be afraid. Stand firm and watch the deliverance the LORD will work for you today. The Egyptians you see today you will never see again."
The LORD will fight for you. You just have to keep quiet.
The LORD said to Moses, "Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to move on."
"As for you — lift your staff, stretch your hand out over the sea, and divide it, so the Israelites can go through the middle of the sea on dry ground."
"And I am about to harden the Egyptians' heart, so they'll go in after them. I'll gain honour through Pharaoh and his whole army, his chariotry and his horsemen."
"Then the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I gain honour through Pharaoh, his chariotry and his horsemen."
The angel of God, who had been going ahead of Israel's camp, moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from in front of them and stood behind them.
It came between the Egyptian camp and the Israelite camp. There was the cloud and the darkness, and it lit up the night, and neither side came near the other all night long.
Moses stretched his hand out over the sea, and all night the LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind. He turned the sea into dry land, and the waters were divided.
The Israelites went into the middle of the sea on dry ground, with the waters a wall for them on their right and on their left.
The Egyptians pursued and went in after them — all Pharaoh's horses, his chariotry and his horsemen — into the middle of the sea.
In the morning watch the LORD looked down on the Egyptian camp through the pillar of fire and cloud, and threw the camp into confusion.
He turned the wheels of their chariots aside so that they drove with difficulty. The Egyptians said, "Let's get away from Israel — the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt."
The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch your hand out over the sea, so the waters come back over the Egyptians, over their chariotry and their horsemen."
Moses stretched his hand out over the sea, and at daybreak the sea came back to its normal flow. The Egyptians were fleeing right into it, and the LORD shook them off into the middle of the sea.
The waters came back and covered the chariotry and the horsemen — Pharaoh's whole army that had gone into the sea after them. Not one of them was left.
But the Israelites had walked on dry ground through the middle of the sea, with the waters a wall for them on their right and on their left.
So that day the LORD delivered Israel from the hand of Egypt, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
Israel saw the great hand the LORD had used against Egypt, and the people feared the LORD, and they trusted the LORD and Moses his servant.

exodus_15.t: Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD: Let me sing to the LORD, for he is highly exalted; horse and its rider he has thrown into the sea.
My strength and my song is the LORD, and he has become my deliverance. This is my God, and I will glorify him, my father's God, and I will lift him high.
The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.
Pharaoh's chariots and his army he threw into the sea, and the pick of his officers were sunk in the Sea of Reeds.
The deeps cover them; they went down into the depths like a stone.
Your right hand, LORD, is glorious in power; your right hand, LORD, shatters the enemy.
In the greatness of your majesty you tear down those who rise against you; you send out your burning anger, and it burns them up like stubble.
By the breath of your nostrils the waters were piled up; the streams stood up like a heap; the deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.
The enemy said, "I'll pursue, I'll overtake, I'll divide the plunder; I'll have my fill of them. I'll draw my sword; my hand will dispossess them."
You blew with your breath, and the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters.
Who is like you among the gods, LORD? Who is like you — glorious in holiness, fearsome in praises, doing wonder?
You stretched out your right hand, and the earth swallowed them.
In your steadfast love you led the people you redeemed; you guided them by your strength to your holy home.
The peoples have heard, and they tremble; writhing has seized the inhabitants of Philistia.
Then the chiefs of Edom were terrified; trembling took hold of Moab's leaders; all the inhabitants of Canaan melted away.
Terror and dread fall on them; by the greatness of your arm they go still as a stone, until your people pass over, LORD, until the people pass over whom you purchased.
You will bring them and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, the place for your dwelling that you made, LORD, the sanctuary, my Lord, that your hands established.
The LORD will reign forever and ever.

For Pharaoh's horses went into the sea with his chariotry and his horsemen, and the LORD brought the sea's waters back over them — while the Israelites walked on dry ground through the middle of the sea.
Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, took the tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.
Miriam sang back to them: Sing to the LORD, for he is highly exalted; horse and its rider he has thrown into the sea.
Moses led Israel out from the Sea of Reeds into the wilderness of Shur. They travelled three days in the wilderness and found no water.
They came to Marah, but they couldn't drink the water there, because it was bitter. That's why the place is called Marah.
The people grumbled against Moses. "What are we supposed to drink?"
He cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a tree. He threw it into the water, and the water turned sweet. There he made a statute and an ordinance for them, and there he tested them.

He said, "If you listen carefully to the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in his eyes, and give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, then I won't put on you any of the sicknesses I put on the Egyptians. I am the LORD who heals you."
They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the water.

exodus_16.t: They set out from Elim, and the whole congregation of the Israelites came to the wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they came out of Egypt.
The whole congregation of the Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness.

The Israelites said to them, "If only we had died by the LORD's hand back in Egypt, sitting by the pot of meat, eating bread till we were full. You've brought us out into this wilderness to starve this whole assembly to death."

The LORD said to Moses, "I'm about to rain down bread from the heavens for you. The people are to go out and gather each day's portion on its day, so I can test them — whether they'll walk in my law or not."
"On the sixth day they're to prepare what they bring in, and it will be double what they gather on the other days."
Moses and Aaron said to all the Israelites, "This evening you'll know that it was the LORD who brought you out of Egypt,
"and in the morning you'll see the glory of the LORD, because he's heard your grumblings against the LORD. And what are we, that you grumble against us?"

Moses said, "When the LORD gives you meat to eat this evening and bread in the morning to fill you, it's because he's heard the grumblings you're grumbling against him. What are we? Your grumblings aren't against us — they're against the LORD."
Moses said to Aaron, "Tell the whole congregation of the Israelites, 'Draw near before the LORD, because he's heard your grumblings.'"
As Aaron was speaking to the whole congregation of the Israelites, they turned toward the wilderness — and there the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.
The LORD said to Moses:
"I've heard the grumblings of the Israelites. Tell them, 'At twilight you'll eat meat, and in the morning you'll have your fill of bread. And you'll know that I am the LORD your God.'"
That evening the quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp.
When the layer of dew lifted, there on the surface of the wilderness was something fine and flaking, fine as frost on the ground.
When the Israelites saw it they said to each other, "What is it?" — they didn't know what it was. Moses said to them, "It's the bread the LORD has given you to eat."
"This is what the LORD has commanded: gather what each of you can eat — an omer a head, by the number of people you have. Each of you take for those in his tent."
The Israelites did that, and they gathered — some a lot, some a little.
When they measured it by the omer, whoever gathered a lot had nothing over, and whoever gathered a little had no shortfall. Each had gathered what he could eat.
Moses said to them, "No one is to leave any of it until morning."
But they didn't listen to Moses. Some left part of it until morning, and it bred worms and stank, and Moses was angry with them.
They gathered it morning after morning, each according to what he could eat, and when the sun grew hot it melted.
On the sixth day they gathered double the bread, two omers each, and all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses.

He said to them, "This is what the LORD said: tomorrow is a sabbath observance, a sabbath of holiness to the LORD. Bake what you're going to bake, boil what you're going to boil, and set the rest aside to be kept until morning."
They set it aside until morning, as Moses had commanded, and it didn't stink, and there were no maggots in it.
Moses said, "Eat it today, because today is a sabbath to the LORD. You won't find it in the field today."
"Six days you gather it, but on the seventh day, the sabbath, there'll be none."
On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, and found none.
The LORD said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?"
"See that the LORD has given you the sabbath. That's why on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Each of you stay put; nobody go out from his place on the seventh day."
So the people rested on the seventh day.
The house of Israel called it manna. It was like coriander seed, white, and it tasted like a wafer made with honey.
Moses said, "This is what the LORD has commanded: keep a full omer of it for your generations, so they can see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of Egypt."
Moses said to Aaron, "Take a jar, put a full omer of manna in it, and set it before the LORD, to be kept for your generations."
As the LORD had commanded Moses, Aaron set it before the testimony, to be kept.
The Israelites ate the manna for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land — they ate the manna until they reached the border of the land of Canaan.
An omer is a tenth of an ephah.

exodus_17.t: The whole congregation of the Israelites set out from the wilderness of Sin by stages, at the LORD's command, and camped at Rephidim. There was no water for the people to drink.
The people quarrelled with Moses and said, "Give us water to drink." Moses said to them, "Why are you quarrelling with me? Why are you testing the LORD?"
But the people were thirsty there for water, and they grumbled against Moses: "Why did you do this? You brought us up from Egypt to kill me and my children and my livestock with thirst."
Moses cried out to the LORD, "What am I supposed to do with this people? A little more and they'll stone me."
The LORD said to Moses, "Go on ahead of the people and take some of the elders of Israel with you. Take the staff you struck the River with, and go."
"I'll be standing there in front of you on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it, and the people will drink." Moses did it in front of the elders of Israel.
He called the place Massah and Meribah, because of the Israelites' quarrelling and because they tested the LORD, saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"
Then Amalek came and made war on Israel at Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, "Choose men for us and go out and fight Amalek. Tomorrow I'll be standing on top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand."
Joshua did what Moses told him and fought Amalek, while Moses, Aaron and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
Whenever Moses lifted his hand, Israel prevailed; whenever he let his hand rest, Amalek prevailed.
But Moses' hands were heavy, so they took a stone and put it under him and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on each side. So his hands were steady until sunset.
So Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.
The LORD said to Moses, "Write this down as a reminder in the book, and put it in Joshua's ears: I will completely wipe out the remembrance of Amalek from under the heavens."
Moses built an altar and called it "The LORD is my banner."
He said, "For a hand is on the throne of the LORD: the LORD has war against Amalek from generation to generation."

exodus_18.t: Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law, heard everything God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, and that the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had taken in Zipporah, Moses' wife, after he had sent her away,
and her two sons. One was named Gershom, because he had said, "I've become a sojourner in a foreign land";
and the other was named Eliezer, "because my father's God was my help, and he delivered me from Pharaoh's sword."
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness, where he was camped at the mountain of God.
He sent word to Moses: "I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you, and your wife and her two sons are with her."
Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, bowed down and kissed him. They asked after each other's welfare and went into the tent.
Moses told his father-in-law everything the LORD had done to Pharaoh and Egypt for Israel's sake, all the hardship that had come on them along the way, and how the LORD had delivered them.
Jethro rejoiced over all the good the LORD had done for Israel, delivering them from the hand of Egypt.
Jethro said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you from the hand of Egypt and the hand of Pharaoh, who has delivered the people from under the hand of Egypt."
"Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods — for in the very matter in which they acted presumptuously against them."
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took a burnt offering and sacrifices for God, and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God.
The next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood there before him from morning until evening.

When Moses' father-in-law saw everything he was doing for the people, he said, "What is this you're doing for the people? Why are you sitting alone, with all the people standing before you from morning until evening?"
Moses said to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to consult God."
"When they have a dispute, it comes to me, and I judge between a man and his neighbour, and I make known God's statutes and his laws."
Moses' father-in-law said to him, "What you're doing is not good."
"You'll wear yourself out, you and this people with you, because the task is too heavy for you. You can't do it alone."
"Now listen to me. Let me give you advice, and may God be with you. You stand for the people before God, and bring their matters to God."
"Warn them about the statutes and the laws, and show them the way they're to walk and the work they're to do."
"And pick out from all the people men of ability, who fear God, men of truth, who hate unjust gain, and put them over the people as officials of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens."
"Let them judge the people at all times. Every big matter they'll bring to you, and every small matter they'll judge themselves. Lighten your own load, and they'll carry it with you."
"If you do this, and God commands you to, you'll be able to hold up, and all these people will go home in peace."
Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he had said.
Moses chose men of ability from all Israel and made them heads over the people: officials of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.
They judged the people at all times. The hard cases they brought to Moses, and every small matter they judged themselves.
Then Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and he went back to his own land.

exodus_19.t: In the third month after the Israelites came out of Egypt, on that very day, they came to the wilderness of Sinai.
They set out from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai, and camped there in the wilderness, in front of the mountain.
Moses went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain: "This is what you're to say to the house of Jacob and tell the Israelites:
"You've seen for yourselves what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.
"Now, if you'll listen carefully to my voice and keep my covenant, you'll be my treasured possession out of all the peoples — because the whole earth is mine —
"and you yourselves will be for me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." These are the words you are to speak to the Israelites.
Moses came and summoned the elders of the people, and set before them all these words the LORD had commanded him.
All the people answered together, "Everything the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses brought the people's words back to the LORD.

The LORD said to Moses, "I'm about to come to you in the thickness of the cloud, so the people can hear when I speak with you, and so they'll trust you from then on." And Moses told the LORD what the people had said.
The LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and set them apart as holy today and tomorrow, and have them wash their clothes.
"Have them ready for the third day, because on the third day the LORD will come down in the sight of all the people on Mount Sinai.
"Set a boundary for the people all around, and tell them, 'Be careful not to go up the mountain or touch its edge. Anyone who touches the mountain is to be put to death.'
"'No hand is to touch him — he's to be stoned or shot through. Animal or human, it is not to live. When the ram's horn sounds long, they may go up the mountain.'
Moses went down from the mountain to the people, set them apart as holy, and they washed their clothes.
He said to the people, "Be ready for three days. Do not go near a woman."
On the third day, when morning came, there were thunders and lightnings and a heavy cloud on the mountain, and a very loud blast of a ram's horn, and all the people in the camp trembled.
Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain.
The whole of Mount Sinai was smoking, because the LORD had come down on it in fire. Its smoke went up like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain trembled violently.
The sound of the ram's horn grew louder and louder. Moses would speak, and God would answer him with a voice.
The LORD came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain, and summoned Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.
The LORD said to Moses, "Go down and warn the people, so they don't break through to the LORD to look, and many of them fall."
"And the priests who draw near to the LORD are to set themselves apart as holy too, or the LORD will break out against them."
Moses said to the LORD, "The people can't go up Mount Sinai — you warned us yourself: 'Set a boundary for the mountain and set it apart as holy.'"
The LORD said to him, "Go on down, and come up again, you and Aaron with you. But the priests and the people are not to break through and come up to the LORD, or he will break out against them."
So Moses went down to the people and spoke to them.

exodus_20.t: And God spoke all these words:
"I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of a house of slaves.
"You shall have no other gods before me.
"You shall not make yourself a carved image, or any form of what is in the heavens above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth.
"You shall not bow down to them or serve them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of fathers on sons, on the third generation and the fourth, of those who hate me,
"and showing steadfast love to thousands, to those who love me and keep my commandments.
"You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave unpunished anyone who takes his name in vain.
"Remember the sabbath day, to set it apart as holy.
"Six days you shall labour and do all your work,

"but the seventh day is a sabbath to the LORD your God. You shall not do any work — not you, or your son or your daughter, your male servant or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner within your gates.
"For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea and everything in them, and rested on the seventh day. That's why the LORD blessed the sabbath day and set it apart as holy.
"Honour your father and your mother, so that your days may be long on the land the LORD your God is giving you.
"You shall not murder.
"You shall not commit adultery.
"You shall not steal.
"You shall not testify against your neighbour as a false witness.
"You shall not covet your neighbour's house. You shall not covet your neighbour's wife, or his male servant or female servant, or his ox or his donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbour."
All the people were seeing the thunders and the torches and the sound of the ram's horn and the mountain smoking. When the people saw it they trembled, and they stood at a distance.
They said to Moses, "You speak with us, and we'll listen. But don't let God speak with us, or we'll die."
Moses said to the people, "Don't be afraid. God has come to test you, and so that the fear of him will be before you, and you won't sin."
The people stood at a distance, and Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.
The LORD said to Moses, "This is what you're to say to the Israelites: You've seen for yourselves that I spoke with you from the heavens.
"You shall not make gods of silver alongside me, and you shall not make yourselves gods of gold.

"Make me an altar of earth, and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your cattle. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you.
"And if you make me an altar of stones, don't build it of dressed stone — if you take your tool to it, you've profaned it.
"And don't go up to my altar by steps, so that your nakedness isn't uncovered on it."

exodus_21.t: These are the rulings you are to set before them.
When you buy a Hebrew slave, he serves six years. In the seventh he goes free, and it costs him nothing.
If he came in on his own, he leaves on his own. If he's married, his wife leaves with him.
If his master gave him a wife and she has borne him sons or daughters, the woman and her children belong to her master, and he leaves on his own.
But if the slave says outright, "I love my master, my wife, and my children. I'm not going free,"
then his master brings him to God, takes him to the door or the doorpost, and pierces his ear with the awl. And he serves him for life.
When a man sells his daughter as a female slave, she does not go free the way the male slaves do.
If she does not please her master, who had designated her for himself, he has to let her be bought back. He cannot sell her to a foreign people — he has broken faith with her.
If he designates her for his son, he treats her according to the custom for daughters.
If he takes another woman, he cannot cut back her food, her clothing, or her conjugal right.
If he does not do those three things for her, she goes free — no money changes hands.
Anyone who strikes a person and the person dies is to be put to death.
But if he was not lying in wait, and God let it come about through his hand, I will appoint a place for you where he can flee.
But when a man acts deliberately against his neighbour, to kill him by cunning, you take him from my altar and put him to death.
Anyone who strikes his father or his mother is to be put to death.
Anyone who steals a person and sells him — or is found still holding him — is to be put to death.
Anyone who reviles his father or his mother is to be put to death.
When men quarrel and one hits the other with a stone or his fist, and the man does not die but is laid up in bed,
if he gets up and walks about outside with his staff, the man who struck him is clear. He only has to pay for the time lost and see that he is fully healed.
When a man beats his slave or his female slave with the rod and the slave dies under his hand, it is to be avenged.
But if the slave survives a day or two, it is not avenged — the slave is his money.
When men are fighting and they strike a pregnant woman so that she gives birth prematurely, and there is no harm, he is to be fined whatever the woman's husband imposes, paid as the judges determine.
But if there is harm, you give life for life —
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.
When a man strikes his slave's eye or his female slave's eye and destroys it, he sets the slave free in place of the eye.
And if he knocks out his slave's tooth or his female slave's tooth, he sets the slave free in place of the tooth.
When an ox gores a man or a woman and the person dies, the ox is stoned and its meat is not eaten. The owner is in the clear.
But if the ox had been prone to gore before, and its owner had been warned and did not keep it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox is stoned and the owner is put to death too.
If a ransom is imposed on him, he pays the redemption price for his life, whatever is imposed.
Whether it gores a son or a daughter, the same ruling applies to him.
If the ox gores a slave or a female slave, the owner gives thirty shekels of silver to the slave's master, and the ox is stoned.
When someone opens a pit, or digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls in,
the owner of the pit makes compensation — he pays silver to the animal's owner and keeps the dead animal.
When one man's ox strikes his neighbour's ox and it dies, they sell the live one and split the proceeds, and split the dead animal too.
But if it was known the ox had been prone to gore before and its owner did not keep it in, he pays in full — ox for ox — and keeps the dead one.

exodus_22.t: When someone steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters or sells it, he pays back five head of cattle for the ox and four sheep for the sheep.
If a thief is caught breaking in and is struck and dies, no bloodguilt attaches.
If the sun has already risen, there is bloodguilt. The thief has to make restitution; if he has nothing, he is sold to pay for his theft.
If the stolen animal is found alive in his hands — ox, donkey, or sheep — he pays back double.
When someone grazes a field or a vineyard and turns his livestock loose so they graze in another man's field, he makes compensation from the best of his own field and vineyard.
When a fire breaks out and catches in thornbushes and burns up stacked sheaves, standing grain, or the field itself, whoever started it makes compensation.
When someone gives a neighbour silver or goods to keep, and it is stolen from that man's house — if the thief is found, the thief pays back double.
If the thief is not found, the owner of the house is brought before God, to settle whether he has laid a hand on his neighbour's property.

In every case of misappropriation — an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a garment, any lost thing that someone claims, "This is it" — the case of both parties comes before God, and whichever one God condemns pays his neighbour back double.
When someone gives a neighbour a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any animal to keep, and it dies or is injured or is driven off, with nobody watching,
an oath before the LORD settles it between the two of them, that he has not laid a hand on his neighbour's property. The owner accepts it, and nothing is repaid.
But if it was stolen from him, he makes restitution to its owner.
If it was torn by a predator, he brings it as evidence. He does not pay for a torn animal.
When someone borrows an animal from a neighbour and it is injured or dies with the owner not there, he has to make restitution.
If the owner was there, he does not pay. If it was hired, the hire covers it.
When a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he pays the bride-price for her, and she becomes his wife.
If her father flatly refuses to give her to him, the man weighs out silver at the bride-price for virgins.
You are not to let a sorceress live.
Anyone who lies with an animal is to be put to death.
Anyone who sacrifices to the gods is devoted to destruction — to none but the LORD alone.
Do not mistreat a sojourner or oppress him — you were sojourners in the land of Egypt yourselves.
Do not afflict any widow or fatherless child.
If you do afflict him, and he cries out to me, I will hear his cry.
My anger will burn, and I will kill you with the sword. Your wives will be widows and your children fatherless.
