"Give me my wives and my children, whom I have served you for, and let me go. You know yourself what service I've done for you."
Laban said to him, "If I have found favour in your eyes — I've learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you."
And he said, "Name your wages, and I'll pay them."
He said to him, "You know yourself how I've served you, and how your livestock has fared with me."
"The little you had before I came has burst out into abundance, and the LORD has blessed you wherever I turned. So when do I get to provide for my own household?"
He said, "What shall I give you?" Jacob said, "You needn't give me anything. If you'll do this one thing for me, I'll go back to pasturing your flock and keeping it."
"Let me pass through your whole flock today and take out every speckled and spotted sheep, every dark one among the lambs, and the spotted and speckled among the goats. That will be my wages."
"And my honesty will speak for me later on, when you come to look over my wages: any animal with me that isn't speckled or spotted among the goats, or dark among the lambs, is stolen."
And Laban said, "Good. Let it be as you say."

But that same day he removed the striped and spotted male goats and all the speckled and spotted female goats — every one with white on it — and every dark one among the lambs, and handed them over to his sons.
And he put three days' journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob pastured the rest of Laban's flock.
Then Jacob took fresh rods of poplar, almond and plane, and peeled white strips into them, baring the white wood on the rods.
And he set the rods he had peeled in the troughs, in the watering channels where the flock came to drink, right in front of them; and they went into heat when they came to drink.
The flock went into heat at the rods, and the flock bore striped, speckled and spotted young.
And Jacob separated the lambs, and he set the flock facing the striped ones and every dark one in Laban's flock. He made flocks of his own, kept apart, and he didn't put them with Laban's flock.
And whenever the sturdy ones in the flock went into heat, Jacob would set the rods in front of them in the troughs, so they'd mate at the rods.
But when the flock were feeble he wouldn't set them out; so the feeble ones went to Laban, and the sturdy ones to Jacob.
So the man increased greatly, and he came to have large flocks, maidservants and menservants, camels and donkeys.

genesis_31.t: Now he heard what Laban's sons were saying: "Jacob has taken everything our father had, and out of what was our father's he has made all this wealth."
And Jacob saw Laban's face, and it wasn't toward him as it had been before.
And the LORD said to Jacob, "Go back to the land of your fathers, to your kindred, and I'll be with you."
So Jacob sent and called Rachel and Leah out to the open country, to his flock.
He said to them, "I can see your father's face — it isn't toward me as it was before. But the God of my father has been with me."
"And you know yourselves that I've served your father with all my strength."
"And your father has made a fool of me and changed my wages ten times, but God didn't let him do me harm."
"If he said, 'The speckled will be your wages,' then the whole flock bore speckled; and if he said, 'The striped will be your wages,' then the whole flock bore striped."
"So God took away your father's livestock and gave it to me."
"And at the time the flock went into heat, I lifted my eyes and saw in a dream: the he-goats mounting the flock were striped, speckled and mottled."
"And the angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob,' and I said, 'Here I am.'"
"And he said, 'Look up and see: all the he-goats mounting the flock are striped, speckled and mottled. I have seen everything Laban is doing to you.'"
"'I am the God of Beth-el, where you anointed a pillar and made your vow to me. Now get up, leave this land, and go back to the land of your kindred.'"
Then Rachel and Leah answered him, "Do we still have any share or inheritance in our father's house?"
"Doesn't he treat us as foreign women? He has sold us, and he has consumed our money completely."
"All the wealth God has taken away from our father is ours and our children's. So now — do whatever God has told you."
Then Jacob got up and lifted his children and his wives onto the camels,
and he drove off all his livestock and all the goods he'd accumulated — the livestock he had acquired in Paddan-aram — to come to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.
Now Laban had gone to shear his flock, and Rachel stole the teraphim, her father's household gods.
And Jacob stole the heart of Laban the Aramean by not telling him he was running.
So he fled with everything he had. He got up, crossed the River, and set his face toward the hill country of Gilead.
On the third day Laban was told that Jacob had fled.
So he took his kinsmen with him and pursued him for seven days' journey, and he caught up with him in the hill country of Gilead.
But God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream that night and said to him, "Take care: do not speak with Jacob, from good to bad."
So Laban overtook Jacob. Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban pitched camp with his kinsmen in the hill country of Gilead.
And Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done? You stole my heart and led away my daughters like captives taken by the sword."
"Why did you hide in order to run, and steal away from me, and not tell me? I'd have sent you off with gladness and songs, with tambourine and lyre."
"And you didn't let me kiss my sons and my daughters. You've acted foolishly in doing this."
"I have it in my power to do you harm, but the God of your father spoke to me last night: 'Take care not to speak with Jacob, from good to bad.'"
"And now you've gone — of course you have, since you longed for your father's house. But why did you steal my gods?"
Jacob answered Laban, "Because I was afraid. I thought you'd tear your daughters away from me."
"Whoever you find your gods with shall not live. In front of our kinsmen, point out what of yours is with me, and take it." Now Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.
So Laban went into Jacob's tent, into Leah's tent, and into the tent of the two maidservants, and he didn't find them. Then he came out of Leah's tent and went into Rachel's tent.
Now Rachel had taken the teraphim, put them in the camel's saddlebag, and sat on them; and Laban felt all through the tent and didn't find them.
And she said to her father, "Don't be angry, my lord, that I can't rise before you — the way of women is upon me." And he searched and didn't find the teraphim.
Then Jacob was angry and quarrelled with Laban. "What is my transgression?" he said. "What is my sin, that you've pursued me so hotly?"
"You've felt through everything I own — what have you found of all your household goods? Put it here in front of my kinsmen and yours, and let them decide between us."
"Twenty years I've been with you. Your ewes and your she-goats haven't miscarried, and I've never eaten the rams of your flock."
"I never brought you an animal killed by beasts; I bore that loss myself. You required it from my hand, whether it was stolen by day or by night."
"This is how it was for me: by day the heat consumed me, by night the frost, and sleep fled from my eyes."
"That's twenty years I've had in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times."

"If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been for me, you'd have sent me away empty-handed. God has seen my affliction and the labour of my hands, and last night he gave his decision."

Laban answered Jacob, "The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flock is my flock — everything you see is mine. But as for my daughters, what can I do for them today, or for the children they've borne?"
"So now — come, let's cut a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between us."
So Jacob took a stone and raised it up as a pillar.
And Jacob said to his kinsmen, "Gather stones." So they took stones and made a heap, and they ate there by the heap.
And Laban called it Yegar Sahadutha, and Jacob called it Galeed.
And Laban said, "This heap is a witness between me and you today." That is why its name was called Galeed —
and Mizpah, because he said, "May the LORD keep watch between me and you when we are out of each other's sight,"
"if you mistreat my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters — no one is here with us — look, God is witness between me and you."
And Laban said to Jacob, "Look at this heap, and look at the pillar I have set up between me and you."
"This heap is a witness and the pillar is a witness: I will not pass beyond this heap to you, and you will not pass beyond this heap and this pillar to me, to do harm."
"The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor — may they judge between us, the God of their father." And Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
Then Jacob offered a sacrifice in the hill country and called his kinsmen to eat bread. They ate bread and stayed the night in the hill country.
Early in the morning Laban rose and kissed his sons and his daughters and blessed them. Then Laban went back to his place.

genesis_32.t: Jacob went on his way, and God's angels met him.
When Jacob saw them he said, 'This is God's camp.' So he called the place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau, in the land of Seir, the country of Edom.
He gave them their orders: 'Say this to my lord Esau: Your servant Jacob says, I've been living with Laban all this time, right up to now.'
I've come to own oxen and donkeys, flocks, and servants, men and women. I'm sending word to my lord so I can find favour with you.
The messengers came back to Jacob and said, 'We went to your brother Esau. He's on his way to meet you now, and there are four hundred men with him.'
Jacob was badly frightened, and it pressed on him. He split the people with him, and the flocks and herds and camels, into two camps.
He thought, 'If Esau comes at the one camp and attacks it, the other camp can still get away.'
Then Jacob prayed, 'God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac — LORD, you told me, "Go back to your land and your kindred, and I will do you good."'
'I'm not worth the least of the loyalty and faithfulness you've shown your servant. I crossed this Jordan with nothing but my staff, and now I've become two camps.
'Please rescue me from my brother, from Esau. I'm afraid of him — that he'll come and strike us down, mothers along with children.
'And you said it yourself: "I will do you good, and I'll make your offspring like the sand of the sea — too many to count."'
He spent that night there, and out of what he'd come to own he picked out a gift for his brother Esau.
two hundred she-goats and twenty he-goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty nursing camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten young ones.
He handed them over to his servants, each drove on its own, and told them, 'Go on ahead of me, and leave a gap between the droves.'
He told the first one, 'When my brother Esau meets you and asks, "Who do you belong to? Where are you going? And whose are these up ahead?" —
then say, "They belong to your servant Jacob. It's a gift sent to my lord Esau, and he's right behind us."'
He gave the same orders to the second and the third and to everyone following the droves: 'Say the same thing to Esau when you find him;
'and say, "Your servant Jacob is right behind us."' He was thinking, 'I'll cover his face with the gift going on ahead of me, and afterwards I'll see his face. Maybe he'll accept me.'
So the gift went on ahead of him, and he spent that night in the camp.
That night he got up, took his two wives, his two maidservants and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them and sent them across the stream, and sent everything he had across as well.
Jacob was left by himself, and a man wrestled with him until dawn came up.
When he saw that he couldn't overpower him, he touched the socket of Jacob's thigh, and it was thrown out of joint as they wrestled.
Then he said, 'Let me go — dawn is up.' But Jacob said, 'I won't let you go unless you bless me.'
He said to him, 'What is your name?' He answered, 'Jacob.'
Then he said, 'Your name won't be Jacob any longer, but Israel — because you've struggled with God and with men, and you've come through.'
Then Jacob asked, 'Tell me your name.' But he said, 'Why do you ask my name?' And he blessed him there.
So Jacob called the place Peniel: 'I have seen God face to face, and my life has been spared.'
The sun came up on him as he passed Penuel, and he was limping from his thigh.
That is why to this day the people of Israel do not eat the hip sinew that lies on the socket of the thigh — because he touched the socket of Jacob's thigh at that sinew.

genesis_33.t: Jacob looked up and there was Esau coming, four hundred men with him. He divided the children among Leah, Rachel and the two maidservants.
He put the maidservants and their children in front, Leah and her children after them, and Rachel and Joseph last.
He went on ahead of them himself and bowed to the ground seven times as he came near his brother.
But Esau ran to meet him. He threw his arms around him, fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept.
Then he looked up and saw the women and the children and asked, 'Who are these with you?' Jacob said, 'The children God has graciously given your servant.'
The maidservants came up with their children and bowed down.
Then Leah came up with her children and they bowed down, and after that Joseph came up, and Rachel, and they bowed down.
Then Esau said, 'What was all that company I met?' Jacob said, 'To find favour with my lord.'
But Esau said, 'I have plenty, my brother. Keep what's yours.'
Jacob said, 'No, please. If I have found favour with you, take my gift from my hand. Seeing your face has been like seeing the face of God, and you have received me.'
'Please take my blessing, the one brought to you — God has been good to me, and I have everything.' He kept pressing him, and Esau took it.
Then Esau said, 'Let's set out and go, and I'll travel alongside you.'
But Jacob said, 'My lord knows the children are young, and the flocks and herds in my care are nursing. If they're driven hard for even one day, the whole flock will die.'
'Let my lord go on ahead of his servant. I'll come slowly, at the pace of the livestock ahead of me and the pace of the children, until I reach my lord at Seir.'
Esau said, 'Then let me leave some of my people with you.' But Jacob said, 'Why do that? Let me just find favour with my lord.'
So Esau went back that same day, on his way to Seir.
But Jacob set out for Succoth. He built himself a house and made shelters for his livestock, and that is why he called the place Succoth.
Jacob arrived safely at the city of Shechem, in the land of Canaan, coming from Paddan Aram, and he camped in front of the city.
He bought the piece of ground where he had pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, for a hundred pieces of money.
There he set up an altar, and he named it El-Elohe-Israel — God, the God of Israel.

genesis_34.t: Dinah, Leah's daughter, whom she had borne to Jacob, went out to see the women of the land.
Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the chief of that land, saw her. He took her, lay with her and forced her.
He became attached to Dinah, Jacob's daughter. He loved the girl, and he spoke to her heart.
Shechem said to his father Hamor, 'Get me this girl for a wife.'
Jacob heard that he had defiled his daughter Dinah, but his sons were out in the field with his livestock, so Jacob said nothing until they came in.
Then Hamor, Shechem's father, went out to speak with Jacob.
Jacob's sons came in from the field when they heard. They were grieved and they burned with anger, because he had done an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter. Such a thing is not done.
Hamor spoke with them: 'My son Shechem has set his heart on your daughter. Please give her to him for a wife.
'Intermarry with us. Give us your daughters, and take our daughters for yourselves.
'Live with us. The land will be open to you — live in it, trade in it, acquire property in it.'
Then Shechem said to her father and her brothers, 'Let me find favour with you. Whatever you tell me, I will give.
'Set the bride-price and the gift as high as you like — I'll pay whatever you say. Only give me the girl for a wife.'
But Jacob's sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor with deceit when they spoke, because he had defiled their sister Dinah.
They said to them, 'We can't do this — give our sister to a man who has a foreskin. It would be a reproach to us.
'We'll agree to you on one condition only: that you become like us, with every male among you circumcised.
'Then we'll give you our daughters and take your daughters for ourselves. We'll live with you and become one people.
'But if you won't listen to us and be circumcised, we'll take our daughter and go.'
Their words seemed good to Hamor and to Shechem son of Hamor.
The young man lost no time doing it, because he delighted in Jacob's daughter — and he was the most honoured in his father's whole household.
So Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of their city and spoke to the men of the city:
'These men are at peace with us. Let them live in the land and trade in it — there's room enough for them on all sides. We'll take their daughters as wives for ourselves, and give them ours.
'They'll agree to live with us and become one people on one condition only: that every male among us be circumcised, just as they are.
'Won't their livestock and their property and all their animals become ours? Only let us agree with them, and they'll live with us.'
Everyone who went out of the gate of his city listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised — everyone who went out of the gate of that city.
On the third day, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob's sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, each took his sword. They came on the city unopposed and killed every male.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword, took Dinah out of Shechem's house and left.
Jacob's sons came on the dead and plundered the city, because there their sister had been defiled.
They took their flocks, their herds and their donkeys, and whatever was in the city and in the field.
All their wealth, all their children and their wives they carried off, and they plundered everything in the houses.

Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, 'You have brought trouble on me — you've made me a stench to the people of this land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I have few men. They'll band together against me and attack me, and I'll be destroyed, I and my household.'
But they said, 'Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?'

genesis_35.t: God said to Jacob, 'Get up, go to Bethel and settle there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you were running from your brother Esau.'
So Jacob said to his household and everyone with him, 'Get rid of the foreign gods you have among you. Cleanse yourselves and change your clothes.
'Let's get up and go to Bethel. I'll make an altar there to the God who answered me in the day of my distress and has been with me everywhere I've gone.'
They handed Jacob all the foreign gods they had and the rings from their ears, and Jacob buried them under the terebinth near Shechem.
Then they set out, and the terror of God fell on the cities around them, so no one pursued Jacob's sons.
So Jacob came to Luz, in the land of Canaan — that is, Bethel — he and everyone with him.
He built an altar there and called the place El-bethel, because that was where God revealed himself to him when he was running from his brother.
Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died and was buried below Bethel under the oak. They called it Allon Bacuth.
God appeared to Jacob again when he came from Paddan Aram, and blessed him.
God said to him, 'Your name is Jacob. You will not be called Jacob any longer — Israel will be your name.' So he named him Israel.
God said to him, 'I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation, a whole assembly of nations, will come from you, and kings will come from your own body.
'The land I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and to your offspring after you I will give the land.'
Then God went up from him, at the place where he had spoken with him.
Jacob set up a pillar at the place where he had spoken with him — a pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it, and poured oil on it.
And Jacob named the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
They set out from Bethel, and while there was still some way to go to Ephrath, Rachel went into labour, and it went hard for her.
And when her labour was at its hardest, the midwife said to her, 'Don't be afraid — this one is a son for you too.'
And as her life was leaving her — for she died — she named him Ben-oni; but his father called him Benjamin.
So Rachel died, and she was buried on the road to Ephrath — that is, Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar over her grave. That is the pillar of Rachel's grave to this day.
Israel set out and pitched his tent beyond Migdal Eder.
While Israel was living in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard of it. — Jacob had twelve sons.
Leah's sons: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, then Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun.
Rachel's sons: Joseph and Benjamin.
Bilhah's sons — Rachel's maidservant — Dan and Naphtali.
Zilpah's sons — Leah's maidservant — Gad and Asher. These are Jacob's sons, born to him in Paddan Aram.
Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, Kiriath-arba — that is, Hebron — where Abraham and Isaac had lived as aliens.
Isaac lived a hundred and eighty years.
Isaac breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days, and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.

genesis_36.t: These are the generations of Esau — that is, Edom.
Esau took his wives from among the women of Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite; Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon the Hivite;
and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.
Adah bore Eliphaz to Esau, and Basemath bore Reuel.
Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam and Korah. These are Esau's sons, born to him in the land of Canaan.

Esau took his wives, his sons and daughters, everyone in his household, his livestock, all his animals and everything he had accumulated in the land of Canaan, and he went to a land away from his brother Jacob.
They had too much property to live together, and the land where they were living as aliens could not support them, because of their livestock.
So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.
These are the generations of Esau, the father of Edom, in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz, son of Esau's wife Adah, and Reuel, son of Esau's wife Basemath.
Eliphaz's sons were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz.
Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz son of Esau, and she bore him Amalek. These are the sons of Adah, Esau's wife.
These are Reuel's sons: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. These were the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife.
These were the sons of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: she bore Esau Jeush, Jalam and Korah.
These are the chiefs among Esau's sons. From the sons of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn: chief Teman, chief Omar, chief Zepho, chief Kenaz,
chief Korah, chief Gatam, chief Amalek. These are the chiefs from Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Adah.
These are the sons of Reuel son of Esau: chief Nahath, chief Zerah, chief Shammah, chief Mizzah. These are the chiefs from Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife.
These are the sons of Oholibamah, Esau's wife: chief Jeush, chief Jalam, chief Korah. These are the chiefs from Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, Esau's wife.
These are Esau's sons, and these are their chiefs. That is Edom.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who lived in the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
and Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. These are the Horite chiefs, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom.
Lotan's sons were Hori and Hemam, and Lotan's sister was Timna.
These are Shobal's sons: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam.
These are Zibeon's sons: Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness while he was pasturing his father Zibeon's donkeys.
These are Anah's children: Dishon, and Oholibamah, Anah's daughter.
These are Dishan's sons: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran and Keran.
These are Ezer's sons: Bilhan, Zaavan and Akan.
These are Dishan's sons: Uz and Aran.
These are the Horite chiefs: chief Lotan, chief Shobal, chief Zibeon, chief Anah,
chief Dishon, chief Ezer, chief Dishan. These are the Horite chiefs, chief by chief, in the land of Seir.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the people of Israel.
Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom, and his city was called Dinhabah.
Bela died, and Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.
Jobab died, and Husham from the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.
Husham died, and Hadad son of Bedad reigned in his place. He defeated Midian in the country of Moab, and his city was called Avith.
Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.
Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the River reigned in his place.
Shaul died, and Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place.
Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place. His city was called Pau, and his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Me-zahab.
These are the names of Esau's chiefs, by clan and by place, name by name: chief Timna, chief Alvah, chief Jetheth,
chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon,
chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar,
chief Magdiel, chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, by their dwelling places in the land they possessed. That is Esau, the father of Edom.

genesis_37.t: Jacob settled in the land where his father had lived as an alien, the land of Canaan.

These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph was seventeen, shepherding the flock with his brothers — he was still a youth — with the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph brought their father a bad report about them.
Israel loved Joseph more than all his other sons, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a long tunic.
When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they hated him, and they could not say a peaceable word to him.
Joseph had a dream and told his brothers about it, and they hated him all the more.
He said to them, 'Listen to this dream I had.'
'We were binding sheaves out in the field, and my sheaf stood up — it stood upright — and your sheaves gathered round and bowed down to my sheaf.'
His brothers said to him, 'So you're going to reign over us? You're going to rule us?' And they hated him all the more, for his dreams and for what he said.
Then he had another dream and told it to his brothers. 'I've had another dream,' he said. 'The sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me.'
He told it to his father and his brothers, and his father rebuked him: 'What is this dream you've had? Are we really to come — I and your mother and your brothers — and bow to the ground to you?'
His brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind.
His brothers went off to pasture their father's flock at Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, 'Your brothers are pasturing at Shechem, aren't they? Come — I'll send you to them.' He answered, 'Here I am.'
He said, 'Go and see whether it's well with your brothers and well with the flock, and bring me back word.' So he sent him from the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
A man found him wandering in the open country and asked him, 'What are you looking for?'
He said, 'I'm looking for my brothers. Tell me where they're pasturing.'
The man said, 'They've moved on. I heard them say, "Let's go to Dothan."' So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
They saw him from a distance, and before he reached them they plotted against him, to kill him.
They said to each other, 'Here comes the dream-master.'
'Come on, let's kill him and throw him into one of the pits, and say a wild animal ate him. Then we'll see what becomes of his dreams.'
But Reuben heard, and he rescued him from their hand. 'Let's not take his life,' he said.
Reuben said to them, 'Don't shed blood. Throw him into this pit out in the wilderness, but don't lay a hand on him' — so that he could rescue him from them and take him back to his father.
When Joseph reached his brothers, they stripped him of his tunic — the long tunic he was wearing —
and they took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty — there was no water in it.
Then they sat down to eat. They looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, camels loaded with gum, balm and ladanum, on their way down to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, 'What do we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood?
'Come on, let's sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him ourselves. He is our brother, our own flesh.' And his brothers listened to him.
Then some Midianite traders passed by. They drew Joseph up out of the pit and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and they took Joseph to Egypt.
When Reuben came back to the pit and Joseph was not in it, he tore his clothes.
He went back to his brothers and said, 'The boy is gone. And I — where do I go now?'
They took Joseph's tunic, killed a male goat and dipped the tunic in the blood.
They sent the long tunic and brought it to their father and said, 'We found this. Look at it — is it your son's tunic or not?'
He recognised it and said, 'It's my son's tunic. A wild animal has eaten him. Joseph has been torn to pieces.'
Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth round his waist and mourned for his son for many days.
All his sons and all his daughters got up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. 'I will go down to my son, mourning, to Sheol,' he said. And his father wept for him.
Meanwhile the Medanites sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, one of Pharaoh's officials, the commander of the guard.

genesis_38.t: At that time Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to an Adullamite named Hirah.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite named Shua. He took her, and he went in to her.
She conceived and bore a son, and he named him Er.
She conceived again and bore a son, and she named him Onan.
She had one more son and named him Shelah. He was at Kezib when she bore him.
Judah got a wife for Er his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.
But Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.
Then Judah said to Onan, 'Go in to your brother's wife and do the brother-in-law's duty for her, and raise up offspring for your brother.'
But Onan knew the offspring would not count as his, so whenever he went in to his brother's wife he spilled it on the ground, so as not to give his brother offspring.
What he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD, and he put him to death too.

Then Judah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law, 'Stay a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up' — because he thought, 'He may die too, like his brothers.' So Tamar went and lived in her father's house.
After a long while Judah's wife, the daughter of Shua, died. When Judah had been comforted, he went up to his sheepshearers at Timnah, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
Tamar was told, 'Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.'

So she took off her widow's clothes, covered herself with a veil and wrapped herself up, and sat at the entrance of Enaim, on the road to Timnah — because she had seen that Shelah had grown up and she had not been given to him as a wife.
When Judah saw her, he took her for a prostitute, because she had covered her face.
He turned aside to her by the road and said, 'Come now, let me go in to you' — he did not know she was his daughter-in-law. She said, 'What will you give me for coming in to me?'
He said, 'I'll send you a young goat from the flock.' She said, 'Only if you give me a pledge until you send it.'
He said, 'What pledge shall I give you?' She said, 'Your seal and your cord and your staff — the one in your hand.' So he gave them to her, went in to her, and she conceived by him.
Then she got up and went away, took off her veil and put her widow's clothes back on.
Judah sent the young goat by his friend the Adullamite to get the pledge back from the woman; but he did not find her.
He asked the local men, 'Where is the shrine prostitute who was at Enaim, by the road?' They said, 'There has been no shrine prostitute here.'
So he went back to Judah and said, 'I couldn't find her. And the men of the place said, "There has been no shrine prostitute here."'
Judah said, 'Let her keep them, or we'll be made a laughing-stock. Look — I sent this young goat, and you didn't find her.'
About three months later Judah was told, 'Tamar your daughter-in-law has acted as a prostitute, and she is pregnant by it.' Judah said, 'Bring her out and let her be burned.'
As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law: 'I am pregnant by the man these belong to.' And she said, 'Look at them — whose are these, the seal, the cord and the staff?'
Judah recognised them and said, 'She is more in the right than I am — I did not give her to my son Shelah.' And he did not know her again.
When the time came for her to give birth, there were twins in her womb.
And as she gave birth, one of them put out a hand. The midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it on his hand, saying, 'This one came out first.'
But as he drew his hand back, his brother came out. She said, 'How you have broken out — a breach upon you!' So he was named Perez.
Afterwards his brother came out, the one with the scarlet thread on his hand, and he was named Zerah.

genesis_39.t: Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, one of Pharaoh's officials, the commander of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there.
The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, there in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master saw that the LORD was with him, and that the LORD made everything he did succeed in his hand.
So Joseph found favour with him and served him. He put him in charge of his household and gave everything he had into his hand.

From the time he put him in charge of his household and everything he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house because of Joseph. The blessing of the LORD was on everything he had, in the house and in the field.
So he left everything he had in Joseph's hand, and with Joseph there he gave no thought to anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and handsome to look at.
After this, his master's wife looked at Joseph and said, 'Lie with me.'
But he refused. He said to his master's wife, 'Look — with me here my master gives no thought to what is in the house, and everything he has he has put into my hand.
'He is no greater in this house than I am, and he has withheld nothing from me except you, since you are his wife. How could I do this great evil, and sin against God?'
And though she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her — would not lie beside her, would not be with her.
One such day he came into the house to do his work, and none of the household men were there in the house.
She caught hold of his clothing and said, 'Lie with me.' But he left the clothing in her hand and fled, and went outside.
When she saw that he had left the clothing in her hand and had fled outside,
she called out to the men of her household: 'See — he has brought us a Hebrew man to mock us. He came to me to lie with me, and I called out with a loud voice.
'And when he heard me raise my voice and call out, he left the clothing beside me and fled, and went outside.'
She kept the clothing beside her until his master came home.
Then she spoke to him in the same words: 'The Hebrew servant you brought us came in to me to mock me.
'And when I raised my voice and called out, he left the clothing beside me and fled outside.'
When his master heard his wife's words — 'This is what your servant did to me' — his anger burned.
So Joseph's master took him and put him in the prison house, the place where the king's prisoners were held; and there he stayed, in the prison house.
But the LORD was with Joseph. He extended steadfast love to him and gave him favour with the commander of the prison house.
The commander of the prison house put all the prisoners in the prison into Joseph's hand, and whatever was done there, he was the one who did it.
The commander of the prison house looked into nothing at all that was in Joseph's hand, because the LORD was with him, and whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed.

genesis_40.t: Later on, the king of Egypt's cupbearer and his baker did something to offend their master.
Pharaoh was furious with two of his officials — the head cupbearer and the head baker.
He had them locked up in the house of the commander of the guard — the prison where Joseph was being held.
The commander of the guard put Joseph in charge of them, and he looked after them. They were in custody a good while.
The same night, both of them had a dream — each his own dream, and each dream meaning something different. This was the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, the two being held in the prison.
When Joseph came in the next morning, he could see they were upset.
So he asked Pharaoh's officials, who were in custody with him in his master's house, "Why the long faces today?"
They told him, "We've had dreams, and there's nobody to interpret them." Joseph said, "Doesn't interpretation belong to God? Tell me about them."
So the head cupbearer told Joseph his dream. "In my dream," he said, "there was a vine right in front of me,
and on the vine were three branches. It budded, the blossom came out, and the clusters ripened into grapes.
Pharaoh's cup was in my hand. I took the grapes, squeezed them into the cup, and put the cup in Pharaoh's hand.
Joseph told him, "Here's what it means. The three branches are three days."
Three days from now Pharaoh will lift up your head and put you back in your post, and you'll be handing him his cup the way you used to when you were his cupbearer.
Just remember me when things go well for you. Do me this kindness: mention me to Pharaoh and get me out of this place.
I was stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, and I've done nothing here either — nothing that should have landed me in this pit.
When the head baker saw the interpretation was a good one, he said to Joseph, "I had a dream too. There were three baskets of ḥori on my head,
and in the top basket was every kind of baked food for Pharaoh — and birds were eating it right out of the basket on my head."
Joseph answered, "Here's what it means. The three baskets are three days."
Three days from now Pharaoh will lift up your head — right off you — and hang you on a tree, and the birds will eat the flesh off you.
Three days later it was Pharaoh's birthday, and he threw a feast for all his servants. There, in front of them, he lifted up the head of the head cupbearer and the head of the head baker.
He put the head cupbearer back in his post, and the man placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand.
But the head baker he hanged, exactly as Joseph had told them.
But the head cupbearer didn't remember Joseph. He forgot him.

genesis_41.t: Two full years later, Pharaoh had a dream. He was standing by the Nile,
and out of the Nile came seven cows, sleek and fat, and they grazed in the reeds.
Then seven more cows came up out of the Nile behind them, ugly and gaunt, and stood next to the first cows on the bank.
And the ugly, gaunt cows ate up the seven sleek, fat ones. Then Pharaoh woke up.
He fell back asleep and dreamed again. Seven ears of grain were coming up on one stalk, plump and good.
Then seven thin ears, scorched by the east wind, sprang up after them.
And the thin ears swallowed up the seven plump, full ones. Then Pharaoh woke up — and it had been a dream.
In the morning he was deeply troubled, so he sent for all the ḥarṭummim of Egypt and all its wise men. Pharaoh told them his dream, but none of them could interpret it for him.
Then the head cupbearer spoke up to Pharaoh. "Today I have to bring up my own failings.
Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put me in custody in the commander of the guard's house — me and the head baker.
We both had a dream the same night, and each dream meant something different.
There was a young Hebrew with us, a slave belonging to the commander of the guard. We told him, and he interpreted our dreams for us, each one according to its own dream.
And it turned out exactly as he interpreted: I got my post back, and he was hanged.
So Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and they rushed him out of the pit. He shaved, changed his clothes, and came in to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I've had a dream, and there's no one to interpret it. But I've heard it said of you that you only have to hear a dream and you can interpret it."
Joseph answered Pharaoh, "It isn't in me. God is the one who will answer, for Pharaoh's good."
So Pharaoh told him, "In my dream I was standing on the bank of the Nile,
and out of the Nile came seven cows, fat and well-formed, and they grazed in the reeds.
Then seven more cows came up after them, weak and misshapen and lean. I've never seen anything so bad in all the land of Egypt.
And the lean, ugly cows ate the seven fat ones that came first.
They went right inside them, but you couldn't tell they had — they looked just as bad as before. Then I woke up.
Then in my dream I saw seven ears of grain coming up on one stalk, full and good.
Then seven more ears sprang up after them, ṣenumot, thin, scorched by the east wind.
And the thin ears swallowed the seven good ones. I told all this to the ḥarṭummim, but none of them could tell me what it meant."
Joseph said to Pharaoh, "Pharaoh's dream is one dream. God has told Pharaoh what he's about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years. It's one dream.
And the seven lean, ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, and so are the seven empty ears scorched by the east wind. They will be seven years of famine.
This is what I meant when I told Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what he's about to do.
Seven years are coming, and there'll be great plenty all through the land of Egypt.
Then seven years of famine will come after them. All the plenty in Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will consume the land.
No one will remember the plenty in the land, because of the famine that follows — it will be that severe.
And the reason the dream came to Pharaoh twice is that the matter is settled with God, and God is moving quickly to do it.
So now Pharaoh should look for a discerning, wise man and put him in charge of the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh should act. He should appoint officers over the land and take a fifth of what Egypt produces during the seven years of plenty.
Let them gather all the food from these good years that are coming and store the grain under Pharaoh's authority, as food in the cities, and let them guard it.
The food will be a reserve for the land through the seven years of famine coming on Egypt, so the land won't be wiped out by the famine.
Pharaoh liked the plan, and so did all his servants.
Pharaoh said to his servants, "Could we find another man like this, one who has the spirit of God in him?"
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has made all this known to you, there's no one as discerning and wise as you are.
You will be over my house, and all my people will take their orders from your mouth. Only the throne makes me greater than you."
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Look — I have set you over the whole land of Egypt."
Pharaoh took the signet ring off his own hand and put it on Joseph's, dressed him in fine linen, and put the gold chain around his neck.
He had Joseph ride in his second chariot, with men calling out ahead of him, "Abrek!" That is how he set him over all the land of Egypt.
And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh — and without your word no one in all Egypt will lift a hand or a foot."
Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah, and gave him Asenath, daughter of Poti-phera, the priest of On, as his wife. And Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt. He left Pharaoh's presence and travelled through the whole land of Egypt.
During the seven years of plenty the land produced by the handful.
He gathered all the food of the seven years that came to the land of Egypt and stored it in the cities. The food from the fields around each city he stored inside that city.
Joseph piled up grain like sand on the seashore — so much that he stopped keeping count, because it was past counting.
Two sons were born to Joseph before the year of famine came. Asenath, daughter of Poti-phera the priest of On, bore them to him.
Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh — "because God has made me forget all my hardship, and my father's whole household."
The second he named Ephraim — "because God has made me fruitful in the land where I was afflicted."
Then the seven years of plenty in Egypt came to an end.
And the seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in every land, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
When the whole land of Egypt grew hungry, the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh told all Egypt, "Go to Joseph. Whatever he tells you, do it."
The famine covered the whole land. Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to Egypt, and the famine grew worse there.
And people from every land came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine was severe everywhere.

genesis_42.t: When Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why are you all standing there looking at each other?"
He said, "I've heard there's grain in Egypt. Go down and buy some for us, so we can live instead of dying."
So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain in Egypt.
But Jacob didn't send Benjamin, Joseph's brother, along with them. He said, "Something might happen to him."
So Israel's sons came to buy grain along with everyone else who was coming, because the famine had reached the land of Canaan.
Now Joseph was the ruler of the land, the one who sold grain to all its people. His brothers came and bowed down to him, faces to the ground.
Joseph saw his brothers and recognised them, but he made himself a stranger to them and spoke harshly. "Where have you come from?" he said. "From the land of Canaan," they said, "to buy food."
Joseph recognised his brothers, but they did not recognise him.
Then Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed about them, and he said, "You're spies. You've come to see where the land lies open."
They said, "No, my lord. Your servants have come to buy food."
"We're all sons of one man. We're honest men. Your servants have never been spies."
But he said, "No. You came to see where the land lies open."
They said, "Your servants are twelve brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is with our father right now, and one of us is gone."
Joseph said, "It's exactly what I told you. You are spies."
"Here is how you'll be tested. By the life of Pharaoh, you're not leaving this place unless your youngest brother comes here."

"Send one of you to fetch your brother. The rest of you stay locked up, and your words will be tested — we'll see whether the truth is with you. And if not, then by the life of Pharaoh, you're spies."
And he put them all in custody for three days.
On the third day Joseph said to them, "Do this and you'll live. I fear God."
"If you're honest men, let one of your brothers be held where you're being kept, and the rest of you go and take grain for your starving households,
"and bring your youngest brother to me. Then your words will be confirmed, and you won't die." And they agreed to it.
They said to each other, "We really are guilty about our brother. We saw how distressed he was when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen. That's why this distress has come on us."
Reuben answered, "Didn't I tell you not to sin against the boy? You wouldn't listen. And now his blood is being called to account."
They didn't know Joseph could understand them, because there had been an interpreter between them.
He turned away from them and wept. Then he came back, spoke to them, and took Simeon from among them and had him bound in front of them.
Then Joseph gave orders: fill their containers with grain, put each man's silver back in his sack, and give them provisions for the road. And that was done for them.
They loaded their grain on their donkeys and set off.
At the place they stopped for the night, one of them opened his sack to feed his donkey, and there was his silver, sitting in the mouth of the bag.
He said to his brothers, "My silver's been put back — look, here it is in my bag!" Their hearts sank, and they turned to each other shaking. "What is this that God has done to us?"
They came back to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan and told him everything that had happened:
"The man who is lord of that land spoke harshly to us and treated us like spies scouting out the land.
"We told him, 'We're honest men. We've never been spies.
"'We're twelve brothers, sons of one father. One of us is gone, and the youngest is with our father right now in Canaan.'
"And the man who is lord of the land said to us, 'This is how I'll know you're honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, take grain for your starving households, and go.
"'And bring your youngest brother to me, and I'll know you're not spies but honest men. Then I'll give your brother back, and you can trade in the land.'"
Then, as they emptied their sacks, there was each man's bundle of silver in his own sack. When they and their father saw the bundles of silver, they were afraid.
Their father Jacob said to them, "You're taking my children from me. Joseph is gone, Simeon is gone, and now you'd take Benjamin. It has all come down on me."
Then Reuben said to his father, "You can put my two sons to death if I don't bring him back to you. Put him in my hands, and I'll bring him back."
But he said, "My son is not going down with you. His brother is dead and he's the only one left. If harm comes to him on the road you're taking, you'll bring my grey head down in sorrow to Sheol."

genesis_43.t: The famine was severe in the land.
When they had eaten up the grain they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them, "Go back and buy us a little food."
But Judah said to him, "The man gave us a solemn warning: 'You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.'
"If you'll send our brother with us, we'll go down and buy food for you.
"But if you won't send him, we're not going down, because the man told us, 'You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.'"
Israel said, "Why did you do this to me — telling the man you had another brother?"

They said, "The man kept questioning us about ourselves and our family — 'Is your father still alive? Do you have a brother?' We just answered his questions. How could we have known he'd say, 'Bring your brother down'?"
Then Judah said to his father Israel, "Send the boy with me and we'll get up and go, so we can live instead of dying — us, and you, and our children.
"I'll stand surety for him myself. Hold me answerable. If I don't bring him back to you and set him in front of you, then the guilt is mine for the rest of my life.
"If we hadn't held back, we could have been there and back twice by now."

Then their father Israel said, "If it has to be, then do this: take some of the land's best products in your containers and carry a gift down to the man — a little balm and a little honey, gum and myrrh, pistachios and almonds.
"Take double the silver with you, and take back the silver that was returned in the mouths of your sacks. Maybe it was a mistake.
"Take your brother too. Get up and go back to the man.
"And may God Almighty give you compassion in front of the man, so he sends back your other brother, and Benjamin too. As for me — if I'm bereaved, I'm bereaved."
So the men took the gift, took double the silver with them, and took Benjamin. They set out, went down to Egypt, and stood before Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to his household steward, "Bring these men inside. Slaughter an animal and prepare it — they'll be eating with me at noon."
The man did as Joseph said and brought them into Joseph's house.

The men were afraid at being brought into Joseph's house. They said, "It's because of the silver that was put back in our sacks the first time. We're being brought in so he can fall on us and overpower us and make slaves of us — and take our donkeys."
So they went up to the steward of Joseph's house and spoke to him at the doorway.
They said, "Please, my lord — we did come down the first time to buy food.
"When we got to the place we stayed and opened our sacks, there was each man's silver in the mouth of his sack — our silver, the full weight of it. We've brought it back with us.
"And we've brought more silver with us to buy food. We don't know who put our silver in our sacks."
He said, "Peace to you. Don't be afraid. Your God, the God of your father, gave you treasure in your sacks. Your silver reached me." And he brought Simeon out to them.
The man brought them into Joseph's house, gave them water to wash their feet, and gave their donkeys fodder.
They got the gift ready for when Joseph came at noon, since they'd heard they would be eating there.
When Joseph came into the house, they brought in the gift they had with them and bowed down to the ground before him.
He asked how they were, and said, "Is your old father well, the one you told me about? Is he still alive?"
They said, "Your servant our father is well. He's still alive." And they bowed low, down to the ground.
Then he looked up and saw his brother Benjamin, his own mother's son, and he said, "Is this your youngest brother, the one you told me about?" And he said, "God be gracious to you, my son."
Joseph hurried out — feeling for his brother welled up in him and he had to weep. He went into an inner room and wept there.
Then he washed his face and came out. He held himself in check and said, "Serve the meal."
They served him on his own, the brothers on their own, and the Egyptians who ate with him on their own — because Egyptians cannot eat with Hebrews; it is an abomination to them.
They were seated in front of him, the eldest by his birthright down to the youngest by his youth, and they stared at each other in astonishment.
Portions were carried over to them from his table, and Benjamin's portion was five times the size of anyone else's. And they drank and got drunk with him.

genesis_44.t: Then Joseph told his household steward, "Fill the men's sacks with as much food as they can carry, and put each man's silver in the mouth of his sack.
"And put my cup — the silver one — in the mouth of the youngest one's sack, along with his grain money." And he did exactly as Joseph had said.
As soon as it was light, the men were sent on their way with their donkeys.
They had just left the city and were not far off when Joseph said to his steward, "Get up and go after those men. When you catch them, say to them, 'Why have you repaid evil for good?
"'Isn't this the cup my lord drinks from, the one he uses for divination? What you've done is evil.'"
He caught up with them and said all this to them.
They said to him, "Why does my lord say such things? Your servants would never do anything like that!
"Look — the silver we found in the mouths of our sacks, we brought it back to you all the way from Canaan. Why would we steal silver or gold from your master's house?
"Whoever of your servants it's found with, let him die — and the rest of us will be my lord's slaves."
He said, "All right, let it be as you say — except that the one it's found with becomes my slave, and the rest of you go free."
They hurried, each lowering his sack to the ground and opening it.
He searched them, starting with the eldest and finishing with the youngest. And the cup was found in Benjamin's sack.
They tore their clothes, each man loaded his donkey, and they went back to the city.
Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house — he was still there — and they fell to the ground in front of him.
Joseph said to them, "What is this you've done? Didn't you know that a man like me can find things out by divination?"

Judah said, "What can we say to my lord? What can we speak? How can we clear ourselves? God has uncovered your servants' guilt. Here we are — my lord's slaves, all of us, along with the one the cup was found with."
But he said, "Far be it from me. The man the cup was found with will be my slave. The rest of you go up in peace to your father."
Then Judah came up close to him and said, "Please, my lord — let your servant say one word in my lord's hearing, and don't let your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself.
"My lord asked his servants, 'Do you have a father, or a brother?'
"And we said to my lord, 'We have an old father, and a young child born to him in his old age. His brother is dead; he's the only one of his mother left, and his father loves him.'
"And you said to your servants, 'Bring him down to me so I can see him for myself.'
"And we said to my lord, 'The boy can't leave his father. If he leaves him, his father will die.'
"And you said to your servants, 'If your youngest brother doesn't come down with you, you will not see my face again.'
"So when we went up to your servant my father, we told him what my lord had said.
"And our father said, 'Go back and buy us a little food.'
"And we said, 'We can't go down. If our youngest brother comes with us, we'll go — because we can't see the man's face unless our youngest brother is with us.'
"And your servant my father said to us, 'You know my wife bore me two sons.
"'One of them left me, and I said, "He must have been torn to pieces." I haven't seen him since.
"'And if you take this one from me too, and harm comes to him, you'll bring my grey head down to Sheol in grief.'
"So now, if I come back to your servant my father without the boy — and his life is bound up with the boy's —
"then when he sees the boy isn't there, he will die, and your servants will have brought the grey head of your servant our father down to Sheol in sorrow.
"Your servant went surety for the boy with my father. I said, 'If I don't bring him back to you, the guilt is mine before my father for the rest of my life.'
"So now, let your servant stay in the boy's place as my lord's slave, and let the boy go up with his brothers.
"How could I go up to my father without the boy? I could not bear to see what it would do to my father."

genesis_45.t: Then Joseph could not hold himself in any longer in front of everyone standing there, and he cried out, "Get everyone out of here!" So no one was with him when Joseph made himself known to his brothers.
He wept aloud, and the Egyptians heard it, and Pharaoh's household heard it.
Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?" But his brothers could not answer him. They were terrified of him.
Then Joseph said to his brothers, "Come closer to me." And they came closer. And he said, "I am Joseph your brother — the one you sold into Egypt.
"So now, don't be grieved, and don't be angry with yourselves for selling me here. God sent me ahead of you to preserve life.
"The famine has been in the land two years now, and there are five more coming with no ploughing and no harvest.
"God sent me ahead of you to leave you a remnant on the earth, and to keep you alive for a great deliverance.
"So it wasn't you who sent me here — it was God. He made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of his whole household, and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
"Hurry, go up to my father and tell him, 'This is what your son Joseph says: God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me — don't delay.
"'You'll live in the land of Goshen and be near me — you, your sons, your grandsons, your flocks and herds, everything you have.
"'And I'll provide for you there, since there are five more years of famine — so that you and your household and everything you have aren't reduced to nothing.'
"And look — you can see with your own eyes, and so can my brother Benjamin, that it is my own mouth speaking to you.
"Tell my father about all my honour in Egypt, and everything you've seen. Then hurry and bring my father down here."
Then he threw his arms around his brother Benjamin's neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck.
He kissed all his brothers and wept over them. After that his brothers were able to talk with him.
Word reached Pharaoh's household: "Joseph's brothers have come." And Pharaoh and his servants were pleased.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Tell your brothers, 'Do this: load your animals and go back to the land of Canaan,
"'and bring your father and your households and come to me. I'll give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you'll eat the fat of the land.'
"And you are ordered to do this: take carts from the land of Egypt for your children and your wives, bring your father, and come.
"'And don't worry about your belongings — the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.'"
Israel's sons did so. Joseph gave them carts, as Pharaoh had ordered, and provisions for the journey.
He gave each of them changes of clothing, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothing.
And to his father he sent as much again: ten donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt, and ten she-donkeys loaded with grain and bread and food for his father's journey.
So he sent his brothers off, and as they went he said, "Don't quarrel on the way."
So they went up from Egypt and came to the land of Canaan, to their father Jacob.
They told him, "Joseph is still alive — he is ruler over all the land of Egypt." But his heart went numb; he did not believe them.
But when they repeated everything Joseph had said to them, and he saw the carts Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of Jacob their father revived.
And Israel said, "Enough. My son Joseph is alive. I'll go and see him before I die."

genesis_46.t: So Israel set out with everything he had. He came to Beersheba and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
And God spoke to Israel in visions of the night. "Jacob, Jacob." And he said, "Here I am."
He said, "I am God, the God of your father. Don't be afraid to go down to Egypt — I will make you into a great nation there.
"I will go down with you to Egypt myself, and I will surely bring you up again. And Joseph will close your eyes with his own hand."
Then Jacob set out from Beersheba. His sons carried their father Jacob, along with their children and their wives, in the carts Pharaoh had sent to carry him.
They took their livestock and the possessions they had acquired in Canaan, and came to Egypt — Jacob and all his offspring with him:
his sons and grandsons, his daughters and granddaughters — all his offspring he brought with him to Egypt.
These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt — Jacob and his sons: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn;
Reuben's sons: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
Simeon's sons: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jakin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of the Canaanite woman.
Levi's sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Judah's sons: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah — though Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And Perez's sons were Hezron and Hamul.
Issachar's sons: Tola, Puvah, Iob, and Shimron.
Zebulun's sons: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These are Leah's sons, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, along with his daughter Dinah. In all, his sons and daughters numbered thirty-three.
Gad's sons: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
Asher's sons: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah, with their sister Serah. And Beriah's sons: Heber and Malchiel.
These are Zilpah's sons, whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah. She bore these to Jacob — sixteen persons.
The sons of Rachel, Jacob's wife: Joseph and Benjamin.
And in the land of Egypt, Asenath, daughter of Poti-phera the priest of On, bore Joseph two sons: Manasseh and Ephraim.
Benjamin's sons: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
These are Rachel's sons, born to Jacob — fourteen persons in all.
Dan's sons: Hushim.
Naphtali's sons: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These are Bilhah's sons, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel. She bore these to Jacob — seven persons in all.
All those who came to Egypt with Jacob, his own direct descendants, not counting the wives of Jacob's sons, numbered sixty-six.
Joseph's sons, born to him in Egypt, were two. In all, the household of Jacob that came to Egypt numbered seventy.
He sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph, to get directions to Goshen, and they came into the land of Goshen.
Joseph harnessed his chariot and went up to Goshen to meet his father Israel. He appeared before him, threw his arms around his neck, and wept on his neck a long while.
Israel said to Joseph, "Now I can die — I have seen your face, and you are still alive."
Joseph said to his brothers and his father's household, "I'm going up to tell Pharaoh. I'll say to him, 'My brothers and my father's household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
"'The men are shepherds — they've always kept livestock — and they've brought their flocks and herds and everything they own.'
"And when Pharaoh summons you and asks what your occupation is,

"say, 'Your servants have kept livestock from our youth until now, we and our fathers before us' — so that you can settle in the land of Goshen, since every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians."

genesis_47.t: Then Joseph came and told Pharaoh, "My father and my brothers have come from the land of Canaan with their flocks and herds and everything they own, and they're now in the land of Goshen."
From among his brothers he took five men and presented them to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to his brothers, "What is your occupation?" They said, "Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were."

They said to Pharaoh, "We've come to stay in the land as sojourners, because there's no pasture for your servants' flocks — the famine is severe in Canaan. So please let your servants settle in the land of Goshen."
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Your father and your brothers have come to you.

"The land of Egypt is open to you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best part of it — let them live in the land of Goshen. And if you know of capable men among them, put them in charge of my own livestock."
Then Joseph brought his father Jacob in and presented him to Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Jacob, "How many are the days of the years of your life?"

Jacob said to Pharaoh, "The days of the years of my sojournings are a hundred and thirty. Few and hard have been the days of the years of my life, and they haven't reached the years my fathers lived in their sojournings."
Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and left his presence.
So Joseph settled his father and his brothers, giving them a holding in the best part of the land of Egypt, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.
And Joseph provided food for his father, his brothers, and his father's whole household, according to the number of their children.
There was no food anywhere in the land — the famine was crushing — and the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan wasted away because of it.
Joseph gathered up all the silver to be found in Egypt and Canaan, in payment for the grain people were buying, and brought it into Pharaoh's house.
When the silver of Egypt and Canaan was spent, all Egypt came to Joseph and said, "Give us food! Why should we die in front of you? The silver is gone."
Joseph said, "Bring me your livestock, and I'll give you food for them, since the silver is gone."
So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for their horses, flocks, herds, and donkeys. That year he kept them fed in exchange for all their livestock.

When that year was over, they came to him the next year and said, "We won't hide it from my lord: the silver is spent, and the herds are my lord's. There's nothing left for my lord but our bodies and our ground.

"Why should we die in front of you, we and our ground with us? Buy us and our ground for food, and we and our ground will be Pharaoh's slaves. Just give us seed, so we can live instead of dying, and so the ground doesn't go to waste."
So Joseph bought all the ground of Egypt for Pharaoh. Every Egyptian sold his field, because the famine bore down on them, and the land became Pharaoh's.
And the people he moved into the cities, from one end of Egypt's territory to the other.
Only the priests' ground he did not buy. The priests had an allowance from Pharaoh and lived on it, so they did not sell their ground.
Then Joseph said to the people, "Look — today I have bought you and your ground for Pharaoh. Here is seed for you. Sow the ground.
"At harvest you'll give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four parts will be yours — for seed, for your own food, for your households, and for your children to eat."
They said, "You have kept us alive. May we find favour with my lord, and we'll be Pharaoh's slaves."
And Joseph made it a standing law for the ground of Egypt, still in force today: a fifth goes to Pharaoh. Only the priests' ground did not become Pharaoh's.
So Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in Goshen. They acquired holdings there, and they were fruitful and multiplied greatly.
Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years, and the days of Jacob, the years of his life, came to a hundred and forty-seven.

When the time came near for Israel to die, he called for his son Joseph and said, "If I have found favour with you, put your hand under my thigh and deal with me in loyalty and faithfulness — don't bury me in Egypt.
"When I lie down with my fathers, carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place." And he said, "I'll do as you say."
And he said, "Swear it to me." So he swore to him. And Israel bowed down at the head of the bed.

genesis_48.t: Some time after this, Joseph was told that his father was ill. So he took his two sons with him, Manasseh and Ephraim.
Jacob was told, "Your son Joseph has come to you." And Israel gathered his strength and sat up on the bed.
Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me,
"and he said to me, 'I am going to make you fruitful and multiply you, and make you into a company of peoples, and I will give this land to your offspring after you as a holding for all time.'
"And now your two sons, born to you in Egypt before I came to you here, are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, just like Reuben and Simeon.
"Any children born to you after them will be yours; they'll be reckoned under their brothers' names in their inheritance.
"As for me — when I came from Paddan, Rachel died on me in the land of Canaan, on the road, still some way short of Ephrath. And I buried her there, on the road to Ephrath, that is Bethlehem."
When Israel saw Joseph's sons, he said, "Who are these?"
Joseph said to his father, "They're my sons, the ones God gave me here." And he said, "Bring them to me, and I'll bless them."
Israel's eyes were failing with age and he could not see. So Joseph brought them close to him, and he kissed them and embraced them.
Israel said to Joseph, "I never expected to see your face, and now God has let me see your children too."
Then Joseph took them from between his knees and bowed down with his face to the ground.
Joseph took the two of them — Ephraim in his right hand, facing Israel's left, and Manasseh in his left hand, facing Israel's right — and brought them close to him.
But Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on Ephraim's head — the younger one — and his left hand on Manasseh's head. He crossed his hands, since Manasseh was the firstborn.
And he blessed Joseph and said: "The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has shepherded me my whole life until this day,

"the angel who redeems me from all harm — may he bless these boys. Let my name be named over them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and let them multiply into a great crowd in the midst of the earth."
When Joseph saw his father laying his right hand on Ephraim's head, he was displeased, and he took hold of his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head over to Manasseh's.
Joseph said to his father, "Not like that, father — this is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head."

But his father refused. "I know, my son, I know. He too will become a people, and he too will be great — but his younger brother will be greater, and his offspring will become a multitude of nations."
So he blessed them that day, saying, "By you Israel will pronounce blessings: 'May God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh.'" And he set Ephraim ahead of Manasseh.
Then Israel said to Joseph, "I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers.
"And to you I give one ridge of land more than to your brothers — the one I took from the Amorites with my sword and my bow."

genesis_49.t: Then Jacob called his sons together and said, "Gather round, and let me tell you what will happen to you in the days to come.
Gather in and hear, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father.
Reuben, you are my firstborn — my strength, the first of my vigour, first in dignity, first in power.
Unruly as water, you will not excel, because you went up onto your father's bed — you defiled it. He went up onto my couch.
Simeon and Levi are brothers — their swords are weapons of violence.
Let me have no part in their council; let me not join their assembly — in their anger they killed a man, and for their pleasure they hamstrung an ox.
Cursed be their anger — it is fierce — and their wrath — it is cruel. I will divide them in Jacob, scatter them in Israel.
Judah — your brothers will praise you. Your hand will be on your enemies' neck. Your father's sons will bow down to you.
Judah is a lion's cub. From the kill, my son, you have gone up. He crouched, he lay down like a lion, like a lioness — who would rouse him?
The staff will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's rod from between his feet, until tribute comes to him, and the obedience of the peoples is his.
He ties his donkey to the vine, his donkey's colt to the choicest vine; he washes his clothes in wine, his robe in the blood of grapes.
His eyes darker than wine, his teeth whiter than milk.
Zebulun will live by the shore of the seas, a haven for ships, with his flank toward Sidon.
Issachar is a strong-boned donkey, lying down between the sheepfolds.
He saw that rest was good and the land was pleasant, so he bent his shoulder to the load and became a labouring serf.
Dan will judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel.
Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a viper on the path, biting the horse's heels so the rider topples backward.
I wait for your deliverance, the LORD.
Gad — raiders will raid him, but he will raid at their heel.
Asher's food will be rich; he will supply a king's delicacies.
Naphtali is a doe set free, and gives beautiful sayings.
Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring; its branches run over a wall.
The archers dealt bitterly with him, shot at him and harassed him.
But his bow held firm, and his arms were made supple by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob — from there, the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel —
from the God of your father, who will help you, and with the Almighty, who will bless you: blessings of the heavens above, blessings of the deep lying beneath, blessings of breasts and womb.

Your father's blessings have prevailed over the blessings of my forebears, to the bounty of the ancient hills. May they rest on Joseph's head, on the crown of the head of the nazir among his brothers.
Benjamin is a ravening wolf — in the morning he devours the prey, at evening he divides the spoil.
All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father said to them as he blessed them, giving each the blessing suited to him.
Then he charged them: "I am about to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers, in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
in the cave in the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre in the land of Canaan — the field Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial holding.
There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah.
The field and the cave in it were bought from the sons of Heth.
When Jacob had finished charging his sons, he drew his feet up into the bed, breathed his last, and was gathered to his people.

genesis_50.t: Then Joseph fell on his father's face and wept over him and kissed him.
Joseph ordered his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father, and the physicians embalmed Israel.
It took forty days, the full time for embalming, and the Egyptians mourned him for seventy days.
When the days of weeping were over, Joseph spoke to Pharaoh's household: "If I have found favour with you, please speak to Pharaoh for me and say,
"'My father made me swear an oath: "I am about to die. Bury me in the grave I dug for myself in the land of Canaan." So let me go up and bury my father, and I will come back.'"
Pharaoh said, "Go up and bury your father, just as he made you swear."
So Joseph went up to bury his father, and with him went all Pharaoh's servants, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt,
along with Joseph's whole household, his brothers, and his father's household. Only their children and their flocks and herds were left behind in Goshen.
Chariots and horsemen went up with him too. It was a very large company.
They came to the threshing floor of Atad, across the Jordan, and there they made a great and heavy lamentation. He observed seven days of mourning for his father.
When the Canaanites who lived there saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, they said, "This is a heavy mourning for Egypt." So the place was named Abel-mizraim, which is across the Jordan.
So his sons did for him exactly as he had commanded them.
His sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave in the field of Machpelah, the field Abraham had bought as a burial holding from Ephron the Hittite, facing Mamre.
Then Joseph returned to Egypt, he and his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father, after burying his father.
When Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, "What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back in full for all the harm we did him?"
So they sent word to Joseph: "Before he died, your father left this command:

"'Say this to Joseph: Please forgive your brothers' transgression and their sin, for they dealt you evil. And now forgive the transgression of the servants of the God of your father.'" And Joseph wept as they spoke to him.
