When this sound came, the crowd gathered and were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.
They were astonished and amazed, and said to each other, "Look, aren't all these people who are speaking Galileans?
Then how is it that each of us hears them in the language we were born into?
Parthians, Medes and Elamites; people living in Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia;
Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; visitors from Rome,
Jews and converts, Cretans and Arabs — we hear them telling the great things God has done, in our own languages!"
They were all astonished and at a loss, saying to one another, "What can this mean?"
But others jeered, "They're full of new wine."
Then Peter stood up with the eleven, raised his voice and addressed them: "Men of Judea, and all of you living in Jerusalem, know this, and listen closely to my words.
These people aren't drunk, as you suppose — it's only nine in the morning —
but this is what was said through the prophet Joel:

'And it will be in the last days, God says: I will pour out from my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy, and your young men will see visions, and your old men will dream dreams.
Even on my male servants and my female servants I will pour out from my Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy.
And I will give wonders in the sky above and signs on the earth below — blood and fire and a mist of smoke.
The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the day of the Lord comes, the great and glorious day.
And then everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.'
"Men of Israel, listen to these words. Jesus of Nazareth was a man God set out plainly before you by acts of power and wonders and signs that God did through him among you — as you yourselves know.
This man, handed over by God's settled purpose and foreknowledge — you killed him, nailing him up by the hand of lawless men.
God raised him up, releasing him from the pains of death, because it wasn't possible for him to be held by it.
For David says about him: 'I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand so that I will not be shaken.
That is why my heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced; and my flesh, too, will rest in hope,
because you will not abandon my life to the grave, or let your holy one see decay.
You have shown me the ways of life; you will fill me with gladness in your presence.'
"Brothers, I can tell you plainly about the patriarch David: he died, he was buried, and his tomb is here among us to this day.
So he was a prophet, and he knew that God had sworn him an oath to seat one of his descendants on his throne —
so he saw ahead and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ: that he was not abandoned to the grave and his flesh did not see decay.
This Jesus God raised up — and all of us are witnesses to it.
So he was lifted up to God's right hand, and he received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit, and he has poured out what you now see and hear.
For David did not go up into the heavens, but he himself says: 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand,
until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet."'
So let the whole house of Israel know for certain: God has made him both Lord and Christ — this Jesus, the one you crucified."
When they heard this it cut them to the heart, and they said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, "Brothers, what should we do?"
Peter said to them, "Change your minds, and every one of you be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins — and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
The promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off — for as many as the Lord our God calls to himself."
He went on testifying with many other words and urging them: "Be saved from this crooked generation."
So the ones who welcomed his message were baptised, and about three thousand were added that day.
They kept at the apostles' teaching and the shared life, the breaking of the bread and the prayers.
Awe came over everyone, and many wonders and signs kept happening through the apostles.
All the believers were together and had everything in common,
and they would sell their property and possessions and share the proceeds with everyone, as anyone had need.
Day after day they kept meeting with one mind in the temple, and they broke bread from house to house and shared their food with glad and simple hearts,
praising God and enjoying the goodwill of all the people. And day by day the Lord added to their number those who were being saved.

acts_3.t: Peter and John were on their way up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour.
A man who had been lame from birth was being carried along. Every day they would set him down at the temple gate called Beautiful, to ask for handouts from the people going into the temple.
When he saw Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked for something.
Peter, with John, looked straight at him and said, "Look at us."
He gave them his attention, expecting to get something from them.
But Peter said, "Silver and gold I don't have. But what I do have, I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk."
He took him by the right hand and raised him up, and at once his feet and ankles were made firm.
He jumped up, stood, and started walking; and he went into the temple with them — walking and leaping and praising God.
All the people saw him walking and praising God,
and they knew him — he was the one who used to sit begging at the temple's Beautiful Gate — and they were filled with amazement and astonishment at what had happened to him.
While he was still holding on to Peter and John, all the people came running to them in the colonnade called Solomon's, completely astonished.
When Peter saw it he answered the people: "Men of Israel, why are you amazed at this? Why are you staring at us as if we had made him walk by our own power or godliness?

The God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob, the God of our ancestors, has glorified his servant Jesus — the one you handed over and disowned to Pilate's face, when Pilate had decided to release him.
You disowned the holy and righteous one and asked to have a murderer granted to you,
and you killed the pioneer of life — whom God raised from the dead. We are witnesses of that.
And it is by trust in his name that his name has made this man strong — the man you see and know. The trust that comes through him has given him this complete health, right in front of you all.
And now, brothers, I know you acted in ignorance, and so did your rulers.
But this is how God fulfilled what he foretold through the mouth of all the prophets — that his Christ would suffer.
So change your minds and turn back, so your sins can be wiped out,
so that times of relief may come from the Lord's presence, and he may send the Christ appointed for you — Jesus,
Heaven must receive him until the time when everything is restored — which God spoke about long ago through the mouth of his holy prophets.
Moses said, 'The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. Listen to him in everything he says to you.
And then everyone who does not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people.'
And all the prophets from Samuel on, every one who spoke, announced these days too.
You are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant God made with your ancestors when he said to Abraham, 'And in your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.'
God raised up his servant and sent him to you first, to bless you by turning each one of you from your wicked ways."

acts_4.t: While they were still speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came up to them,
annoyed that they were teaching the people and announcing in Jesus the resurrection from the dead —
so they arrested them and held them in custody until the next day, since it was already evening.
But many who heard the message trusted, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
The next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered in Jerusalem,
along with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and everyone from the high-priestly family.
They stood them in the middle and questioned them: "By what power or in what name did you people do this?"
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, "Rulers of the people and elders,
if we are being examined today about a good deed done to a sick man, and about how this man was made well,

then let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel: it is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth — whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — it is by him that this man stands here in front of you, healthy.
This is the stone that you builders rejected, and it has become the cornerstone.
And there is salvation in no one else — there is no other name under heaven given among people by which we must be saved."
When they saw how boldly Peter and John spoke, and realised they were uneducated, ordinary men, they were amazed; and they recognised them as men who had been with Jesus.
And with the man who had been healed standing right there with them, they had nothing to say back.
So they ordered them out of the council and talked it over among themselves,
saying, "What are we to do with these men? Everyone living in Jerusalem can see that a remarkable sign has happened through them, and we can't deny it.
But to keep it from spreading any further among the people, let us warn them, with threats, to speak to no one any more in this name."
So they called them in and ordered them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John answered them, "Whether it's right in God's sight to listen to you rather than to God — you decide.
We can't stop speaking about what we have seen and heard."
So they threatened them again and let them go, since they could find no way to punish them — because of the people, who were all glorifying God over what had happened.
The man this sign of healing had happened to was over forty years old.
When they were let go they went to their own people and reported everything the chief priests and elders had said to them.
When they heard it they raised their voice to God with one mind: "Master, you are the God who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,
who said through the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of our ancestor David your servant: 'Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot in vain?
The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.'
For truly, in this very city, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the nations and the peoples of Israel, were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed,
to do whatever your hand and your plan had decided beforehand should happen.
And now, Lord, look at their threats, and let your servants speak your word with complete boldness,
as you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders happen through the name of your holy servant Jesus."
When they had prayed, the place where they were gathered shook, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke God's word with boldness.
The whole group of those who trusted were one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything he owned was his own — they had everything in common.
And with great power the apostles kept giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great favour was on them all.
There was not a needy person among them, because everyone who owned land or houses would sell them and bring the money from the sale
and lay it at the apostles' feet; and it was handed out to each one as anyone had need.
Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas — which means son of encouragement — a Levite, a Cypriot by birth,
sold a field he owned, brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet.

acts_5.t: But a man named Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property,
and he held back part of the price for himself — his wife knew — and he brought some of it and laid it at the apostles' feet.
But Peter said, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and hold back part of the price of the land?
While it was unsold, wasn't it yours? And once it was sold, wasn't it yours to do with as you liked? What made you put this thing in your heart? You didn't lie to people; you lied to God."
When Ananias heard these words he fell down and stopped breathing. And great fear came over everyone who heard about it.
The younger men got up, wrapped him, carried him out and buried him.
About three hours later his wife came in, not knowing what had happened.
Peter said to her, "Tell me, did you sell the land for this much?" "Yes," she said, "for that much."
Peter said to her, "Why did the two of you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord? Listen — the feet of the men who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out."
She fell down at his feet at once and stopped breathing. The young men came in, found her dead, carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
And great fear came over the whole community and over everyone who heard about these things.
Many signs and wonders kept happening among the people through the apostles' hands. And they were all together with one mind in Solomon's colonnade,
None of the others dared join them, but the people spoke highly of them.
More than that, crowds of men and women who trusted the Lord kept being added,
so much so that they would carry the sick out into the streets and lay them on cots and mats, so that when Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them.
Crowds came in from the towns around Jerusalem too, bringing the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, and every one of them was healed.
Then the high priest rose up, and all those with him — the party of the Sadducees — and they were filled with jealousy,
and they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.
But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out and said,
"Go, stand in the temple, and tell the people all the words of this life."

So at daybreak they went into the temple and began teaching. Meanwhile the high priest and those with him arrived and called the council together — the whole senate of the sons of Israel — and sent to the jail to have them brought.
But when the officers got there they did not find them in the prison. They went back and reported,
"We found the jail locked up tight and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened it we found no one inside."
When the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard this they were completely at a loss about them, wondering what would come of it.
Then someone came and reported to them, "Look — the men you put in prison are standing in the temple teaching the people."
So the captain went off with the officers and brought them in — but not by force, because they were afraid the people would stone them.
They brought them in and stood them before the council, and the high priest questioned them:
"We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name — and look, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you mean to bring this man's blood down on us."
Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than people.
The God of our ancestors raised Jesus, whom you laid hands on and killed by hanging him on a tree.
God exalted him at his right hand as leader and saviour, to give Israel a change of mind and forgiveness of sins.
And we are witnesses of these things — and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
When they heard this they were furious and wanted to kill them.
But a Pharisee named Gamaliel stood up in the council — a teacher of the law honoured by all the people — and ordered the men put outside for a short while,
and said to them, "Men of Israel, be careful what you are about to do to these men.
Some time back Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and about four hundred men joined him. He was killed, and everyone who was persuaded by him broke up and came to nothing.
After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew people away after him. He was destroyed too, and everyone who was persuaded by him was scattered.
So now I tell you: keep away from these men and leave them alone. If this plan or this work is of human origin it will be destroyed,
but if it is from God, you won't be able to destroy them — you may even find yourselves fighting against God." They were persuaded by him.
So they called in the apostles, had them beaten, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
So they went out from the council rejoicing, because they had been counted worthy to be dishonoured for the Name.
And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they never stopped teaching and announcing the good news that the Christ is Jesus.

acts_6.t: In those days, as the disciples were growing in number, the Greek-speakers began complaining against the Hebrews, because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution.
So the twelve called the whole body of disciples together and said, "It isn't right for us to leave the word of God to wait on tables.
So, brothers and sisters, pick out seven men from among you who are well spoken of, full of the Spirit and wisdom, and we'll put them in charge of this need;
and we will give ourselves to prayer and to the service of the word."

The whole group liked the proposal, and they chose Stephen, a man full of trust and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip and Prochorus and Nicanor and Timon and Parmenas and Nicolaus, a convert from Antioch.
They set these men before the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.
And the word of God kept growing, and the number of disciples in Jerusalem grew fast, and a large group of the priests were becoming obedient to the faith.
Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
But some men from what is called the Synagogue of the Freedmen — Cyrenians and Alexandrians and people from Cilicia and Asia — stood up and began arguing with Stephen,
and they could not hold their own against the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.
Then they secretly put men up to say, "We have heard him speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God."
They stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came at him, seized him and brought him before the council.
They put forward false witnesses, who said, "This man never stops speaking words against this holy place and the law.
We've heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will tear this place down and change the customs Moses handed down to us."
Everyone sitting in the council fixed their eyes on him, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

acts_7.t: The high priest said, "Is this so?"
He said, "Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our ancestor Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran,
and said to him, 'Leave your land and your relatives, and come to the land I will show you.'
So he left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. And from there, after his father died, God moved him into this land where you are living now.
He gave him no inheritance in it — not even a foot of ground — but he promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his offspring after him, even though he had no child.
This is how God put it: his offspring would be foreigners in a land belonging to others, and they would enslave them and mistreat them for four hundred years.
'And I will judge the nation they serve as slaves,' God said, 'and after that they will come out and worship me in this place.'
And he gave him the covenant of circumcision; and so Abraham fathered Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob the twelve patriarchs.
The patriarchs were jealous of Joseph and sold him into Egypt. But God was with him,
and rescued him out of all his troubles, and gave him favour and wisdom in front of Pharaoh king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over his whole household.
Then a famine came over the whole of Egypt and Canaan, and with it great distress, and our ancestors couldn't find food.
When Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt he sent our ancestors there the first time.
On the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Pharaoh learned about Joseph's family.
Joseph sent and called for his father Jacob and all his relatives — seventy-five people in all.
So Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, and so did our ancestors,
and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.
As the time drew near for the promise God had made to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
until another king rose over Egypt who did not know Joseph.
He dealt craftily with our people and mistreated our ancestors, making them abandon their babies so they wouldn't survive.
That was when Moses was born, and he was beautiful before God. He was brought up three months in his father's house,
and when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter took him up and brought him up as her own son.
Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was powerful in his words and deeds.
When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to go and see his brothers, the sons of Israel.
Seeing one of them being wronged, he stepped in to defend him and got justice for the man being ground down, by striking the Egyptian down.
He assumed his brothers would understand that God was giving them deliverance through his hand — but they didn't understand.
The next day he came upon some of them fighting, and he tried to make peace between them: 'Men, you are brothers. Why are you wronging each other?'
But the one who was wronging his neighbour shoved him away and said, 'Who made you ruler and judge over us?
You don't want to kill me the way you killed the Egyptian yesterday, do you?'
At that Moses fled and became a foreigner in the land of Midian, where he fathered two sons.
When forty years had gone by, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush.
When Moses saw it he was amazed at the sight; and as he came closer to look, the voice of the Lord came:
'I am the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.' Moses began to tremble and did not dare look.
The Lord said to him, 'Take the sandal off your feet, because the place where you are standing is holy ground.
I have seen, I have really seen how my people in Egypt are being mistreated, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to rescue them. So now — come, I will send you to Egypt.'
This Moses, whom they rejected when they said, 'Who made you ruler and judge?' — this is the man God sent as both ruler and deliverer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
This is the man who led them out, doing wonders and signs in the land of Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.
This is the Moses who said to the sons of Israel, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.'
This is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness, with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai and with our ancestors; he is the one who received living words to give to us.
Our ancestors would not obey him. They pushed him away, and in their hearts they turned back to Egypt,
saying to Aaron, 'Make us gods to go ahead of us. As for this Moses who brought us out of the land of Egypt — we don't know what has happened to him.'
In those days they made a calf and brought a sacrifice to the idol, and they celebrated over the works of their own hands.

So God turned and handed them over to worship the army of the sky, as it is written in the book of the prophets: 'Did you bring me slaughtered animals and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?
You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan — the figures you made to worship. And I will deport you beyond Babylon.'
Our ancestors had the tent of testimony in the wilderness, just as the one who spoke to Moses had told him to make it, following the pattern he had seen.
And our ancestors, in their turn, brought it in with Joshua when they took possession from the nations God drove out before them, until the days of David.
David found favour before God and asked to find a dwelling place for the house of Jacob.
But it was Solomon who built him a house.
Yet the Most High does not live in things made by hands, as the prophet says:
'Heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or where is the place of my rest?
Wasn't it my hand that made all these things?'
"You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in hearts and ears! You are always resisting the Holy Spirit. Just as your ancestors did, so do you.
Which of the prophets did your ancestors not persecute? They killed the ones who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One — and now you have become his betrayers and murderers —
you who received the law by the direction of angels, and did not keep it."
When they heard this they were furious in their hearts, and they ground their teeth at him.
But he, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into the sky and saw God's glory, and Jesus standing at God's right hand,
and he said, "Look — I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand."
But they shouted at the top of their voices, covered their ears, and rushed at him all together.
They threw him out of the city and started stoning him. And the witnesses laid their clothes at the feet of a young man called Saul.
And they went on stoning Stephen as he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."
Then he knelt down and cried out at the top of his voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

acts_8.t: And Saul approved of his killing. On that day a great persecution broke out against the community in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered through the regions of Judea and Samaria — all except the apostles.
Devout men buried Stephen and mourned loudly over him.
But Saul was tearing the community apart — going into house after house, dragging off men and women, handing them over to prison.
So the ones who had been scattered went about announcing the good news of the word.
Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them.
The crowds listened with one mind to what Philip said, as they heard him and saw the signs he was doing.
For with many who had unclean spirits, the spirits came out, crying with a loud voice; and many paralysed and lame people were healed.
And there was great joy in that city.
Now there was a man named Simon who had been in the city practising magic and astonishing the people of Samaria, claiming to be someone great.
Everyone from the least to the greatest listened to him, and they said, "This man is the power of God that is called Great."
They listened to him because he had astonished them with his magic for a long time.
But when they trusted Philip as he announced the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptised, both men and women.
Simon himself trusted too, and after he was baptised he stuck close to Philip; and when he saw signs and great acts of power happening, he was astonished.
When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them.
They went down and prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit —
because it hadn't yet fallen on any of them; they had only been baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus.
Then they laid their hands on them, and they were receiving the Holy Spirit.
When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the apostles' laying on of hands, he brought them money
and said, "Give me this authority too, so that whoever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit."
But Peter said to him, "May your silver be destroyed along with you, because you thought you could buy God's gift with money.
You have no part or share in this matter, because your heart is not straight before God.
So change your mind about this wickedness of yours, and beg the Lord — maybe the intention of your heart can be forgiven you.
For I can see you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of injustice."
Simon answered, "You beg the Lord for me, so that none of what you have said comes on me."
So when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they went back to Jerusalem, announcing the good news to many Samaritan villages.
An angel of the Lord spoke to Philip: "Get up and go south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." (This is a desert road.)
So he got up and went. And there was an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a court official of Candace queen of the Ethiopians, in charge of all her treasury. He had come to Jerusalem to worship,
and he was on his way back, sitting in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and keep close to this chariot."
Philip ran up and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah, and said, "Do you actually understand what you're reading?"
He said, "How could I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
The passage of scripture he was reading was this: 'Like a sheep he was led to slaughter; and like a lamb silent before the one who shears it, so he does not open his mouth.
In his humiliation justice was taken from him. Who will tell of his generation? For his life is taken from the earth.'
The eunuch said to Philip, "Please tell me — who is the prophet saying this about? Himself, or someone else?"
So Philip opened his mouth and, starting from this scripture, announced to him the good news about Jesus.
As they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "Look — water! What's to stop me being baptised?"
[Philip said, "If you trust with your whole heart, it's permitted." And he answered, "I trust that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."]
He ordered the chariot to stop, and the two of them went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptised him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch never saw him again; he went on his way rejoicing.
But Philip turned up at Azotus, and as he passed through he announced the good news to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.

acts_9.t: But Saul, still breathing out threat and murder against the Lord's disciples, went to the high priest
and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found anyone who belonged to the Way, men or women, he could have them bound and brought to Jerusalem.
As he travelled, he was getting near Damascus, when suddenly a light from the sky flashed around him.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
He said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said, "I am Jesus, the one you are persecuting. [It's hard for you to kick against the goads.]"
[Trembling and astonished he said, "Lord, what do you want me to do?" And the Lord said to him,] "But get up and go into the city, and you'll be told what you must do."
The men travelling with him stood there speechless — they heard the voice but saw no one.
Saul got up from the ground, and though his eyes were open he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
And for three days he could not see, and he did not eat or drink.
There was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." "Here I am, Lord," he said.
The Lord said to him, "Get up and go to the street called Straight, and look for a man from Tarsus named Saul at the house of Judas — because he is praying,
and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias coming in and laying hands on him so he can see again."
But Ananias answered, "Lord, I've heard from many people about this man, how much harm he has done to your holy people in Jerusalem.
And he's here with authority from the chief priests to bind everyone who calls on your name."
But the Lord said to him, "Go — this man is a chosen instrument of mine, to carry my name before the nations and kings and the sons of Israel.
I'm the one who will show him how much he must suffer for my name."

So Ananias went and entered the house, laid his hands on him and said, "Brother Saul, the Lord has sent me — Jesus, the one who appeared to you on the road you were travelling — so you can see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit."
At once something like scales fell from his eyes, and he could see again; and he got up and was baptised,
and after he had eaten he got his strength back. He was with the disciples in Damascus for some days,
and straight away he was proclaiming Jesus in the synagogues — that he is the Son of God.

Everyone who heard was astonished, and they said, "Isn't this the man who destroyed those in Jerusalem who call on this name? And hadn't he come here for that very thing — to bring them bound to the chief priests?"
But Saul grew stronger and stronger, and he threw the Jews living in Damascus into confusion by proving that this man is the Christ.
After many days had gone by, the Jews there plotted to kill him,
but their plot got back to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night to kill him,
so his disciples took him at night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.
When he arrived in Jerusalem he tried to join the disciples, and they were all afraid of him — they didn't believe he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took hold of him and brought him to the apostles, and told them how he had seen the Lord on the road, and that he had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.
So he was with them, coming and going in Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus,
talking and arguing with the Greek-speakers; but they were trying to kill him.
When the brothers and sisters found out, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

So the community throughout the whole of Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up; and living in the fear of the Lord and in the encouragement of the Holy Spirit, it kept growing.
As Peter travelled around through all those places, he came down to the holy people living in Lydda as well.
There he found a man named Aeneas, who had been lying on a mat for eight years, paralysed.
Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your own bed." And he got up right away.
And everyone living in Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha — which translated means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of mercy that she kept doing.
In those days she got ill and died. They washed her and laid her in an upstairs room.
Lydda was near Joppa, so when the disciples heard Peter was there they sent two men to him, urging him, "Don't put off coming to us."

Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived they took him up to the upstairs room, and all the widows stood round him, weeping and showing the tunics and coats Dorcas used to make while she was with them.
Peter put them all outside, knelt down and prayed. Then he turned to the body and said, "Tabitha, get up." She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
He gave her his hand and helped her up; then he called the holy people and the widows and presented her alive.
It became known all over Joppa, and many trusted in the Lord.
And he stayed on in Joppa for many days with a man named Simon, a tanner.

acts_10.t: There was a man in Caesarea named Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort called the Italian.
He was devout, and he feared God — he and his whole household; he gave many gifts of mercy to the people and prayed to God all the time.
About three in the afternoon he saw plainly, in a vision, an angel of God come in to him and say, 'Cornelius.'
He stared at him, terrified, and said, 'What is it, sir?' The angel said to him, 'Your prayers and your gifts of mercy have gone up as a memorial before God.'
Now send men to Joppa and send for a man named Simon, the one who is called Peter.
He is staying with a tanner named Simon, whose house is by the sea. He will tell you what you must do.'
When the angel who spoke to him had gone, he called two of his household slaves and a devout soldier from among his attendants,
explained the whole thing to them, and sent them off to Joppa.
The next day, while they were on the road and getting near the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray, about noon.
He got hungry and wanted something to eat. While they were getting it ready, a trance came over him,
and he sees the sky opened and something coming down like a great sheet, let down to the ground by its four corners.
In it were all the four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth and birds of the sky.
And a voice came to him: 'Get up, Peter — kill and eat.'
But Peter said, 'By no means, Lord. I have never eaten anything common or unclean.'
And the voice came to him a second time: 'What God has made clean, you must not call common.'
This happened three times, and at once the thing was taken up into the sky.
While Peter was still puzzling over what the vision he had seen might mean — look: the men Cornelius had sent had asked their way to Simon's house, and there they were at the gate.
They called out and asked whether Simon called Peter was staying there.
While Peter was still turning the vision over, the Spirit said to him, 'Look — three men are looking for you.
Get up, go down, and go with them, without hesitating at all, because I am the one who sent them.'
Peter went down to the men and said, 'Look, I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason you are here?'

They said, 'Cornelius — a centurion, a just man who fears God, well spoken of by the whole nation of the Jews — was told by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear words from you.'
So he invited them in and put them up. The next day he got up and went off with them, and some of the brothers and sisters from Joppa went along with him.
The following day he came into Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them; he had called together his relatives and his close friends.
As Peter was coming in, Cornelius met him, fell at his feet and bowed low.
But Peter pulled him up, saying, 'Stand up. I'm a man myself.'
Talking with him, he went in and found a lot of people gathered there.
He said to them, 'You know it's taboo for a Jewish man to associate with a foreigner or to go near one. And God has shown me that I am to call no human being common or unclean.
That's why I came without objection when I was sent for. So let me ask: why did you send for me?'
Cornelius said, 'Four days ago, at this very hour, I was fasting and praying at three in the afternoon in my house, and there — a man stood in front of me in shining clothing
and says, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your gifts of mercy have been remembered before God.
So send to Joppa and call for Simon, the one who is called Peter. He is a guest in the house of Simon the tanner, by the sea.'
So I sent to you at once, and you were good to come. So now we're all here in front of God to hear everything the Lord has commanded you.'
Peter opened his mouth and said, 'I truly see it: God does not go by the face,
but in every nation the one who fears him and works rightness is acceptable to him.
The word he sent to the sons of Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ — he is Lord of all —
you know what happened all through Judea, starting from Galilee after the baptism John proclaimed:
Jesus of Nazareth — how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, and he went about doing good and healing everyone who was under the devil's tyranny, because God was with him.
And we are witnesses of everything he did, both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem — and they killed him by hanging him on a tree.
God raised him on the third day and let him be seen —
not by all the people, but by witnesses God had chosen beforehand — by us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
And he ordered us to proclaim to the people and to testify that this is the one God has marked out as judge of living and dead.
To him all the prophets testify: that everyone who believes in him receives release from sins through his name.'
While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on everyone who was listening to the message.
The believers from the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the nations,
because they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God. Then Peter answered:
'Can anyone hold back the water and stop these people being baptised — people who received the Holy Spirit just as we did?'
So he ordered that they be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay on for a few days.

acts_11.t: The apostles and the brothers and sisters throughout Judea heard that the nations too had received the word of God.
So when Peter came up to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision took issue with him,
saying, 'You went in to men who have a foreskin, and you ate with them.'
So Peter started at the beginning and laid it out for them in order:
'I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision — something coming down like a great sheet, let down from the sky by its four corners, and it came right down to me.
I looked hard into it and saw the four-footed animals of the earth, the wild beasts, the reptiles and the birds of the sky.
And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Get up, Peter — kill and eat.'
But I said, 'By no means, Lord. Nothing common or unclean has ever gone into my mouth.'
But the voice answered from heaven a second time: 'What God has made clean, you must not call common.'
This happened three times, and then the whole thing was pulled back up into the sky.
And right then three men turned up at the house where we were, sent to me from Caesarea.
The Spirit told me to go with them without making any distinction. These six brothers came with me too, and we went into the man's house.
He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying, 'Send to Joppa and fetch Simon who is called Peter.
He will speak words to you by which you will be saved — you and your whole household.'
And as I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as it did on us at the beginning.
And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptised with water, but you will be baptised in the Holy Spirit.'
So if God gave them the same gift he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ — who was I to stand in God's way?'
When they heard this they went quiet, and they gave glory to God: 'So God has given the nations, too, a change of mind that leads to life.'
Now those who had been scattered by the persecution that arose over Stephen travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the message to nobody but Jews.
But some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, came to Antioch and began speaking to the Greek-speaking Jews as well, announcing the good news of the Lord Jesus.
And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.
News about them reached the ears of the community in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas out as far as Antioch.
When he arrived and saw the grace of God he was glad, and he urged them all to hold to the Lord with settled hearts,
for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of trust. And a sizeable crowd was added to the Lord.
He went off to Tarsus to hunt for Saul,

and when he found him he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met together in the community and taught a sizeable crowd — and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first publicly styled Christians.
In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them named Agabus stood up and indicated through the Spirit that a great famine was about to come over the whole inhabited world — which it did, under Claudius Caesar.
So the disciples decided, each of them according to what he could afford, to send help to the brothers and sisters living in Judea.
And that is what they did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

acts_12.t: About that time Herod the king laid hands on some who belonged to the community, to do them harm.
He killed James, John's brother, with a sword.
And when he saw that this pleased the Jews, he went on to seize Peter as well. These were the days of unleavened bread.
He arrested him and put him in prison, handing him over to four squads of four soldiers to guard him; he meant to bring him out to the people after the Passover.
So Peter was kept in the prison — but the community was praying hard to God for him.
On the night before Herod was going to bring him out, Peter was asleep between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and guards in front of the door were watching the prison.
And look: an angel of the Lord stood there, and light shone in the cell. He struck Peter's side and woke him: 'Get up — quickly.' And the chains fell off his hands.
The angel said to him, 'Get dressed and put on your sandals.' He did. And he says to him, 'Throw your cloak round you and follow me.'
He went out and followed, and he didn't know that what was happening through the angel was real; he thought he was seeing a vision.

They passed the first guard and the second and came to the iron gate that leads into the city, and it opened for them by itself. They went out and walked down one street, and all at once the angel left him.
Then Peter came to himself and said, 'Now I know for sure — the Lord sent his angel and got me out of Herod's hand, and out of everything the people of the Jews were expecting.'
Once he had worked that out, he went to the house of Mary the mother of John who is called Mark, where a good many had gathered and were praying.
When he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer.
She knew Peter's voice, and out of sheer joy she didn't open the gate but ran back in and announced that Peter was standing at the gateway.
They said to her, 'You're out of your mind.' But she kept insisting it was so. And they kept saying, 'It's his angel.'
Peter kept on knocking. When they opened, they saw him and were astounded.
He waved them quiet with his hand and told them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, 'Report this to James and to the brothers.' Then he left and went somewhere else.
When day came there was no small commotion among the soldiers about what had become of Peter.
Herod searched for him and didn't find him. He interrogated the guards and ordered them led away; then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

Herod was furious with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came to him together, and after winning over Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace — because their country was fed from the king's.
On an appointed day Herod put on royal clothing, sat on the platform and made a public speech to them.
And the assembled people kept shouting, 'The voice of a god and not of a man!'
At once an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give the glory to God, and he was eaten by worms and died.
But the word of God kept growing and multiplying.
And Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem, having completed their service, and they took John who was called Mark along with them.

acts_13.t: In the community at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius the Cyrenian, Manaen who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
While they were serving the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, 'Set Barnabas and Saul apart for me, for the work I have called them to.'
Then, after fasting and praying and laying their hands on them, they let them go.
So, sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia and from there sailed for Cyprus.
When they reached Salamis they announced the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. They also had John as their assistant.
They went through the whole island as far as Paphos, and there they found a man who was a magician, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Bar-Jesus.
He was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man, who called for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the magician — that's how his name is translated — stood against them, trying to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
But Saul, who is also Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked straight at him
and said, 'You are full of every kind of deceit and every kind of fraud — son of the devil, enemy of all rightness! Will you never stop twisting the straight ways of the Lord?

And now, look: the hand of the Lord is on you, and you will be blind, and not see the sun, for a time.' Straight away mist and darkness fell on him, and he went about looking for people to lead him by the hand.
Then the proconsul saw what had happened and believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
Paul and his companions put to sea from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. But John left them and went back to Jerusalem.
They went on from Perga and arrived at Antioch in Pisidia, and on the sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
After the reading of the law and the prophets, the synagogue rulers sent to them: 'Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.'
Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and said: 'Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen.
The God of this people Israel chose our fathers, and he lifted the people high while they were living as foreigners in the land of Egypt; and with a raised arm he brought them out of it.
And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness.
And he destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan and gave them their land as an inheritance,
over about four hundred and fifty years. After that he gave them judges, up to Samuel the prophet.
And then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
He removed him and raised up David to be their king, and he testified about him: 'I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do everything I want.'
From this man's seed God brought Israel a saviour, Jesus, just as he had promised.
Before he came, John had proclaimed in advance a baptism of a change of mind to all the people of Israel.
As John was finishing his course he kept saying, 'What do you suppose me to be? I am not the one. But look, there is one coming after me whose sandal I am not worthy to untie.'
Brothers — sons of Abraham's family, and those among you who fear God — it is to us that the message of this rescue has been sent.
For those living in Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognise him, and by judging him they fulfilled the words of the prophets that are read every sabbath.
And though they found no ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him executed.
When they had finished everything written about him, they took him down from the tree and put him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead,
and for many days he was seen by the people who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, and they are now his witnesses to the people.
And we bring you the good news that the promise made to the fathers —
God has fulfilled it for us, their children, by raising Jesus, as it is also written in the second psalm: 'You are my son; today I have fathered you.'
And that he raised him from the dead, never to go back to decay — this is how he said it: 'I will give you the holy and faithful things of David.'
That is why he also says somewhere else: 'You will not give your holy one to see decay.'
For David served God's purpose in his own generation, and then he fell asleep and was gathered to his fathers and saw decay.
But the one God raised did not see decay.
So let it be known to you, brothers: through this man release from sins is announced to you;
and everything you could not be freed from by the law of Moses — in this man everyone who believes is freed.
So watch out that what is said in the prophets does not come on you:
'Look, you scoffers — be amazed, and vanish; because I am doing a work in your days, a work you will never believe even if someone spells it out to you.'
As they were going out of the synagogue of the Jews, the nations kept urging that these things be spoken to them on the next sabbath.
When the gathering broke up, many of the Jews and of the devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas, who talked with them and urged them to stay with the grace of God.
On the following sabbath nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
When the Jews saw the crowds they were filled with jealousy, and they contradicted what Paul was saying — contradicting and slandering.

So Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly: 'It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. Since you push it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life — look, we are turning to the nations.
For this is what the Lord has commanded us: 'I have set you as a light of nations, that you may be for rescue to the end of the earth.'
When the nations heard this they were glad and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed.
And the word of the Lord was carried right through the region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, and they raised a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and threw them out of their district.
So they shook the dust off their feet against them and went to Iconium.
And the disciples were being filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

acts_14.t: In Iconium the same thing happened: they went into the synagogue of the Jews and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed.
But the Jews who would not be persuaded stirred up the minds of the nations and turned them against the brothers and sisters.
So they spent a good while there speaking openly, leaning on the Lord, who testified to the message of his grace and granted signs and wonders to happen through their hands.
The city's people were split: some were with the Jews, some with the apostles.
When both the nations and the Jews, along with their rulers, made a move to mistreat them and stone them,
they realised it and got away to the Lycaonian cities, Lystra and Derbe and the country round about,
and there they went on announcing the good news.
In Lystra there was a man sitting who had no power in his feet: he had been lame from his mother's womb and had never walked.
He listened to Paul speaking. Paul looked straight at him and saw that he had trust to be made well,
and said in a loud voice, 'Stand up straight on your feet.' And he jumped up and started walking about.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done they raised their voices, saying in Lycaonian, 'The gods have come down to us in human form!'
They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, since he was the one leading the talking.
And the priest of the Zeus whose temple stood in front of the city brought bulls and garlands to the gates, and he and the crowds wanted to sacrifice.
When the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their clothes and rushed out into the crowd, shouting

'Men, why are you doing this? We're human beings too, with the same nature as you, and we're bringing you good news — to turn you from these empty things to the living God, who made the sky and the earth and the sea and everything in them.
In the generations that have gone by he let all the nations go their own ways,
and yet he didn't leave himself without a witness: doing good, giving you rain from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.'
Even saying this, they barely stopped the crowds from sacrificing to them.
But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and after winning the crowds over they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead.
But when the disciples had gathered round him he got up and went into the city; and the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.
They announced the good news in that city and made a good number of disciples, and then they went back to Lystra and Iconium and Antioch,
strengthening the disciples and urging them to stay in the faith — and telling them that we have to go through many pressures to enter the kingdom of God.
They appointed elders for them in each community, and with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord they had come to believe in.
They passed through Pisidia and came into Pamphylia,
and after speaking the message in Perga they went down to Attalia.
From there they sailed to Antioch — where they had been handed over to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.
When they arrived they called the community together and reported everything God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of trust to the nations.
And they stayed on there with the disciples — and not for a short time.

acts_15.t: Some men came down from Judea and started teaching the brothers and sisters, 'Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you can't be saved.'

There was no small dissension and dispute between Paul and Barnabas and them — so they arranged for Paul and Barnabas and some others of their number to go up to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem about this question.

So the community sent them on their way, and they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria telling the whole story of how the nations had turned, and they brought great joy to all the brothers and sisters.
When they arrived in Jerusalem they were welcomed by the community and the apostles and the elders, and they reported everything God had done with them.
But some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and said they had to be circumcised and told to keep the law of Moses.
The apostles and the elders gathered to look into this matter.

After a long dispute Peter stood up and said to them, 'Brothers, you know that in the early days God made his choice among you: that through my mouth the nations should hear the message of the good news and believe.
And God, who knows the heart, testified for them by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us,
and he made no distinction between us and them; he cleansed their hearts by trust.
So now, why are you testing God by putting a yoke on the disciples' necks that neither our fathers nor we have had the strength to carry?
No — we believe we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way they are.'
The whole gathering went quiet, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul describing all the signs and wonders God had done through them among the nations.
After they had finished, James answered: 'Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has told us how God first visited the nations to take from them a people for his name.
And the words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written:
'After this I will come back and rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will rebuild its ruins and set it upright again,
so that the rest of humanity may seek out the Lord, and all the nations on whom my name has been called, says the Lord who does these things,
known from of old.'
So my judgement is this: we should not make trouble for those of the nations who are turning to God,
but write to them to keep away from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood.
For from ancient generations Moses has had people proclaiming him in every city, read aloud in the synagogues every sabbath.'

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole community, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, leading men among the brothers and sisters,
writing by their hand: 'The apostles and the elders, brothers, to the brothers and sisters from the nations throughout Antioch and Syria and Cilicia: greetings.
Since we have heard that some of our number went out and unsettled you with words, upsetting your minds — and we gave them no such instructions —
it seemed good to us, once we had come to one mind, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have handed over their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
So we have sent Judas and Silas, and they will tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things:
to keep away from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from what is strangled and from sexual immorality. Keep yourselves from these and you will do well. Farewell.
So they were sent off and went down to Antioch, and they gathered the crowd together and handed over the letter.
When they read it they were glad at the encouragement.
Judas and Silas, being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers and sisters with a long message and strengthened them.
After they had spent some time there, the brothers and sisters sent them off in peace, back to those who had sent them.
[But it seemed good to Silas to stay on there.]
Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and announcing the good news of the word of the Lord, along with many others.
After some days Paul said to Barnabas, 'Let's go back and visit the brothers and sisters in every city where we announced the word of the Lord, and see how they are.'
Barnabas wanted to take John called Mark along with them,
but Paul thought it right not to take along a man who had walked out on them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.
There was a sharp clash, so that they separated from each other; and Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus.
Paul chose Silas and left, handed over by the brothers and sisters to the grace of the Lord.
He travelled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the communities.

acts_16.t: He came down to Derbe and to Lystra. And there was a disciple there named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman, but his father was a Greek.
The brothers and sisters in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him.
Paul wanted this man to go out with him, so he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews in those places — they all knew his father was a Greek.
As they travelled through the cities they passed on to them the decisions the apostles and elders in Jerusalem had reached, for them to keep.
So the communities were being strengthened in the faith, and they were growing in number every day.
They went through the Phrygian and Galatian region — the Holy Spirit had stopped them from speaking the message in Asia.
When they came opposite Mysia they tried to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus wouldn't let them.
So they passed by Mysia and came down to Troas.
And a vision appeared to Paul during the night: a Macedonian man was standing there, urging him, 'Cross over into Macedonia and help us.'
And once he had seen the vision, we set about at once finding a way over into Macedonia, since we had worked out that God had called us to announce the good news to them.
So we put to sea from Troas and ran a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis,
and from there to Philippi, which is a city of the first district of Macedonia, a colony. We stayed in this city some days.
On the sabbath day we went outside the gate to a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and talked with the women who had gathered.
And one woman named Lydia was listening — a dealer in purple from the city of Thyatira, a worshipper of God — and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what Paul was saying.
When she and her household were baptised, she urged us: 'If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.' And she pressed us into it.
As we were going to the place of prayer, a slave girl met us who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners a great deal of money by telling fortunes.
She kept following Paul and us, shouting, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, and they're announcing to you a way of rescue.'
She did this for many days. Paul, worn down by it, turned and said to the spirit, 'I order you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour.
When her owners saw that their hope of profit had gone out, they grabbed Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers.
They brought them to the magistrates and said, 'These men are throwing our city into an uproar. They're Jews,
and they're announcing customs it isn't lawful for us to accept or practise, since we're Romans.'
The crowd joined in the attack on them, and the magistrates tore their clothes off them and ordered them beaten with rods.
After laying many blows on them they threw them into prison, and ordered the jailer to keep them securely.
Given an order like that, he threw them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison shook. At once all the doors came open, and everyone's chains came loose.
The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, thinking the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul called out at the top of his voice, 'Don't do yourself any harm — we're all here.'
He called for lights and rushed in, and trembling he fell down in front of Paul and Silas.
He brought them outside and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'
They said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved — you and your household.'
And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to everyone in his house.
He took them at that hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he and all his household were baptised right there and then.
He brought them up into his house and set a table for them, and he and his whole household were overjoyed that he had come to believe in God.
When day came the magistrates sent the rod-bearers with the message, 'Release those men.'
The jailer reported this to Paul: 'The magistrates have sent word that you're to be released. So come out now and go in peace.'

But Paul said to them, 'They beat us in public without a trial — men who are Roman citizens — and threw us into prison; and now they're throwing us out on the quiet? No. Let them come themselves and bring us out.'
The rod-bearers reported this to the magistrates, and they took fright when they heard they were Romans.
They came and appealed to them, and after bringing them out they asked them to leave the city.
So they went out of the prison and went to Lydia's house; and when they had seen the brothers and sisters they encouraged them and left.

acts_17.t: They travelled through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews.
As he always did, Paul went in to them, and for three sabbaths he argued with them from the scriptures,
opening them up and laying it out: that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that 'this Jesus, whom I announce to you, is the Christ.'
Some of them were persuaded and threw in their lot with Paul and Silas — along with a great number of the devout Greeks, and quite a few of the leading women.

But the Jews became jealous, and they picked up some worthless men from the marketplace, got a mob together and set the city in an uproar. They attacked Jason's house, trying to bring them out to the assembly.
When they didn't find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers and sisters before the city officials, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too,
and Jason has taken them in. Every one of them acts against the decrees of Caesar — they say there is another king, Jesus.'
They stirred up the crowd and the city officials who heard this,
and after taking a security payment from Jason and the rest, they let them go.
The brothers and sisters sent Paul and Silas away at once, by night, to Berea; and when they got there they went into the synagogue of the Jews.
These were more open-minded than the ones in Thessalonica: they took the message in with real eagerness, and they went through the scriptures every day to see whether it was so.
So many of them believed — and not a few of the Greek women of high standing, and men too.
But when the Jews from Thessalonica found out that the word of God had been announced by Paul in Berea as well, they came there too, shaking up and stirring the crowds.
So the brothers and sisters sent Paul off at once to go as far as the sea, while Silas and Timothy stayed on there.
The men escorting Paul brought him as far as Athens, and then they left, with instructions for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked inside him as he looked at the city full of idols.
So he argued in the synagogue with the Jews and with those who worshipped God, and in the marketplace, every day, with whoever happened to be there.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers took him on. Some said, 'What's this seed-picker trying to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign divinities' — because he was announcing the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.
They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus: 'Can we find out what this new teaching of yours is?
You're bringing some strange things to our ears, and we want to know what they mean.'
Now all the Athenians and the foreigners staying there spent their time on nothing but telling or hearing something newer.
Paul stood up in the middle of the Areopagus and said: 'Men of Athens, I can see that in every way you are very religious.

For as I was going about, looking closely at the objects of your worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: To an unknown god. What you worship without knowing — that is what I am announcing to you.
The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by hands;
and he isn't served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.
And from one man he made every nation of humanity to live over the whole face of the earth, marking out set times and the boundaries of where they live,
so that they would look for God — feel their way to him, perhaps, and find him — though he is not far from any one of us.
For in him we live and move and exist; as some of your own poets have said, 'For we are also his offspring.'
So if we are God's offspring, we ought not to think the divine is like gold or silver or stone — an image shaped by human skill and imagination.
So God overlooked the times of ignorance; but now he tells people that everyone everywhere is to change their mind,
because he has set a day on which he is going to judge the inhabited world in rightness, by a man he has marked out — and he has given everyone proof of it by raising him from the dead.'
When they heard about a resurrection of the dead, some sneered, but others said, 'We'll hear you on this again.'
And with that Paul went out from among them.
But some men joined him and believed — among them Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

acts_18.t: After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.
There he found a Jew named Aquila, a Pontian by birth, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome; and he went to them.
And because they had the same trade he stayed with them and worked — they were tentmakers by trade.
He argued in the synagogue every sabbath and tried to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was taken up with the message, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.
When they set themselves against him and slandered him, he shook out his clothes and said to them, 'Your blood is on your own head. I'm clean. From now on I'm going to the nations.'
He moved on from there and went into the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshipper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
And Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believed in the Lord, and his whole household with him; and many of the Corinthians who heard believed and were baptised.
One night the Lord said to Paul in a vision, 'Don't be afraid — speak, and don't be silent,
because I am with you, and nobody will lay a hand on you to hurt you; because I have many people in this city.'
So he settled there for a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose up against Paul with one accord and brought him to the tribunal,
saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'
Paul was just about to open his mouth when Gallio said to the Jews, 'If it were some crime or wicked fraud, Jews, it would be reasonable for me to bear with you.
But if these are questions about a word and names and your own law — see to it yourselves. I don't want to be a judge of such things.'
And he drove them away from the tribunal.
Then they all seized Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, and beat him right in front of the tribunal; and none of it mattered to Gallio.

Paul stayed on a good many days more, then said goodbye to the brothers and sisters and sailed for Syria, and Priscilla and Aquila with him. He had his head shaved at Cenchreae, because he was under a vow.
They came to Ephesus, and he left them there; but he himself went into the synagogue and argued with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay longer he would not agree,
but said goodbye, saying, 'I must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem. I'll come back to you again, God willing.' And he put to sea from Ephesus.
He landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the community, and went down to Antioch.
After spending some time there he set out, going through the Galatian region and Phrygia one place after another, strengthening all the disciples.
A Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, arrived at Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, and powerful in the scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and he was on fire in spirit; he spoke and taught accurately the things about Jesus — though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.

When he wanted to cross over into Achaia, the brothers and sisters urged him on and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he got there he was a great help to those who had come to believe through grace,
because he took the Jews on in public and refuted them thoroughly, showing from the scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

acts_19.t: While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul went through the inland regions and came down to Ephesus, and he found some disciples there.
He said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' They said, 'No — we haven't even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.'
He said, 'Into what, then, were you baptised?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.'
Paul said, 'John baptised with a baptism of a change of mind, telling the people to believe in the one coming after him — that is, in Jesus.'
When they heard this they were baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus,
and when Paul laid his hands on them the Holy Spirit came on them, and they were speaking in tongues and prophesying.
There were about twelve men in all.
He went into the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, arguing and persuading about the kingdom of God.

But when some grew hard and would not be persuaded, running the Way down in front of the crowd, he pulled away from them and took the disciples apart, arguing every day in the lecture hall of a man named Tyrannus.
This went on for two years, so that everyone living in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.
And the works of power God was doing through Paul's hands were no ordinary ones,
so that even handkerchiefs and work-aprons that had touched his skin were carried off to the sick, and the diseases left them, and the evil spirits went out.
Some travelling Jewish exorcists took it upon themselves to name the name of the Lord Jesus over people who had evil spirits, saying, 'I bind you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.'
There were seven sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva doing this.
But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I'm acquainted with — but who are you?'
And the man with the evil spirit in him jumped on them, overpowered them all and got the better of them, so that they ran out of that house naked and wounded.
This became known to everyone living in Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks; fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
And many of those who had believed came and confessed and told openly what they had been doing.

And a good number of those who had practised magic arts brought their books together and burned them in front of everyone. They added up the prices and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So, with real force, the word of the Lord kept growing and gaining ground.
When all this was over, Paul resolved in the spirit to go to Jerusalem, passing through Macedonia and Achaia, and he said, 'After I've been there, I must see Rome too.'
He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, into Macedonia, while he himself stayed on for a while in Asia.
About that time there was no small disturbance about the Way.
For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no small business to the craftsmen.
He got them together, along with the workers in similar trades, and said, 'Men, you know our prosperity comes from this business,

and you can see and hear for yourselves that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has talked a sizeable crowd round and turned them away, saying that gods made by hands are not gods.

And the danger isn't only that this line of ours will fall into disrepute, but that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and that she will be brought down from her magnificence — she whom the whole of Asia and the inhabited world worships.'
When they heard this they were filled with rage and kept shouting, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'
The city was filled with confusion, and they rushed all together into the theatre, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's travelling companions.
Paul wanted to go in to the assembled people, but the disciples wouldn't let him.
Some of the Asiarchs too, who were friends of his, sent to him and urged him not to risk himself in the theatre.
