So some were shouting one thing and some another, because the assembly was in confusion, and most of them didn't know why they had come together.
Some of the crowd briefed Alexander, whom the Jews had pushed forward. Alexander motioned with his hand and wanted to make a defence to the people.
But when they realised he was a Jew, one voice went up from them all, for about two hours, shouting, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'

The city secretary quietened the crowd down and says, 'Men of Ephesus, is there anyone alive who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple-keeper of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from the sky?
Since nobody can contradict that, you ought to keep calm and do nothing rash.
You have brought these men here, and they are neither temple-robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a case against anyone — court days are held, and there are proconsuls: let them bring charges against each other.
And if you're after anything further, it will be settled in the lawful assembly.
As it is, we're in danger of being charged with rioting over today, since there's no cause we'll be able to give an account for concerning this gathering.'
And when he had said this, he dismissed the assembly.

acts_20.t: After the uproar had died down, Paul sent for the disciples, encouraged them, said his goodbyes, and left to travel to Macedonia.
He travelled through those regions, encouraging the people there at length, and came into Greece.
He spent three months there; and when a plot was formed against him by the Jews just as he was about to put out to sea for Syria, he decided to go back by way of Macedonia.
Sopater son of Pyrrhus, from Beroea, went with him as far as Asia; and from the Thessalonians Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and from Asia Tychicus and Trophimus.
These men went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas.
We ourselves sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we reached them at Troas, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul was talking with them; and since he meant to leave the next day he kept on speaking until midnight.
There were a good many lamps in the upstairs room where we had gathered.

A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window, sinking into a deep sleep; and as Paul talked on and on, the sleep carried him under and he fell from the third storey down, and was picked up dead.
Paul went down, threw himself on him, took him in his arms and said, "Stop making a commotion — his life is in him."
Then he went back up, broke the bread and ate, and talked with them a long while, until daybreak, and then he left.
And they took the boy away alive, and were comforted more than a little.
We went on ahead to the ship and set sail for Assos, meaning to take Paul aboard there; he'd arranged it that way, intending to go on foot himself.
When he met us at Assos we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, the next day we arrived opposite Chios; the day after we crossed over to Samos and stayed at Trogyllium; and the following day we came to Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that he wouldn't have to spend time in Asia; he was in a hurry to be in Jerusalem, if he possibly could, on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent word to Ephesus and called for the elders of the community.
When they arrived he said to them: "You know for yourselves how I lived among you the whole time, from the first day I set foot in Asia —
serving the Lord as a slave serves, with all lowliness and with tears, through the trials that came to me from the plots of the Jews;
how I held back nothing that was for your good, but announced it to you and taught you, in public and from house to house,
testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about the change of mind that turns toward God, and about trust in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And now, look: bound in the spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, and I don't know what will meet me there —
except that in city after city the Holy Spirit testifies to me that chains and hardships are waiting for me.
But I count my own life of no value to myself, if only I may finish my course and the service I received from the Lord Jesus — to testify to the good news of God's grace.
And now, look: I know that none of you, among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom, will see my face again.
So I testify to you this very day that I am clean of the blood of everyone.
For I did not hold back from announcing to you the whole purpose of God.
Keep watch over yourselves and over the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit set you as overseers — to shepherd the community of God, which he obtained with his own blood.
I know that after I'm gone savage wolves will come in among you, and they won't spare the flock;
and from among your own number men will rise up and speak twisted things, to drag the disciples away after themselves.
So stay awake, and remember that for three years, night and day, I never stopped warning each one of you, with tears.
And now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who have been made holy.
I coveted nobody's silver or gold or clothing.
You know for yourselves that these hands served my own needs and the needs of the men with me.
In everything I showed you that by working like this we must take hold of the weak, and remember the words of the Lord Jesus — that he himself said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
When he had said this he knelt down with them all and prayed.
They all wept a great deal, and they threw their arms around Paul's neck and kissed him,
grieving most of all over what he had said — that they would never see his face again. And they went with him down to the ship.

acts_21.t: When we had torn ourselves away from them and put out to sea, we ran a straight course and came to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
We found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, went aboard, and put out to sea.
We sighted Cyprus, left it behind on our left, and sailed on to Syria and put in at Tyre — the ship was to unload its cargo there.
We looked for the disciples and found them, and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to set foot in Jerusalem.
When our days there were up we left and went on our way, and all of them, with their wives and children, walked us out of the city; and we knelt down on the beach and prayed
and said goodbye to one another. Then we went aboard the ship, and they went back home.
We finished the voyage from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and sisters and stayed one day with them.
The next day we left and came to Caesarea, and we went into the house of Philip the evangelist, one of the seven, and stayed with him.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
While we were staying there for a number of days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea,

and he came to us, took Paul's belt, tied up his own feet and hands, and said, "This is what the Holy Spirit says: the man whose belt this is — the Jews in Jerusalem will tie him up like this, and hand him over into the hands of the Gentiles."
When we heard this, we and the local people begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and crushing my heart? I'm ready not only to be tied up but to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus."
When he wouldn't be persuaded we fell silent and said, "Let the Lord's will be done."
After those days we got our baggage together and went up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea came with us too, bringing us to the man we were to lodge with — a certain Mnason of Cyprus, a disciple from the early days.
When we arrived in Jerusalem the brothers and sisters welcomed us gladly.
The next day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were there.
He greeted them, and then he went through, one by one, the things God had done among the Gentiles through his service.
When they heard it they praised God; and they said to him, "You can see, brother, how many tens of thousands there are among the Jews who have come to trust, and they're all zealous for the law.
But they've been told about you that you teach all the Jews among the Gentiles to break away from Moses — telling them not to circumcise their children or to walk in the customs.
So what's to be done? A crowd is bound to gather, because they'll hear that you've come.
So do what we tell you. We have four men here who are under a vow.

Take these men, be purified along with them, and pay their expenses so they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know there's nothing in what they've been told about you — that you keep in step yourself, guarding the law.

As for the Gentiles who have come to trust, we sent a letter ourselves with our decision that they should keep themselves from what has been offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from sexual immorality."

Then Paul took the men, and the next day he was purified with them and went into the temple, giving notice of when the days of purification would be completed and the offering would be made for each one of them.
When the seven days were almost over, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple, threw the whole crowd into confusion and laid hands on him,

shouting, "Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people and the law and this place — and now he's even brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place."
They had seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with him earlier, and they assumed Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up, the people came running together, and they seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple; and at once the doors were shut.
They were trying to kill him when a report went up to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in turmoil.
He took soldiers and centurions at once and ran down on them; and when they saw the tribune and the soldiers they stopped beating Paul.
Then the tribune came up, arrested him, and ordered him bound with two chains, and started asking who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd were shouting one thing and some another; and since he couldn't learn anything certain because of the uproar, he ordered Paul brought into the barracks.
When he reached the steps, the soldiers had to carry him because of the violence of the crowd;
for the mass of the people kept following and shouting, "Away with him!"
As he was about to be taken into the barracks Paul says to the tribune, "May I say something to you?" He said, "You know Greek?
So you're not the Egyptian who stirred up a revolt a while back and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the desert?"
Paul said, "I'm a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I'm asking you: let me speak to the people."
When he gave permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the people with his hand; and when a deep silence had fallen he spoke to them in the Hebrew language:

acts_22.t: "Brothers and fathers, listen to the defence I'm now making before you."
When they heard him addressing them in the Hebrew language they went quieter still. And he says:
"I'm a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia but brought up in this city, trained at the feet of Gamaliel in the strictness of our ancestral law — and zealous for God, just as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way to the death, tying up and handing over to prison both men and women,

as the high priest and the whole council of elders can testify for me. I got letters from them to the brothers in Damascus, and I was on my way to bring the people there back to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.
As I was travelling and getting near Damascus, about midday, suddenly a great light out of heaven flashed all around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?'
I answered, 'Who are you, Lord?' And he said to me, 'I am Jesus the Nazorean, whom you are persecuting.'
The men with me saw the light, but they didn't understand the voice of the one speaking to me.
I said, 'What am I to do, Lord?' And the Lord said to me, 'Get up and go into Damascus, and there you'll be told about everything that has been appointed for you to do.'
Since I couldn't see, because of the brightness of that light, the men with me led me by the hand and I came into Damascus.
A man named Ananias, devout according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there,
came to me, stood over me and said, 'Brother Saul, look up.' And in that very hour I looked up at him.
He said, 'The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his own mouth;
because you're going to be a witness for him, to all people, of what you have seen and heard.
And now, why are you waiting? Get up, be baptised, and have your sins washed away, calling on his name.'
When I'd returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw him saying to me, 'Hurry — get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they won't accept your testimony about me.'
And I said, 'Lord, they know themselves that I was the one imprisoning and flogging those who trusted in you, synagogue by synagogue;
and when the blood of Stephen your witness was being poured out, I was standing there myself, approving, and guarding the clothes of the men who killed him.'
And he said to me, 'Go — because I'm going to send you far away, to the Gentiles.'"
They listened to him up to this word; and then they raised their voices and said, "Away with such a man from the earth! It was never fit for him to live."
As they were screaming and flinging off their cloaks and throwing dust into the air,
the tribune ordered him brought into the barracks, saying he was to be examined under the lash, so he could find out why they were shouting at him like this.
But when they had stretched him out for the straps, Paul said to the centurion standing there, "Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman, and uncondemned?"
When the centurion heard this he went to the tribune and reported it: "Look what you're about to do — this man is a Roman."
The tribune came and said to him, "Tell me, are you a Roman?" He said, "Yes."
The tribune answered, "I bought this citizenship for a large sum." Paul said, "But I was born into it."
So the men who were about to examine him drew back from him at once; and the tribune took fright too, when he realised that he was a Roman and that he was the one who had bound him.

The next day, wanting to know for certain what he was being accused of by the Jews, he released him from his chains and ordered the chief priests and their whole council to assemble; and he brought Paul down and stood him in front of them.

acts_23.t: Paul looked straight at the council and said, "Brothers, I've lived my whole life before God with a completely good conscience, right up to this day."
The high priest Ananias ordered the men standing beside him to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, "God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there judging me by the law, and you break the law by ordering me to be struck?"
Those standing there said, "Do you insult God's high priest?"
Paul said, "I didn't know, brothers, that he's high priest; for it is written, 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.'"

Paul knew that one part of them were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, so he kept shouting out in the council, "Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is about a hope, and about resurrection of the dead, that I am being judged."
When he said this, a quarrel broke out between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was split.
For Sadducees say there is no resurrection, and no angel or spirit; but Pharisees acknowledge them all.

There was a great outcry, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees' party stood up and argued fiercely: "We find nothing wrong in this man. And if a spirit spoke to him, or an angel — let's not fight against God."
As the quarrel grew violent, the tribune was afraid Paul would be torn apart by them, so he ordered the troops to go down, seize him out of the middle of them, and bring him into the barracks.
The following night the Lord stood over him and said, "Take heart. As you've testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify in Rome as well."
When day came, the Jews formed a conspiracy and put themselves under a curse: they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
There were more than forty who made this sworn plot;
they went to the chief priests and the elders and said, "We've bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we've killed Paul.
So now you, along with the council, notify the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you meant to look into his case more exactly; and we're ready to do away with him before he gets near."
But the son of Paul's sister heard about the ambush, and he came and got into the barracks and told Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, "Take this young man to the tribune; he has something to report to him."
So he took him and brought him to the tribune, and says, "The prisoner Paul called me and asked me to bring this young man to you; he has something to say to you."
The tribune took him by the hand, drew him aside privately, and asked, "What is it you have to report to me?"
He said, "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though it meant to inquire into his case more exactly.

So don't let them persuade you, because more than forty of their men are lying in wait for him; they've put themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they've done away with him, and now they're ready and waiting for your consent."
So the tribune dismissed the young man, ordering him, "Tell no one that you've disclosed this to me."
Then he called two of the centurions and said, "Get two hundred soldiers ready to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, from nine tonight,"
and to provide animals for Paul to ride, so as to bring him through safely to Felix the governor.
And he wrote a letter along these lines:
Claudius Lysias, to His Excellency Governor Felix: greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them, when I came on them with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman.
Wanting to know the charge on which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council.
I found that he was accused about disputed questions of their law, but had no charge against him deserving death or chains.
And when I was informed that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him. Farewell.
So the soldiers took Paul, as they'd been ordered, and brought him through the night to Antipatris.
The next day they let the horsemen go on with him, and they returned to the barracks.
The horsemen came into Caesarea, delivered the letter to the governor, and presented Paul to him as well.
When he'd read it he asked what province he was from; and on learning that he was from Cilicia,
he said, "I'll hear you fully when your accusers arrive too." And he ordered him kept under guard in Herod's praetorium.

acts_24.t: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an advocate named Tertullus, and they laid information against Paul before the governor.
When Paul had been called in, Tertullus opened the case: "Since we enjoy much peace through you, and since reforms are coming to this nation through your foresight,
we welcome it, in every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, with all gratitude.
But so as not to hold you up any longer, I ask you in your fairness to give us a brief hearing.
We have found this man to be a plague, stirring up factions among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazoreans.
He even tried to profane the temple, and we seized him — and we wanted to judge him by our own law.
[But Lysias the tribune came along and, with great violence, took him out of our hands,]
He ordered his accusers to come to you. From him you'll be able, by examining him yourself, to learn about everything we're accusing him of."
The Jews joined in the attack, insisting that this was so.
When the governor motioned to him to speak, Paul answered: "Knowing that you've been a judge over this nation for many years, I make my defence cheerfully.
You can check for yourself that it's not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem.
They didn't find me arguing with anyone in the temple, or gathering a crowd — not in the synagogues, not anywhere in the city;
and they can't produce any evidence to you for the things they're now accusing me of.
But I do admit this to you: that according to the Way — which they call a sect — I serve the God of our fathers, trusting everything laid down in the law and written in the prophets,
and I have a hope toward God — one these men themselves are waiting for — that there is going to be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.
That is why I train myself, too, always to keep a conscience that doesn't stumble, toward God and toward people.
After several years I came to bring charitable gifts to my nation, and offerings.
It was while I was doing this that they found me in the temple, purified — with no crowd and no disturbance.
But it was some Jews from Asia — and they're the ones who ought to be here in front of you bringing a charge, if they have anything against me.
Or let these men here say what wrong they found when I stood before the council —
unless it's this one sentence I shouted out as I stood among them: 'It is about the resurrection of the dead that I am being judged before you today.'"
Felix, who knew the facts about the Way quite exactly, adjourned them: "When Lysias the tribune comes down, I'll settle your case."
He instructed the centurion to keep him in custody but to give him some freedom, and not to stop any of his own people from looking after him.
Some days later Felix arrived with Drusilla, his own wife, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and listened to him about trust in Christ Jesus.
But as he talked about rightness, self-control and the judgment that is coming, Felix became frightened and answered, "That's enough for now — go. When I get an opportunity I'll send for you."
At the same time he was hoping money would be given him by Paul, so he could release him; and so he sent for him quite often and talked with him.
When two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus; and wanting to lay up a favour with the Jews, Felix left Paul in chains.

acts_25.t: So Festus, having taken up his province, went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea three days later,
and the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews laid information before him against Paul. They kept pressing him,
asking as a favour against Paul that he'd have him brought to Jerusalem — while they set an ambush to do away with him along the road.
Festus answered that Paul was being kept at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to leave shortly.
"So," he says, "let those among you who have standing come down with me; and if there's anything out of place in the man, let them accuse him."
After spending not more than eight or ten days among them, he went down to Caesarea; and the next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered Paul brought in.
When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood round him, bringing many serious charges against him which they couldn't prove,
while Paul made his defence: "I've committed no offence against the law of the Jews, or against the temple, or against Caesar."
But Festus, wanting to lay up a favour with the Jews, answered Paul, "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there before me on these charges?"
Paul said, "I'm standing before Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged. I've done the Jews no wrong, as you know perfectly well yourself.

If I'm in the wrong and have done anything deserving death, I don't ask to be spared dying. But if there's nothing in what these men accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them as a favour. I appeal to Caesar."
Then Festus conferred with his council and answered, "You've appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you'll go."
Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and paid their respects to Festus.
Since they were staying there several days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king: "There's a man here left behind as a prisoner by Felix,
about whom, when I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid information, asking for a sentence against him.
I answered them that it isn't the Roman custom to hand over any person as a favour before the accused has met his accusers face to face and been given a chance to defend himself against the charge.
So when they'd come here with me, I made no delay: the next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man brought in.
But when his accusers stood up they brought no charge of the sort of wickedness I'd been expecting.
They had certain disputes with him about their own religion, and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul kept insisting was alive.
I was at a loss how to look into such matters, so I asked whether he'd be willing to go to Jerusalem and be judged there about them.
But when Paul appealed to be kept for His Majesty's decision, I ordered him kept until I could send him up to Caesar."
Agrippa said to Festus, "I'd like to hear the man myself." "Tomorrow," he says, "you'll hear him."
So the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the audience hall, along with the tribunes and the leading men of the city; and at Festus's order Paul was brought in.

And Festus says, "King Agrippa, and all you men here with us: you see this man. The whole crowd of the Jews petitioned me about him, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.
But I found for myself that he'd done nothing deserving death; and when he appealed to His Majesty, I decided to send him.

I have nothing definite to write about him to my lord, so I've brought him out in front of all of you — and especially in front of you, King Agrippa — so that after the examination I'll have something to write.
For it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner on without indicating the charges against him."

acts_26.t: Agrippa said to Paul, "You may speak for yourself." Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defence:
"Concerning everything I'm accused of by Jews, King Agrippa, I count myself fortunate that it's before you I'm to make my defence today,
especially since you're an expert in all the customs and disputed questions among Jews. So I ask you to hear me patiently.
My way of life from my youth — lived from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem — is known to all the Jews.
They've known me from the first, and they could testify if they were willing, that I lived by the strictest party of our religion — as a Pharisee.
And now I stand on trial for the hope of the promise God made to our fathers —
the promise our twelve tribes hope to reach as they serve God earnestly night and day. It's for this hope, King, that I'm accused by the Jews.
Why is it judged unbelievable among you people that God raises the dead?
Now I myself was convinced I had to do many things against the name of Jesus the Nazorean,
and that's what I did in Jerusalem. I shut many of the holy ones up in prisons, on authority I'd received from the chief priests; and when they were being put to death, I cast my vote.
In synagogue after synagogue I punished them again and again, trying to force them to blaspheme; and in a raging fury against them I chased them even to cities outside.
On that business I was travelling to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests,
when at midday along the road I saw, King, a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, blazing around me and those travelling with me.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.'
I said, 'Who are you, Lord?' And the Lord said, 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But get up and stand on your feet. This is why I appeared to you: to appoint you as a servant and a witness, both of what you have seen of me and of what I will show you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you
to open their eyes, so they may turn from darkness to light and from the authority of Satan to God, and so receive release from sins and a share among those who have been made holy by trust in me.'
So, King Agrippa, I did not disobey the heavenly vision.

I announced instead — first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout the whole country of Judea, and to the Gentiles — that they should change their minds and turn to God, doing works worthy of that change of mind.
That's why the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me with their own hands.
But I've had help from God to this very day, and so I stand here testifying to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen —
whether the Christ is subject to suffering, and whether, first from the resurrection of the dead, he would proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles."
As he was making this defence, Festus says in a loud voice, "You're out of your mind, Paul! All that learning is turning you to madness."
But Paul says, "I'm not out of my mind, most excellent Festus. I'm speaking words of truth and sober sense.
The king knows about these things, and I speak to him freely. I don't believe any of this has escaped him — none of it — because it wasn't done in a corner.
Do you trust the prophets, King Agrippa? I know you do."
Agrippa said to Paul, "In a short time you're persuading me to become a Christian?"
Paul said, "I'd pray to God that whether in a little or in much, not only you but all who are listening to me today might become such as I am — except for these chains."
Then the king stood up, and the governor, and Bernice, and those sitting with them;
and as they withdrew they said to one another, "This man is doing nothing that deserves death or chains."
And Agrippa said to Festus, "This man could have been let go, if he hadn't appealed to Caesar."

acts_27.t: When it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan Cohort.
We boarded a ship of Adramyttium that was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, and put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we put in at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul humanely and let him go to his friends and be looked after.
Putting out from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us,
and after sailing across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia we came down to Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy, and put us aboard her.
For a good many days we made slow headway and barely got off Cnidus; and since the wind wouldn't let us get on, we sailed under the lee of Crete, off Salmone,
and coasting along it with difficulty we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.
A good deal of time had been lost, and sailing was already dangerous because the Fast had gone by; so Paul began to warn them,
"Men," he said, "I can see this voyage is going to end in violence and heavy loss — not only of the cargo and the ship but of our lives as well."
But the centurion was persuaded more by the helmsman and the ship's owner than by what Paul said.

And since the harbour was unsuitable for wintering, the majority decided on a plan to put out from there, in the hope of somehow reaching Phoenix — a harbour of Crete facing southwest and northwest — and wintering there.
When a south wind came up gently, they thought they'd got what they wanted; they weighed anchor and began coasting along Crete, close in.
But before long a hurricane-force wind, the one they call the Northeaster, came beating down off the island.
The ship was caught and couldn't face into the wind, so we gave way and were driven along.
Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to get the ship's boat under control.
They hoisted it aboard and then used cables to undergird the ship, frapping the hull; and afraid of running onto the Syrtis, they lowered the sea anchor, and so they were carried along.
The next day, as we were being violently battered by the storm, they began throwing cargo overboard;
and on the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands.
For many days neither sun nor stars appeared, and no small storm lay on us, until in the end all hope of our being saved was being stripped away.
They'd gone a long time without food. Then Paul stood up among them and said, "Men, you should have listened to me and not put out from Crete; you'd have spared yourselves this violence and loss.
But now I urge you to keep your courage up. There'll be no loss of life among you — only of the ship.
For last night there stood beside me an angel of the God whose I am and whom I serve,
and he said, 'Don't be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar — and look, God has granted you all those sailing with you.'
So keep up your courage, men, because I trust God that it will be exactly as I was told.
But we must run aground on some island."
When the fourteenth night came and we were being driven across the Adriatic, about midnight the sailors began to suspect that land was coming up on them.
They took a sounding and found twenty fathoms; a little further on they sounded again and found fifteen.
Afraid we might run onto rocky ground somewhere, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come.
The sailors were trying to get away from the ship, and they lowered the ship's boat into the sea on the pretext of laying out anchors from the bow.
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, "Unless these men stay in the ship, you can't be saved."
So the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship's boat and let it fall away.
Just before daybreak Paul urged them all to take some food: "Today is the fourteenth day you've gone on waiting, without food, taking nothing.
So I urge you to take some food; this is for your survival. Not a hair will be lost from the head of any of you."
When he'd said this he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it, and began to eat.
They all took heart and took some food themselves.
In all there were two hundred and seventy-six of us on the ship.
When they'd eaten enough they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When day came they didn't recognise the land, but they made out a bay with a beach, and they planned to drive the ship onto it if they could.
They cut away the anchors and left them in the sea; at the same time they loosed the lashings of the steering-oars, hoisted the foresail to the wind, and made for the beach.
But they struck a place where two seas met and ran the ship aground. The bow stuck fast and stayed immovable, while the stern began to break up under the force of the waves.
The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, so none of them would swim away and escape.
But the centurion wanted to bring Paul through safely, so he stopped them carrying out the plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land,
and the rest to follow, some on planks and some on pieces of the ship. And so it came about that they all came safely through to land.

acts_28.t: Once we were safely through, we found out that the island was called Malta.
The local people showed us no ordinary kindness: they lit a fire and welcomed us all, because rain had set in and it was cold.
Paul had gathered a bundle of brushwood and was putting it on the fire when a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand.
When the local people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, "This man is certainly a murderer: he came safely through the sea, but Justice hasn't let him live."
But he shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.
They were expecting him to swell up or suddenly drop dead; but after waiting a long time and seeing nothing out of the ordinary happen to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
In the neighbourhood of that place were lands belonging to the leading man of the island, named Publius, who took us in and entertained us hospitably for three days.
It happened that Publius's father was in bed, ill with recurring fever and dysentery; Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him and healed him.
After that happened, the rest of the people on the island who had illnesses came and were cured.
They honoured us with many honours, and when we were putting out to sea they put on board what we needed.
After three months we put to sea in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island, with the Twin Brothers as its figurehead.
We put in at Syracuse and stayed three days,
and from there we cast off and arrived at Rhegium. After one day a south wind came up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli,
where we found brothers and sisters and were urged to stay with them seven days. And so we came to Rome.
The brothers and sisters there heard about us and came out to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns; when Paul saw them he thanked God and took courage.
When we came into Rome, the centurion handed the prisoners over to the commander of the camp; but Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who was guarding him.

Three days later he called together the leading men of the Jews; and when they'd come together he said to them, "Brothers, I'd done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, and yet I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
They examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no ground for a death sentence in my case.
But when the Jews objected, I was forced to appeal to Caesar — not that I had any charge to bring against my own nation.
That's why I asked to see you and talk with you; because it is for the hope of Israel that I have this chain around me."
They said to him, "We've had no letters about you from Judea, and none of the brothers who have arrived has reported or said anything bad about you.
But we think it right to hear from you what you think — because as for this sect, we know it's spoken against everywhere."

They arranged a day with him and came to him at his lodging in even greater numbers; and he laid it out for them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to persuade them about Jesus, from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening.
Some were persuaded by what was said; others did not believe.
They disagreed among themselves and began to leave, after Paul had said one thing: "The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers,
saying: 'Go to this people and say: You will hear and hear, and never understand; you will look and look, and never see.

For this people's heart has grown thick; with their ears they have heard heavily, and their eyes they have shut — so that they might not see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I will heal them.'
So let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they too will listen."
[And when he had said this, the Jews went away, having a great dispute among themselves.]
He stayed two whole years in his own rented lodging, and welcomed everyone who came in to him,
proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness — and nothing to stop him.

colossians_1.t: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by God's will, and Timothy our brother,
to God's people in Colossae — the faithful brothers and sisters in Christ: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
because we heard about your trust in Christ Jesus and about the love you have for all God's people,
because of the hope that's stored up for you in the heavens — the hope you heard about beforehand in the word of the truth of the good news,
the good news that has come to you. Just as it's bearing fruit and growing in all the world, so it is among you too, from the day you heard and came to know God's grace in truth.
That's what you learned from Epaphras, our beloved fellow slave, who is a faithful servant of Christ on your behalf —
and he's the one who told us about your love in the Spirit.
That's why we too, from the day we heard, haven't stopped praying for you and asking that you be filled with the knowledge of his will, in all wisdom and spiritual understanding,
so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing him, bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God,
strengthened with all power, in keeping with the might of his glory, for all endurance and patience — with joy
giving thanks to the Father, who made you fit to share in what has been allotted to God's people in the light —
He rescued us from the authority of darkness and brought us over into the kingdom of the Son he loves,
In him we have release — the forgiveness of sins.
He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation;

because in him all things were created — the ones in the heavens and the ones on the earth, the visible and the invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All of them have been created through him and for him.
And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
And he is the head of the body — the community. He is the beginning, the firstborn from among the dead, so that he himself would come to be first in all things.
because God was pleased to have all the fullness dwell in him,
and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross — through him, whether the things on the earth or the things in the heavens.
And you — you were once estranged and hostile in mind, engaged in evil deeds —
But now he's reconciled you in the body of his flesh, through death, to present you holy, unblemished and free of accusation before him.

— if in fact you continue in the faith, founded and firm, not shifting from the hope of the good news you heard, which was proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and which I, Paul, became a servant of.
Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I fill up in turn what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ, for the sake of his body, which is the community —
which I became a servant of, according to the stewardship God gave me for you — to fulfil the word of God,
the mystery that was hidden from the ages and the generations, but has now been made visible to his people.
To them God chose to make known what the riches of the glory of this mystery among the nations is — and that is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
He's the one we announce, warning everyone and teaching everyone in all wisdom, so that we can present everyone complete in Christ Jesus.
That's what I work hard for, struggling according to his working, which works powerfully in me.

colossians_2.t: I want you to know what a struggle I'm having for you, and for those in Laodicea, and for everyone who hasn't seen my face in the flesh —
so that their hearts may be encouraged, knit together in love and brought to all the riches of full assurance of understanding — to the knowledge of God's mystery, of the Father and of Christ —
In him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden away.
I'm telling you this so that no one deceives you with a persuasive argument.
For even if I'm absent in the flesh, I'm with you in spirit, and I'm glad to see your good order and the solid front of your trust in Christ.
So then — just as you received Christ Jesus the Lord — walk in him,
rooted in him and being built up in him, made firm in the faith just as you were taught, overflowing in it with thanksgiving.
Watch out that no one carries you off through philosophy and empty deceit — following human tradition, following the elemental spirits of the world and not Christ.
because in him all the fullness of deity lives bodily,
and you've been filled in him — and he is the head of every ruler and authority.
In him you were also circumcised — with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ —
buried with him in baptism, and raised with him in it too, through trust in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
And you — you were dead in your trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh — he made alive together with him, and he forgave us all our trespasses.
He wiped out the handwritten note of debt that stood against us with its decrees — the one that was set against us — and he's taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
Having stripped the rulers and the authorities, he made a public example of them, leading them in a triumphal procession in him.
So don't let anyone judge you over food and drink, or over a festival or a new moon or sabbaths.
These are a shadow of what's coming, but the body belongs to Christ.
Don't let anyone disqualify you — someone who delights in self-abasement and the worship of angels, taking his stand on things he has seen, puffed up for no reason by the mind of his flesh,
and not holding on to the head — and it's from the head that the whole body, supplied and held together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that comes from God.
If you died with Christ to the elemental spirits of the world, why do you go on submitting to decrees, as if you were still living in the world:
'Don't handle! Don't taste! Don't touch!'
— and all of it is meant to perish with use — following human commands and teachings.
These things have a reputation for wisdom, with their self-made religion and self-abasement and severity to the body — but they're of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

colossians_3.t: So if you were raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at God's right hand.
Set your minds on the things above, not on the things on the earth.
For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
When Christ, who is your life, is made visible, then you'll be made visible with him too, in glory.
So put to death whatever belongs to the earth in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed — which is idolatry.
That's why God's anger is coming on the sons of disobedience.
You walked in those ways yourselves once, back when you were living in them.
But now you have to put all of it away too: anger, rage, malice, slander, filthy talk out of your mouth.
Don't lie to one another, since you've stripped off the old person with its practices
and put on the new, which is being renewed toward knowledge, after the image of the one who created it.
Here there's no Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free — Christ is all, and in all.
So, as God's chosen ones, holy and loved, put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience —
putting up with one another and forgiving each other if anyone has a complaint against someone. Just as the Lord forgave you, you forgive too.
And over all of these, put on love, which is the bond of completeness.
And let the peace of Christ be the umpire in your hearts — that's what you were called to, in one body. And be thankful.
Let the word of Christ live among you richly, in all wisdom, as you teach and warn one another with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God.
And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
Wives, submit to your own husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
Husbands, love your wives, and don't be harsh with them.
Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing in the Lord.
Fathers, don't provoke your children, so they don't lose heart.
Slaves, obey your masters according to the flesh in everything — not with eye-service, the way people-pleasers do, but with singleness of heart, fearing the Lord.
Whatever you do, work at it from the soul, as for the Lord and not for people,
knowing that from the Lord you'll receive the repayment of the inheritance. It is the Lord Christ you serve as slaves.
For whoever does wrong will be paid back for the wrong he did — and there's no favouritism.

colossians_4.t: Masters, give your slaves what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.
Keep at prayer, staying alert in it with thanksgiving,
and praying for us at the same time, that God would open a door for the word, so we can speak the mystery of Christ — which is why I'm in chains —
so that I can make it visible, as I must speak it.
Walk in wisdom toward those outside, making the most of the opportunity.
Let the way you talk always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so you know how you ought to answer each person.
Tychicus will tell you everything about how I'm doing — he's the beloved brother, faithful servant and fellow slave in the Lord.
I'm sending him to you for exactly this purpose — so you'll know how we are and he can encourage your hearts —
along with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who's one of you. They'll tell you everything that's going on here.
Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and so does Mark, Barnabas's cousin — you got instructions about him: if he comes to you, welcome him.
and so does Jesus, the one they call Justus. These are the only ones from the circumcision among my co-workers for God's kingdom, and they've been a comfort to me.
Epaphras greets you — he's one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus. He's always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand complete and fully assured in everything God wills.
I can testify about him that he's worked hard for you, and for those in Laodicea and those in Hierapolis.
Luke, the beloved doctor, greets you, and so does Demas.
Greet the brothers and sisters in Laodicea, and Nympha and the community that meets in her house.
And once this letter has been read among you, see that it gets read in the assembly of the Laodiceans too, and that you read the one from Laodicea.
And tell Archippus, 'Keep an eye on the service you received in the Lord — see that you fulfil it.'
This greeting is in my own hand — Paul's. Remember my chains. Grace be with you. Amen. [To the Colossians, written from Rome by Tychicus and Onesimus.]

ephesians_1.t: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to God's people who are [in Ephesus] and are faithful in Christ Jesus:
grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, in Christ —
just as he chose us in him before the world was founded, for us to be holy and without blemish before him — in love
having marked us out beforehand for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will,
to the praise of the glory of his grace, which he lavished on us in the Beloved.
In him we have the redemption through his blood, the release from our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace
that he poured out on us. In all wisdom and understanding
he made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he set out in him
for the administration of the fullness of the times: to gather up all things in Christ — the things in the heavens and the things on the earth — in him.
In him we were also given a share, marked out beforehand according to the purpose of the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will,
so that we, who had already put our hope in Christ, might be to the praise of his glory —
and in him you too, when you heard the word of truth — the gospel of your salvation — and when you trusted, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,
who is the down payment on our inheritance, until the redemption of the possession, to the praise of his glory.
That's why I too, ever since I heard about the trust among you in the Lord Jesus and about your love toward all God's people,
haven't stopped giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
asking that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, would give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him,
the eyes of your heart having been enlightened, so that you may know what the hope of his calling is, what the riches of the glory of his inheritance among God's people are,
and what the surpassing greatness of his power is toward us who trust — according to the working of the might of his strength,
which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,
far above every ruler and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named — not only in this age but in the one to come as well.
And he put all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the community,
which is his body — the fullness of the one who fills all things in every way.

ephesians_2.t: And you, dead as you were in your trespasses and sins —
the ones you once walked in, following the age of this world, following the ruler of the authority of the air — the spirit now at work in the sons of disobedience;
and we were all once among them too, living in the desires of our flesh, doing what the flesh and the thoughts wanted; and by nature we were children of wrath, like everyone else.
But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us,
made us alive together with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses — by grace you have been saved —
and raised us up together with him, and seated us together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,
so that in the ages to come he could display the surpassing riches of his grace, in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
For by grace you have been saved, through trust; and this isn't from you — it's God's gift,
not from works, so that no one can boast.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared in advance so that we would walk in them.
So then, remember that you were once the nations in the flesh — called 'the uncircumcision' by what is called 'the circumcision', done in the flesh by human hands —
that at that time you were without Christ, shut out from the citizenship of Israel and strangers to the covenants of the promise, with no hope and without God in the world.
But now, in Christ Jesus, you who were once far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
For he himself is our peace — the one who made both into one and broke down the dividing wall of the fence, the hostility, in his flesh,
abolishing in his flesh the law of commandments in decrees, so that he could create the two in himself into one new humanity, making peace,
and reconcile both of them to God in one body through the cross, killing the hostility by it.
And he came and announced peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near;
because through him we both have our access to the Father in one Spirit.
So then, you're no longer strangers and resident foreigners; you're fellow citizens with God's people and members of God's household,
built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone —
in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord;
and in him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.

ephesians_3.t: That's why I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you, the nations —
assuming you've heard about the administration of God's grace given to me for you,
that the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I wrote briefly before.
By reading it you can see for yourselves what insight I have into the mystery of Christ,
which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit:
that the nations are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers together in the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel —
and I became one who serves it, according to the gift of God's grace given to me according to the working of his power.
To me — less than the least of all God's people — this grace was given: to announce to the nations the untraceable riches of Christ,
and to bring to light for everyone what the administration of the mystery is — the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things;
so that now, through the community, the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the rulers and the authorities in the heavenly places,
according to the purpose of the ages, which he carried out in Christ Jesus our Lord,
in whom we have boldness and confident access through faith in him.
So I ask you not to lose heart over my afflictions on your behalf — they're your glory.
This is why I bend my knees to the Father,
from whom every family in the heavens and on earth is named,
that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
so that Christ may live in your hearts through trust — you having been rooted and grounded in love —
so that you may have full strength to grasp, together with all God's people, what the breadth and length and height and depth are,
and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge — so that you may be filled up to all the fullness of God.
Now to the one who is able to do beyond all things — far more than we ask or think — according to the power at work in us,
to him be the glory in the community and in Christ Jesus, to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

ephesians_4.t: So I urge you — I, the prisoner in the Lord — to walk in a way worthy of the calling you were called with,
with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
making every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
One body and one Spirit — just as you were called in one hope of your calling —
one Lord, one trust, one baptism,
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all of you.
But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ's gift.
That's why it says: 'Having gone up on high, he took captivity captive; he gave gifts to people.'
Now 'he went up' — what does that mean, except that he also went down into the lower regions, the earth?
The one who went down is himself also the one who went up far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.
And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as shepherds and teachers,
for the equipping of God's people for the work of service, for the building up of the body of Christ,
until we all arrive at the unity of the trust and of the knowledge of the Son of God, at a mature person, at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ;
so that we're no longer infants, tossed by waves and carried about by every wind of teaching, by people's trickery, by craftiness in deceitful scheming,
but speaking the truth in love, we're to grow up in every way into him who is the head — Christ —

from whom the whole body, fitted and held together by every supporting ligament, produces its own growth — according to the working of each single part in its measure — for its own building up in love.
So this is what I say, and testify in the Lord: you're no longer to walk as the nations walk, in the futility of their mind,
darkened in their understanding, shut out from the life of God because of the ignorance that's in them, because of the hardness of their heart;
who, having lost all feeling, gave themselves over to indecency, to the practice of every kind of impurity, with greed.
But that's not how you learned Christ —
assuming you heard him and were taught in him, as truth is in Jesus:
that you're to put off, as regards your former way of life, the old person who's being ruined by deceitful desires,
and to be renewed in the spirit of your mind,
and to put on the new person, created according to God in rightness and holiness of the truth.
So, having put off falsehood, each of you speak truth with his neighbour, because we are members of one another.
Be angry, and don't sin; don't let the sun go down on your provocation,
and don't give the devil a place.
Whoever steals must steal no longer; instead let him work hard with his own hands at what is good, so that he has something to share with the one in need.
No rotten word is to come out of your mouth — only what is good for building up where there's need, so that it gives grace to those who hear.
And don't grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness and rage and anger and shouting and slander be taken away from you, along with all malice.
Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you.

ephesians_5.t: So become imitators of God, as beloved children,
and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us — an offering and sacrifice to God, a fragrance of sweet smell.
But sexual immorality and any impurity or greed mustn't even be named among you, as is fitting for God's people;
and no obscenity or foolish talk or coarse joking — they're out of place. Thanksgiving instead.
Know this for certain: no sexually immoral or impure or greedy person — that is, an idolater — has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.
Don't let anyone deceive you with empty words; it's because of these things that the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.
So don't become partners with them.
For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light —
for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness and rightness and truth —
testing what is well-pleasing to the Lord.
And don't take part in the fruitless works of the darkness; expose them instead.
For it's shameful even to speak of the things they do in secret.
But everything exposed by the light is made visible;
for everything that's made visible is light. That's why it says: 'Wake up, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
So watch carefully how you walk — not as unwise but as wise,
buying up the opportunity, because the days are evil.
So don't be foolish; understand what the Lord's will is.
And don't get drunk on wine — that's dissipation — but be filled in the Spirit,
speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making music in your heart to the Lord,
always giving thanks for everything to the God and Father, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
submitting to one another in the fear of Christ —
— wives to your own husbands, as to the Lord;
because the husband is head of the wife, as Christ also is head of the community — he himself being the saviour of the body.
But as the community submits to Christ, so also wives to their husbands, in everything.
Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the community and gave himself up for her,
so that he might make her holy, cleansing her by the washing of water with a word,
so that he might present the community to himself in splendour, with no stain or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but holy and without blemish.
In the same way husbands ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. The one who loves his own wife loves himself;
for no one ever hated his own flesh — he feeds it and cares for it, just as Christ also does the community,
because we are members of his body.
'For this reason a person will leave father and mother and will be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.'
This mystery is great — but I'm speaking about Christ and about the community.
In any case, each one of you is to love his own wife as himself; and the wife is to respect her husband.

ephesians_6.t: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, because this is right.
'Honour your father and mother' — which is the first commandment with a promise —
'so that it may go well for you and you may live long on the earth.'
And fathers, don't provoke your children to anger; bring them up instead in the training and admonition of the Lord.
Slaves, obey your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of heart, as to Christ —
not with eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the soul,
serving with goodwill, as to the Lord and not to people,
knowing that whatever good each one does, he'll receive it back from the Lord — whether slave or free.
And masters, do the same toward them; give up the threatening — knowing that both their Lord and yours is in the heavens, and there's no partiality with him.
Finally, be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his strength.
Put on the full armour of God, so that you can stand against the schemes of the devil;

because our struggle isn't against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
So take up the full armour of God, so that you can withstand on the evil day, and having done everything, stand.
So stand — with your waist belted with truth, and the breastplate of rightness on,
and your feet strapped with the readiness of the gospel of peace;
in all circumstances taking up the shield of trust, with which you'll be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one;
and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God;
praying at every moment in the Spirit, with every kind of prayer and petition; and to that end staying alert with all perseverance and petition for all God's people,
and for me — that a word may be given me when I open my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the gospel,
which I'm an ambassador for, in chains — that in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.
So that you too may know how I am and what I'm doing, Tychicus — the beloved brother and faithful one who serves in the Lord — will make everything known to you.
I sent him to you for this very purpose: so that you may know how things are with us, and so that he may encourage your hearts.
Peace to the brothers and sisters, and love with trust, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruptibility. Amen.

galatians_1.t: Paul, an apostle — not from human beings, and not through a human being either, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead —
and all the brothers and sisters with me, to the communities of Galatia:
grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,
who gave himself for our sins to pull us out of the present evil age, in keeping with the will of our God and Father,
to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
I'm astonished you're deserting so quickly the one who called you by the grace of Christ — for a different gospel —
not that there is another gospel — there are just some people unsettling you, who want to twist the gospel of Christ.
But even if we — or a messenger from heaven — should announce to you a gospel contrary to the one we announced to you: let that person be under a curse.
As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone announces to you a gospel contrary to what you received: let that person be under a curse.
So — am I now trying to win people over, or God? Or am I looking to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I wouldn't be Christ's servant.
I want you to know, brothers and sisters: the gospel I announced isn't something human;
for I didn't get it from any human being, and I wasn't taught it; it came through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
You've heard what my life used to be like in Judaism — how violently I persecuted God's community, how I tried to destroy it,
and I was outstripping many of my own age in my people in Judaism — far more zealous for the traditions handed down from my ancestors.
But when the one who set me apart from my mother's womb, and called me through his grace, was pleased
to reveal his Son in me, so that I might announce him among the nations — I didn't immediately consult flesh and blood,
and I didn't go up to Jerusalem to the ones who were apostles before me. I went off to Arabia instead, and came back again to Damascus.
Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days.
I didn't see any of the other apostles — only James, the Lord's brother.
What I'm writing to you — look, before God — I'm not lying.
Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia,
and I was still unknown by sight to the communities of Judea that are in Christ.
All they kept hearing was, 'the one who used to persecute us is now announcing the faith he once tried to destroy' —
and they were glorifying God because of me.

galatians_2.t: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along too.
I went up because of a revelation, and I put before them the gospel I announce among the nations — privately, though, to the people of repute — in case I was running, or had run, for nothing.
But not even Titus, who was with me, and a Greek — not even he was compelled to be circumcised.
The issue was the false brothers who'd been smuggled in — people who slipped in to spy out the freedom we have in Christ Jesus, so they could enslave us.
We didn't yield to them in submission — not for one hour — so that the truth of the gospel might remain with you.
As for the people of repute — whatever they once were makes no difference to me; God doesn't go by a person's face — those of repute added nothing to me.
Quite the opposite: they saw that I'd been entrusted with the gospel for the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been for the circumcised —
for the one who worked in Peter for a mission to the circumcised worked in me too, for the nations —

and when they recognised the grace given to me, James and Cephas and John — the ones reputed to be pillars — gave me and Barnabas the right hand of partnership: we to the nations, they to the circumcised.
Only this: that we should keep remembering the poor — the very thing I'd been eager to do.
But when Cephas came to Antioch, I stood up to him face to face, because he stood condemned.
Before certain people came from James, he used to eat with the nations. But once they came, he started drawing back and keeping himself separate, because he was afraid of the circumcision group.
And the rest of the Jews joined him in the pretence — so that even Barnabas got carried off with them by their play-acting.

But when I saw they weren't walking straight toward the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas in front of everyone: 'If you're a Jew and you live like the nations and not like a Jew, how can you compel the nations to live like Jews?'
We are Jews by birth, and not sinners from among the nations,

and yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law, but only through faith in Jesus Christ. So we too believed in Christ Jesus — so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law; because by works of the law no flesh will be justified.
But if, in seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves turned out to be sinners — does that make Christ one who serves sin? Absolutely not.
For if I build up again the very things I tore down, I'm showing myself to be a lawbreaker.
For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ.
It's no longer I who live — Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.
I don't set aside God's grace. Because if rightness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.

galatians_3.t: You mindless Galatians! Who put the evil eye on you — you, who had Jesus Christ posted up in public before your very eyes, crucified?
Just one thing I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with trust?
Are you that mindless? You began with the Spirit — are you now being brought to completion by the flesh?
Did you go through so much for nothing — if it really was for nothing?
So then — the one who supplies you with the Spirit and works powers among you: does he do it by works of the law, or by hearing with trust?
It's like Abraham: he trusted God, and it was credited to him as rightness.
So understand this: it's those who live out of trust who are Abraham's sons.
And the Scripture saw it coming — that God would justify the nations by trust — and announced the gospel to Abraham in advance: 'All the nations will be blessed in you.'
So then, those who live out of trust are blessed along with Abraham, who trusted.
For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse. As it is written: 'Cursed is everyone who does not hold to everything written in the book of the law, to do it.'
And it's clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because 'the righteous one will live by trust.'
But the law is not out of trust; rather, 'the person who does these things will live by them.'
Christ bought us out from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — as it is written: 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree' —
so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations, so that through trust we might receive the promise of the Spirit.
Brothers and sisters, let me put it in human terms. Even with a human will: once it's ratified, no one sets it aside or adds provisions to it.
Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It doesn't say 'and to seeds', as of many, but as of one: 'and to your seed' — who is the Christ.
What I mean is this: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not annul a covenant God had already ratified [toward Christ], so as to cancel the promise.
For if the inheritance comes by law, it no longer comes by promise; but God granted it to Abraham through a promise.
So why the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise was made — put in place through messengers, by the hand of an intermediary.
Now an intermediary is not for one party; but God is one.
So is the law against the promises of God? Absolutely not. For if a law had been given that could make alive, then rightness really would have come from the law.
But the Scripture shut everything up under sin, so that the promise, by faith in Jesus Christ, might be given to those who trust.
Before this trust came, we were held in custody under the law, shut up until the coming trust should be revealed.
So the law became our guardian until Christ, so that we might be justified by trust.
But now that this trust has come, we're no longer under a guardian.
For you are all sons of God, through trust, in Christ Jesus.
For all of you who were baptised into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.
There is no Jew or Greek, there is no slave or free, there is no 'male and female' — for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
And if you belong to Christ, then you're Abraham's seed — heirs according to promise.

galatians_4.t: Here's what I mean: as long as the heir is a child, he's no different from a slave — even though he owns everything.
He's under guardians and stewards until the date the father set.
It's the same with us: when we were children, we were enslaved under the elemental things of the world.
But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, born of a woman, born under law,
to buy out those under law, so that we might receive adoption as heirs.
And because you are sons, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying 'Abba! Father!'
So you're no longer a slave but a son — and if a son, then an heir too, through God.
But back then, not knowing God, you were slaves to beings that by nature are not gods.
But now that you've come to know God — or rather, to be known by God — how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elemental things? Do you want to be enslaved to them all over again?
You're observing days and months and seasons and years.
I'm afraid for you — afraid I may have laboured over you for nothing.
Become like me, because I became like you. Brothers and sisters, I'm begging you. You did me no wrong.
You know it was because of a weakness of the flesh that I announced the gospel to you the first time,
and though my condition in the flesh was a trial to you, you didn't despise me or spit me out — you welcomed me as a messenger of God, as Christ Jesus.
So where has it gone, that sense of blessing you had? I can testify about you: if it had been possible, you'd have torn out your own eyes and given them to me.
So have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?
They're courting you — but not honourably. What they want is to shut you out, so that you'll court them.
It's good to be courted in a good cause — always, and not only when I'm there with you.
My children — the ones I'm in labour with all over again, until Christ is formed in you —
I wish I could be with you right now and change my tone, because I'm at a loss about you.
Tell me, you who want to be under law — don't you hear the law?
For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman.
But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through the promise.
These things are being spoken as an allegory: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery — that is Hagar.
Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.
But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.

For it is written: 'Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break out and shout, you who are not in labour — because the children of the deserted woman are many, more than of the one who has a husband.'
And you, brothers and sisters, are children of promise, like Isaac.
But just as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so it is now too.
But what does the Scripture say? 'Drive out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman will certainly not inherit along with the son of the free woman.'
So then, brothers and sisters — we're not children of a slave woman but of the free woman.

galatians_5.t: For freedom Christ set us free. So stand firm — and don't let yourselves be loaded up again with a yoke of slavery.
